audits.title: Animal Welfare on holdings with laying hens and during long distance transport

recommendations.text: Training on the specific technical provisions of Directive 1999/74/EC is provided to inspectors through the available central and regional frameworks.
Cage systems brought into service after 1.1.2003 meet the requirements of Article 8 of Arrêté 01.02.2002 and of Article 6 of Directive 1999/74/EC.

Blinkers which penetrate the nasal septum are not permitted (Chapter C(12) of the Annex to Arrêté 01.02.2002 and point 8 of the Annex to Directive 1999/74/EC). 17 In their response to the draft report, the French CA noted that as the keeping of laying hens is not evenly spread throughout the territory, the shortcomings noted with respect to the flow of information must be interpreted with care. 11
When deficiencies are detected, adequate timely corrective measures and follow- up actions are taken and sanctioning proceedings are initiated, as necessary.
Inspections are taking place throughout the national territory and the results are reported as required by Articles 1 and 2 of Decision 2000/50/EC. Regarding control of route plans:

Adequate controls on route plans are performed to ensure compliance with Article 5(A)(2) of Directive 91/628/EEC, and effective measures are taken to ensure their return. 9. ADDENDUM TO MISSION REPORT DG(SANCO)/7231/2004 In their initial reaction to the recommendations, the central competent authority indicated that: In relation to recommendation (1) that exchange of information is already taking place, both formally and informally and is encouraged. Training will be organised at regional and inter-regional levels, in particular to standardise the practises used by field officials on certain complex technical points. In relation to recommendation (2), that they agreed with the DDSV concerned, who considered that it would not be appropriate to block the installation of cages where works were in progress on 1.1.2003. The regulations on the protection of laying hens are currently applied and monitored. In relation to recommendation (3), that the application of blinkers is not authorised in national and Community regulations. However, this method was only used on veterinary prescriptions after the failure of other attempts intended to prevent cannibalism. In relation to recommendation (4), a note reminding DDSVs to react to all deficiencies detected was issued on 18.3.04 (i.e. shortly before the mission). In relation to recommendation (5), that a computerised system will be set up to facilitate the collection of inspection results. In relation to recommendation (6), the DDSV will be reminded that the itinerary and duration of the journey must be verified before departure of the consignment. 12

To continue developing the Brucella melitensis eradication programme with a view to achieving official freedom from Brucellosis throughout France. To this end the competent authorities should ensure that · all sheep and goat holdings are registered and holding registers are kept; · all sheep and goat herds and all eligible animals are tested within the time intervals foreseen in the Brucella melitensis eradication programme; · the procedures for granting and maintaining the officially free status are enforced; · the compulsory notification of abortions in sheep and goats is enforced by co- operation with the Groupements de Défense Sanitaire; · international livestock transporters keep a register for each vehicle as foreseen by Article 8 of Council Directive 91/68/EEC; · a sufficient number of approved cleansing and disinfection facilities are available to approved transporters in order to meet the requirements of Article 8 of Council Directive 91/68/EEC.

To ensure that ante- and post mortem inspections are carried out as laid down by Article 9 of Council Directive 64/433/EEC and that the veterinary inspections in respect of the health state of the animals delivering milk meet the requirements of Article 13 of Council Directive 92/46/EC.

To strengthen the supervision of the Vétérinaires Sanitaires which play an important role within the Brucella melitensis eradication programme. The French authorities should submit an action plan, detailing the actions taken, and planned, to address the above recommendations within one month of receiving the final translated report. 19 10. ADDENDUM In their response of 23 February 2005 to the draft report, the French Authorities provided some clarification concerning the findings and also commented on the conclusions and recommendations of the report. Where appropriate the text was amended. In respect of the implementation of Article 9 of Council Directive 64/433/EEC regarding ante- and post- mortem inspection, the French CCA has already undertaken to adopt measures to comply with the relevant requirements. 20

audits.title: Control of residues and contaminants in live animals and animal products, including controls on veterinary medicinal products

recommendations.text: To ensure without delay that at least the minimum numbers of samples required by Council Directive 96/23/EC are taken.
To extend the scope of testing under the NRCP to include all necessary substance groups.
To ensure that requirements of Commission Decision 98/179/EC in relation to traceability and integrity are respected.
To ensure that requirements of Commission Decision 98/179/EC in relation to the fact that sampling must be unforeseen and unexpected are respected. With regard to follow-up of non-compliant results

To ensure that follow-up actions are executed in a timely fashion in order to guarantee an adequate follow-up and to ensure that follow-up actions are carried out in accordance with the requirements of Council Directive 96/23/EC. With regard to the laboratories
To ensure, without delay, that all residues laboratories are accredited to ISO 17025.
To ensure that all analytical methods used are appropriately validated in each laboratory in accordance with the requirements in relevant Community legislation.
To ensure that analytical equipment used in all laboratories is sufficient to ensure that analytical performance fulfils the requirements of Community legislation. With regard to VMPs

To ensure that VMPs containing active substances not listed in Annexes I, II or III to Council Regulation (EEC) No 2377/90 are not used in food producing animals, and to remove any such products for food producing animals from the market.
To ensure that Commission Decision 2000/68/EC is fully implemented without delay. 16
To ensure, without delay, that the treatment of bees is in accordance with Community legislation.
Take measures to ensure, without delay, that pigeons and horses treated with VMPs not permitted for use in food producing animals are excluded from slaughter.
To reinforce inspection of veterinary practitioners and farmers, to control the proper distribution and use of VMPs.

To ensure that the requirements of Directive 2001/82/EC in relation to batch numbers are transposed and implemented without delay. _________________ 9. ADDENDUM TO MISSION REPORT 7506/2005: In their comments on the draft report received on 19 September 2005, the French Competent Authorities indicated some actions which were planned, or had already taken place in response to several of the recommendations. Not covered by a specific recommendation ­ relates to NRCP planning: The CA indicates that currently no structure exists to know the sales volumes for VMPs with the exception of antibiotics. The CA states that a project of an overview of VMP sales is in progress. Not covered by a specific recommendation ­ relates to storage of samples in the laboratories: The CA has stated that measures will be implemented to harmonise the periods during which positive samples are stored. These storage periods could differ according to the status of the molecule and the legal obligations in terms of risk management. A draft decree concerning epidemiology will specify these periods. Not covered by a specific recommendation ­ relates to monitoring of turnaround times within laboratories: The CA has stated that the requested indicators of turnaround time will be covered by the laboratory information system (LIMS) currently being purchased. Not covered by a specific recommendation ­ relates to availability of validation data within LERVMD: The CA has indicated that LERMVD will improve its documentary follow-up system. Not covered by a specific recommendation ­ relates to availability of routine filed laboratories to meet detection limits quoted in the NRCP for ionophore coccidiostats. The CA has stated that the LOD (limit of detection) for monensin in the official screening method is 50 µg/kg, whereas the LODs for narasin and salinomycin are 200 µg/kg. It will draw this discrepancy to the attention of the approved laboratories and, assisted by the NRL, check their ability to meet this criterion. Not covered by a specific recommendation ­ relates to top-dressing of VMPs: The CA has stated that these are old marketing authorisations for orally administered powders. The national agency for veterinary medicinal products will therefore revise the references on the labels and the instructions for all of these marketing authorisations. 17 Recommendation 1 The CA has stated that the number of samples will be increased for the year 2006. 100% of the samples required by Directive 96/23 for growth promoters and thyrostatic substances on farms and in slaughterhouses will be scheduled in the control plans for 2006. Account should also be taken of the difficulty in sampling urine on farms, particularly in the case of suckling, animals due to the problem of animal containment and the inherent occupational safety risks for the agents taking the samples. The CA has stated that the Directorate-General for International Affairs has decided to incorporate the management of the residue control plans in 2006 into its computer system (SIGAL). Using the SIGAL database, a system to monitor the rate of plan implementation during the year will be established together with schedules to make it easier to follow the sampling carried out by the DDSVs and the observance of their submission and analysis deadlines. This tool will keep us informed on the progress of the control plans and the DGAL will be able to organise follow-up as needed with the DDSVs. Recommendation 2 Regarding the scope of testing and the inclusion of all necessary substance groups, the CA points out that it relies on the National Reference Laboratory and the National Agency for Veterinary Medicinal Products to advise on issues such as method availability, analysis feasibility and the relevance of this research in France, in view of the use made of veterinary medicinal products for these species. In the case of nitroimidazoles these may be tested for in sheep using the LC-MS-MS method, which is already widespread as a confirmatory method and that TLC could be discontinued as a screening method to increase the performance of the control plan. For coccidiostats (B2b), work is under way to develop an LC-MS-MS method to monitor ionophores. This method will be tested in 2006 on study protocols for chicken livers and eggs. The aim of the method development plan is to establish a multi-family method or several methods covering the majority of molecules for 2008. For coccidiostats used in lambs and kids, a method derived from the one which is currently under development for poultry will be finalised in 2007. For coccidiostats, the LERMVD assumed responsibility for additives just a few years ago. The methodological developments (work by the CRL and other NRLs) in this field of activity, which covers various substance families of different chemical makeup, are being followed very closely by the NRL, as are the MRL proposals made by EFSA. Over the next two years, the NRL will able to improve monitoring in this field under its work plan. Considering the substances authorised within the country but which are currently not tested for (e.g. lasalocid and nicarbazin (poultry and eggs), benzimidazoles (pigs), sulphonamides (horses); quinolones (pigs and bovine) and phenylbutazone (milk and pigs), the CA has stated that the same factors (as described above) need to be considered and they are studying the possibility of including these substances in the 2006 NRCP. Specifically the existing methods for benzimidazoles, sulphonamides and quinolones will also be used for the specified species in 2006. The method under development for ionophore coccidiostats will be used as part of the 2006 NRCP. The use of phenylbutazone in muscle is currently being validated and will be widespread by 2006. Its extension to milk will be tested under a study protocol and introduced in 2006. 18 A detection method for avermectins is being developed and will be used for milk under a study protocol in 2006. Regarding the analysis of nitroimidazoles, the NRL proposes reviewing its position (for example, the discontinuation of TLC screening) once an MRPL has been published for nitroimidazoles (so far, an MRPL of 3µg/kg has been proposed by the CRL in Berlin). Metronidazole will be added to the list of molecules in the nitroimidazole family at the time of the request to reopen the 2005 session of the Residue Application. An LC-MS-MS method for the detection and confirmation of nitroimidazoles was used within the framework of the NRL work plan and validated in accordance with Regulation 2002/657. This method will be introduced and possibly replace the current screening method upon publication of the MRPL for these molecules. Tests for sulphonamides and tylosin in honey are currently being developed. For nitrofurans in honey, the NRL is waiting for the results of work ongoing in the UK before adapting the method. For nitrofurans in milk, the method can be adapted for the purposes of monitoring total residues. An addition to the method will be proposed. A new method for analysis of beta-agonists has been developed using Molecular Imprinting Polymer purification with LC-MS-MS in electrospray positive mode. This will allow CRL-recommended limits to be met whilst maintaining broad spectrum screening of numerous beta-agonists. Recommendation 3: The CA has stated that in the memorandum on the general principles accompanying the specific notes on the control plans, emphasis will be laid on the importance of implementing the control plans and the deadlines for the submission of samples to analysis laboratories in 2006. The memorandum will be submitted for the signature of the DG in December 2005 for implementation from January 2006. In accordance with Commission Decision 98/179/EC, the instructions in the memorandum on the general provisions for 2006 will instruct the DDSVs to close sample bags with numbered seals rather than staples. Reminders a s will be made in the memorandum on general provisions for sending samples for analysis in extreme weather conditio 4: The CA has stated that Memorandum DGAL/SDSPA/N2005- 8165 on the targeting criteria on farms and in slaughterhouses for bovine animals, pigs and poultry was published on 29 June 2005. The Ca has stated that regarding the under-sampling seen in the DDSV visited, corrective action will be taken with the DDSVs. The note on general provisions for 2006 and the specific notes for each plan will reiterate the obligation to ensure a uniform distribution of sampling over the entire calendar year. The introduction of the SIGAL system will likewise ensure the regular monitoring of sampling by each DDSV and their distribution over the year. SIGAL will facilitate the French authorities' task of monitoring the sampling operations carried out by all the DDSVs, compliance with the submission and analysis deadlines and with the deadlines for returning results. 19 Corrective action will be taken with the DDSVs. There will be a reminder in the general note and in the specific notes of the need to meet the set deadlines between sampling, analysis and delivery of results (screening and confirmation). These notes will also include a reminder of the need for samples to be taken at evenly spaced intervals over the entire calendar year. Under SIGAL, "paper" sample forms will be computerised and the transmission of the results between the screening laboratory and the DDSV will take place in the form of electronic data interchange, once laboratories have been categorised for these exchanges. This computer system will make it possible to establish regularly updated schedules showing the intervals between sampling over the year and monitoring the observance of transmission deadlines between sampling, analysis and the delivery of results (screening and confirmation). These schedules will also facilitate the regular monitoring of plan implementation and the number of non- compliances observed. Recommendation 5: The CA has stated that they will introduce follow-up indicators for transfers of samples to laboratories and a response deadline for laboratories in order to improve compliance with the latter and make it shorter, so as to carry out inspections quickly in the event of non-conformity. An inspection grid of veterinary dispensaries also makes it possible to supplement the series of measures to be taken in the event of non-compliance due to prohibited substances (memorandum DGAL/SDSPA/N2005-8188 of 20 July 2005). Recommendation 6: The CA has stated that the draft decree on approved laboratories will be the regulatory basis for the accreditation requirement. It is currently being examined by the Conseil d'Etat, with a view to publication in 1st half of 2006. Recommendation 7: The CA has stated that, in their opinion methods are already appropriately validated in the respective (originating) 8: The CA has stated that LABERCA is planning to purchase several items of new equipment. The examination of the approval dossiers by the Directorate-General for International Affairs in accordance with the draft decree on approved laboratories will make it possible to check that candidate laboratories have the necessary equipment. Publication of the decree is foreseen for the 1st half of 2006. In addition, the publication of official methods and the organisation of inter- laboratory tests by the NRLs contribute to providing these guarantees. recommendations.text: To consider limiting the approval for the relevant categories as follows: Orly airport: Air France: for HC-T(FR), HC-NT, NHC-T(FR), NHC-NT, SFS: HC-T(FR), HC-NT, NHC, France Handling: temporarily suspended by CCA; Le Havre port: Hangar 56: HC-T(CH), HC-T(FR), NHC-T, Dugrand: HC-T(1) , EFBS: HC-T(1) ; Marseille-Port: Hôtel d.... : HC, Hangar 26 : NHC-NT ; Marseille-Fos-sur-Mer: HC-T, NHC-T ; Dunkerque : HC-T(CH), NHC-NT ; 14 if satisfactory guarantees in relation to the correction of the deficiencies found are not received from the CCA within 6 months of the receipt of the final report.

To consider limiting the approvals of Orly, Le Havre, Marseille-Port and Marseille-Fos-sur-Mer to packed products only, if satisfactory guarantees in relation to the correction of the deficiencies found are not received from the CCA within 3months of the receipt of the final report.

To consider listing Dunkerque with two inspection centres for the relevant categories as follows: Dunkerque: Centre 1: HC-T(1), HC-NT, Centre 2: NHC-NT, once satisfactory guarantees in relation to the correction of the deficiencies found are received from the CCA within 6 months of the receipt of the final report. 15 9. ADDENDUM TO MISSION REPORT DG(SANCO)/7522/2005 In their comments to the draft report the CCA indicated the following: The CCA noted the finding of persistent anomalies with regard to facilities at certain border inspection posts and will propose restricting approval for some of them. In their response to the recommendations in Annex 4 the CCA indicated that upon receipt of the final report an action plan with a timetable for the correction of anomalies and will be submitted for assessment by the Commission. The following guarantees were given in advance of the action plan to the followi s: 2: That the instructions from the customs service concerning import controls had been amended and are currently the subject of consultations between the Departments. That a general instruction on the obligation to have plans for cleaning, disinfection and combating harmful organisms as applicable to agri-food establishments is under preparation. 4: That in relation to Beauvais, the French authorities will shortly carry out an additional expert inspection of these facilities and, depending on the position of the manager of the facilities, will forward a plan for bringing them up to standard where appropriate. During 2005, the French authorities will propose to the Commission the authorisation of border inspection posts in the overseas départements of Guadeloupe and Martinique. The applications for authorisation for these facilities are being finalised and will shortly be forwarded to the Commission. A specific control plan is being developed for the département of French Guyana. This plan provides for adapting controls on introduction to Guyanese territory and systematic exit controls, and will make it possible to comply with the provisions of Article 18 of Directive 97/78/EC and the requirements of Article 13 of Directive 91/496/EEC With regard to the département concerned, quarterly inspections have been adopted. Discussions are under way at national level to supplement this system by establishing a second-level control structure. Since the mission, internal audits have been formalised and scheduled at six-monthly intervals. 5: That a joint training campaign bringing together the veterinary services and customs services is planned for the end of 2005 relating to identifying the rules for importing from third countries (animals and animal foodstuffs) into Community territory, intra- Community trade and identification of veterinary and customs procedures and that specialised training for border inspection post officers (veterinarians, engineers and technicians from the veterinary services) is scheduled for 2006. This annual training lasts for five days. This specific training campaign will therefore supplement the training system set out in the pre-inspection questionnaire. This training will be open to specialised customs officers. That an additional veterinarian has been deployed at Orly to provide staff cover and increases in the number of veterinary staff for Marseille-port and Fos-sur-Mer are planned with regard to bringing the facilities into line with standards. 8: Free and customs warehouses and ship suppliers The distinction made necessary by the non-applicability of animal health rules for the introduction of non-compliant products intended for supplying vessels may now be removed in the light of the protection measures adopted in this field in 2004. The decree of 5 May 2000 laying down the procedures for veterinary controls on import, and the decree of 28 July 2004 establishing the list of authorised suppliers, will thus be amended shortly. 16 9: Surveillance of the destruction of kitchen waste from international means of transport is carried out jointly with the customs services. The latter ensures the effective destruction of the goods either directly (with an officer present at the moment of destruction) or indirectly by means of documentation and regular surveys. Surveillance in this area has been stepped up by the customs services or veterinary services according to local characteristics. 11: Le Havre: the French authorities confirm the plan to build new main and ancillary facilities for the Le Havre border inspection post. The solutions proposed for the renovation of these facilities will be presented as an action plan on receipt of the final inspection report. In the meantime, approval of the inspection centres will be restricted to controls on products intended for human consumption and packaged and frozen products HC-T(FR) (1) (2). Dunkerque: The categories of approval for Dunkerque will be amended and, specifically, will include the inspection centre dedicated to controls on products not intended for human consumption. Correction of anomalies in relation to the fitting out of the premises will be presented with the action plan on receipt of the final report. Administrative regularisation is under way with regard to the categories of approval, and the Commission has been informed (see action plan). Fos-sur-Mer: The CCA will restrict approval to controls on packaged products, if the anomalies are not rapidly corrected. If premises in accordance with the provisions of Decision 2001/812/EC are not provided, the CCA will not oppose any additional restriction on the approval of this border inspection post by the European Commission. Marseille-port: With regard to the categories of approval, the CCA propose restricting approval of the live animals inspection centre ("hangar 14") to controls on equidae registered under Directive 90/426/EEC from 31 July 2005. Approval for Marseille- port will be suspended for controls on products of animal origin, whether intended for human consumption or not, from 31 October 2005. A proposed action plan for bringing these facilities into compliance will shortly be forwarded to the Commission for validation prior to implementation. This action plan will include: - a proposal for the fitting out of new premises in accordance with the provisions of Decision 2001/812/EC by operators and managements. This proposal will be accompanied by a precise timetable for the work and completion guarantees; - a proposal for the temporary fitting out of compliant premises while awaiting the implementation of the provisions referred to above Orly: The categories of approval for the Orly border inspection post will be restricted to controls on packaged products and products intended for human consumption for two of the three inspection centres. The CCA confirms the temporary suspension of controls in the France Handling inspection centre while awaiting renovation of the premises. This work should be completed by the end of 2005. As regards the SFS inspection centre, an action plan for correcting the anomalies will be presented by the managing authorities in order to maintain the categories of approval for the centre. 12: That in relation to the border inspection posts at Orly, Le Havre and Dunkerque the inspection centres' technical equipment has been supplemented in order to correct the anomalies noted. 15: Veterinary controls: As for the other facilities, particularly those at Le Havre, the proposed action plan will enable the anomalies to be remedied. 17 Dunkerque ­ identity checks: This pre-notification anomaly has now been corrected That a reminder of the provision in relation to the Reduced physical checks regime had been issued. Controls on live animals: Particular instructions will be issued to border inspection posts approved for controls on live animals Veterinary decision ­ procedure concerning refused consignments: National instructions will correct these difficulties. 17: That the fees for veterinary controls on imports are being reviewed in accordance with the provisions of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

Issuing updated guidance on the plant passport scheme, in order to improve the understanding and implementation by smaller producers and traders. France is requested to report to the Commission two months after receipt of the final report, on action taken and/or planned on the recommendations. For planned action, a deadline for completion should be indicated. 18 ADDENDUM The single authority in France provided detailed comments on the draft report, the full text of which are published separately. In response to recommendation (1) and (2), the single authority stated that "the situation of the Plant Health Office (BSV) will be examined as part of the overall review of the definition of new strategic priorities assigned to the different bodies which form part of the Directorate-General for Food (DGAL). This review is due to be completed by the end of 2005". With regards to the regional plant protection services, DGAL's Sub-directorate for Plant Quality and Plant Protection will carry out a survey to establish how many staff are involved in inspections....the result will be used not only to identify staffing requirements but also to plan and where necessary redeploy staff". In response to recommendation (3)(4) and (5), the single authority stated that "a note is being drafted and distributed to the regional plant protection services and delegated public-sector bodies reminding them of their obligations, particularly regarding those areas in which the FVO identified failings". In addition, the single authority "will remind GNIS/SOC to include the botanical name on plant passports", and in the case of all delegated bodies, "to instruct them to include the single official registration number on plant passports. The regional plant protection services will be sent a letter-ordre de service and the delegated bodies an official letter, reminding them of the specific requirements relating to replacement plant passports". In response to recommendation (7), the single authority stated that "detection tests for latent infection have been carried out since the launch of the 2005 campaign in all plots of land approved for sending susceptible plants to protected zones for Erwinia amylovora". The provisions of the Directive (2000/29/EC) do not indicate what measures need to be taken if positive result are obtained and a decision on what action to take will be made after the results of the first campaign of latent testing are obtained. In response to recommendation (6) and advisory point (8), the single authority stated that "the information leaflet for those in the industry (producers, wholesalers etc.) will be updated in collaboration with the regional plant protection services and distributed in an appropriate manner. The speed at which this can be done will depend on the staffing situation in the Plant Health Office (BSV)". 19

audits.title: Illegal Imports of products of animal origin and live animals

recommendations.text: Competent authorities The Customs authorities, "Direction Générale des Douanes et Droits Indirects (DGDDI)",(2) are within the "Ministère de l'Économie des Finances et de l'Industrie". They carry out certain import controls and check amongst their other tasks for illegal imports of veterinary products and live animals. They have the responsibility for the supervision of non-BIP-entry points. Supervision of BIP-entry points is carried out jointly with DGAL, who are responsible for checking products of animal origin and live animals.

Legislative and administrative measures The CCA stated that EU Regulations and Decisions are directly applicable and instructions to ensure harmonised application are issued by DGAL. Customs issue similar instructions to their services. The responsibilities for controls under Regulation (EC) No 745/2004 are not yet clearly defined. Specific administrative procedures have been put in place by all the involved services for its implementation. An instruction was issued by DGAL regarding the provisions of Regulation (EC) No 745/2004 on the 24 January 2005. This foresees targeted checks on certain third countries identified according to their perceived risk regarding Avian Influenza and Foot and Mouth Disease (FMD). These checks are to be carried out in the framework of local co-operation agreements in place with customs. Customs have not yet issued specific instructions in relation to Regulation (EC) No 745/2004 and continue to operate under an instruction dating from 20 November 2003, which prioritises countries which presented a FMD disease risk at that time. During the mission it was not possible to receive a list of designated points of entry according to Art. 38 of Council Regulation (EEC) No 2913/92(e). However, information was provided that freight may be presented for customs (2) In their comments to the draft report the French CCA clarified that the DGDDI is not a "competent authority" within the meaning of Community terminology. It is responsible solely for controls on imports given its presence at the external borders of the European Union. 4 formalities at 242 offices and that 108 airports are considered as entry points for passengers. Customs is responsible for checks on pet animals according to Regulation (EC) No 998/2003(f) and any point of entry is allowed to receive pet animals.

Co-operation between different authorities At central level co-operation between Customs and DGAL is formalised in a general agreement between the services dating from May 2001, which lays a framework for co-operation and joint activities between the two services. Regular liaison meetings are foreseen under this agreement; however, information was provided after the mission that the last such meeting was in October 2004. Co-operation with other authorities involved is inadequate, in particular regarding the provision of information by travel operators regarding requirements for introduction of products of animal origin for personal consumption. Although DGAL, with Customs approval, wrote to the involved bodies in January 2005, no further action has been implemented as yet. Although it was indicated at the opening meeting that the above agreement was supplemented by local level agreements between Customs and the DGAL, this was not in place in most cases(3). Centrally neither customs nor DGAL has an overview as to the number and quantity of illegally imported consignments of animal origin and live animals seized for each point of entry. No system has been put in place to accurately record all seizures in order to furnish the information required under Art. 5 of Regulation (EC) No 745/2004, as, in general, customs only enter in their database seizures in those cases where there is an infringement procedure. 5.2. CHECKS ON ILLEGAL IMPORTS "Illegal imports" in the context of this report, is the introduction onto the territory of the Community of products of animal origin or live animals which, either accidentally or intentionally, have not been subject to, and cleared following, the veterinary checks foreseen in Community legislation. 5.2.1. Organisation and operation of Customs The administrative levels of management of Customs are organised on a central, interregional and regional basis. Into 10 interregional and 42 regional Directorates, each containing on average 3 Divisions. There are nationally 385 inspection units who carry out controls. Customs control freight, personal luggage and post sent to private persons. They carry out checks for illegal imports as part of their general inspection tasks. No specific measures are in place or specific staff allocated for the detection of illegal imports of animals or animal products. (3) In their comments to the draft report the French CCA clarified that eleven regional customs directorates have signed cooperation protocols with the DDSV and four, including Orly and Roissy, are preparing to do so. The difficulties encountered in establishing these protocols are due to the different administrative organisations in terms of the geographical competence of the customs and veterinary districts. 5 Although it is foreseen that joint controls with veterinary services take place, in practice these did not take place in all points of entry visited and where they were carried out, it was not at a high frequency(4). Customs have locally maintained databases for seizures of personal consignments. However, the information contained in these databases is only in relation to those cases where the customs officials have decided to take an infringement procedure against the offender. In cases, where there is voluntary abandonment or where no infringement procedure is entered into, no record is kept. The information retained is quite general and specific information regarding the nature and origin of the products/animals is not retained (5). In the customs computerised system (SOFI), used for free release of consignments, the relevant CN codes were linked with the requirements for veterinary checks contained in the positive list of Commission Decision 2002/349/EC(g). The customs database used for transit (NCTS) does not contain a link to veterinary checks. SOFI is also used by Customs to identify consignments which will be subject to further documentary or physical checks. These consignments will be routed for checking by Customs officials by the system before free release is possible. 5.2.2. Imports of products for personal consumption 5.2.2.1. Background Customs are responsible for personal baggage checks of travellers in all points of entry. Not all points of entry are permanently staffed by customs and deployment is on the basis of perceived risk. Customs do maintain a permanent presence at the main ports and airports. No specific risk assessment has been carried out in relation to products of animal origin or live animals(6). No specific training in the area of illegal imports was provided to customs(7). However, joint training of customs and veterinary officials in the area of (4) In their comments to the draft report the French CCA clarified that the DGDDI does not have staff specifically for this type of check, which is carried out as part of the general inspections conducted by the customs officers. (5) In their comments to the draft report the French CCA clarified that the statistics available at present do not permit them to provide all the information requested by the FVO. The seizure of goods is only recorded in the event of a customs infringement. For example, in the case of voluntary abandonment of goods transported by travellers, no statistical record is kept. Currently, customs does not have figures, in this specific field, on illegal imports, joint controls carried out with the DSV (Direction des services vétérinaires) in 2004, controls carried out on transit goods, controls carried out on freight, cases where goods detected as being animal products have not been declared as such, results of controls (Roissy), seizures of products of animal origin in postal packages and express freight. The DGDDI is aware of these gaps in the statistics on controls of illegal imports of foods of animal origin and has undertaken to resolve the problem by drawing instructions. (6) In their comments to the draft report the French CCA clarified that risk analysis in place to control foods of animal origin is not the sole responsibility of the DGDDI. The DGAL is also involved. (7) In their comments to the draft report the French CCA clarified that the training effort made by DGDDI is real and significant but the wide range of its tasks does not allow it to develop specific training for each one, training is provided after an analysis of the needs and on the basis of the numerous tasks performed by customs. 6 veterinary checks was introduced in the year 2004 and is planned to continue in 2005. 5.2.2.2.Information to passengers/travellers Information to travellers has been provided in the form of a limited number of the posters foreseen in Regulation (EC) No 745/2004 distributed to those points of entry where a BIP is located. This was because the only posters available were those provided by the Commission services. The number being insufficient to cover all points of entry. These posters were present in the points of entry visited in a number of languages though not always in appropriate locations. In some locations an outdated version of the poster continued to be displayed(8). Posters in relation to the requirements for live animals were drawn up by DGAL and were displayed at the entry points visited. No specific leaflets have been drawn up providing information to travellers in relation to personal imports of products of animal origin. There is, however, some general information, which does not fully reflect the provisions of Regulation (EC) No 745/2004, included in a simplified leaflet, from Customs, containing a number of overall requirements for travellers entering France(9). No further initiatives were taken in order to increase public awareness as no information reflecting the provisions of the above Regulation is distributed to the passengers in aircrafts or ships. A mechanism has not yet been put in place to ensure that operators of international means of transport provide the information to travellers foreseen in Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 745/2004. However, on 14 March 2005 a letter was sent jointly from "Ministère de l'Equipement des transports de l'aménagement du territoire du tourisme et de la mer" and from "La direction générale de l'aviation civile" to the airline companies outlining their responsibilities to provide information to travellers. 5.2.2.3.Organisation of controls/sanctions Customs stated that in case of the airports, arriving flights from third countries are selected on the basis of origin, and luggage for checking is selected on the basis of general customs criteria. Other than where joint checks with veterinary services are carried, out no specific priority is given to products of animal origin; these are included in the general customs checks. Customs stated that checks are carried out for all items using a risk based approach. Each point of entry has its own criteria set locally(10). (8) In their comments to the draft report the French CCA clarified that the number of posters distributed by the Commission was insufficient to cover all points of entry. Consequently, only the BIPs were supplied with the new posters. For the other points it was requested that the old posers should be kept to draw attention of the public to the existence of regulations in this area, particularly since the new rules resulting from Regulation (EC) No 745/2004 do not differ fundamentally from the old. (9) In their comments to the draft report the French CCA clarified that travellers can obtain additional information by contacting the customs information centres whose details are given on the brochure. (10) In their comments to the draft report the French CCA clarified that while each customs control unit has its own risk analysis criteria they apply a national control plan, adapted to local level, 7 National figures for joint checks carried out in 2004 could not be provided. During 2003, the CCA stated that 149 such checks were carried out at the 25 most used entry points out leading to seizure of 5,800 kg of products of animal origin. Passengers are not liable for the cost of destruction of seized consignments. Penalties and sanctions are foreseen at the discretion of the head of local Customs Division. This is in the case that the illegal consignment is seized after being discovered by customs and a decision is taken that the offence constitutes an infringement. In the case of voluntary abandonment no further action is taken. There are varying interpretations of the rules in relation to permitted importations for personal consumption. At one BIP-airport-entry-point customs stated that in many cases passengers were unaware that the products of animal origin in their luggage were illegal and posed a health risk. In one BIP-airport-entry-point up to one kg of any product of animal origin was permitted by officials on the spot for personal consumption. In another portal- entry-point there were no defined criteria as there were no facilities in place for disposal of seized product. If the quantity is large then it is returned on the vessel of arrival, passengers being allowed to retain small quantities. In the two other airports visited, one BIP and one non-BIP, the criteria were applied correctly regarding the prohibitions in relation to meat and milk, but no system was in place to determine the eligibility of the country of origin in relation to other products. Customs stated that in the event that they have doubts about the eligibility or otherwise, they refer to the BIP veterinarians. Mass scanning of luggage with a view to detect products of animal origin is not carried out. Scanners are available but are used in the context of targeted searching rather than mass scanning. Sniffer dogs are not used to screen volumes of luggage for products of animal origin. At the non-BIP-airport-entry-point visited there were some direct third country flights and also interline baggage was received; this baggage was not systematically checked for illegal imports. Passengers arriving directly from third countries were directed to a separate arrival hall where there were posters on display. Third country passengers arriving via another French airport were directed to the domestic arrival hall where no posters in relation to products of animal origin were displayed and no checks were carried out on their baggage for products of animal origin. In the BIP-airport-entry-point seized consignments were retained in secure rooms pending collection for incineration. Amnesty bins for passengers voluntarily abandoning products of animal origin are not used as they are considered to present a security risk. In the non-BIP-airport-entry-point there on the basis of the traffic which they are aware of consequently, most of the units carry out controls on the basis of similar criteria (selection of flights on the basis of place of departure). The selection criteria for controls on passengers are based on the normal customs criteria. 8 had been no seizures, so no specific measures had been put in place for destruction. Although there was documentation available to show that consignments were sent for incineration, there was no system in place to confirm that destruction had taken place in accordance with the requirements of Regulation (EC) No 1774/2002(h). In one BIP-airport-entry-point of entry eight joint checks took place in 2003 and none in 2004(11). In the other BIP-airport-entry-point 26 such checks took place in 2004 concerning 49 flights. In this airport the total seizures for that year were 7,068 kg of products of animal origin and 11 kg of live caterpillars, 26 kg of live snails and 10 live birds. In a non-BIP-airport-entry-point visited no joint checks had taken place, however, in this case three joint checks had taken place at an adjacent ferry port and five joint checks had taken place on roads as the veterinary services do not have the authority to stop traffic. In another non-BIP-airport (not visited) the team was informed that three such joint checks with staff based at a local BIP had taken place in 2004. In two BIP-port-entry-points 100% ferries and cruise ships are checked by customs and 50 - 60% of ferry passengers are checked (not specifically for products of animal origin). 5.2.3. Import and transit of freight The selection of consignments subject to veterinary checks is performed by SOFI, which in general will identify and flag the requirement for veterinary checks on those consignments destined for free release. It is also used to select consignments for physical and documentary checking based on customs criteria e.g. CN code, origin, value, importer, destination etc. Some criteria are set nationally; others are determined by the regionally based "Centres de renseignement, d'orientation et des contrôles" (CERDOC), who define the regional criteria, and others may be set locally by the head of each inspection unit on the basis of flow of consignments. In the case of veterinary consignments under customs transit procedure there is almost full reliance on information provided by the importer or handling agents as the NCTS system used does not flag the requirement for veterinary checks. The mission team were informed by Customs' staff that the NCTS system does not contain sufficient information to allow for optimal targeting of consignments for customs general checking of consignments under customs transit procedure. Introduction of veterinary consignments to temporary storage under Art. 50 of Council Regulation (EEC) No 2913/92(i), as described in point 5.2.7.2 of report DG(SANCO) 7522/2005 is allowed prior to veterinary checks. (11) In their comments to the draft report the French CCA clarified that, controls of this type did take place at other nearby entry points, and in any case, the customs services regularly call on the veterinary services during controls on products of animal origin. As the customs officials are not experts in this field, it is preferable, in cases of doubt, to rely on the competent authorities responsible in this sector. 9 At the BIP-airport-entry-points the SOFI system mainly is used to select consignments for physical and documentary checking. These entry-points have no computerised system in place with details of all arriving consignments. In one BIP-airport-entry-point the targeting unit was visited, which since it was set up in January 2004 has been involved in the general targeting of freight. Specific targeting work had been done in relation to CITES animals and products; however, no specific targeting has been carried out for products of animal origin in general. This unit examines the cargo manifests before arrival of the flight in order to target consignments for checking by the control units before they enter one of the 40 warehouses in the airport environs. In one of the above airports 95% of consignments are customs released for importation and of these approximately 80% are automatically cleared for free release by SOFI. The remaining 20% being routed for either documentary or physical checking. The CCA stated that approximately 2% of the consignments are subject to a physical check based on the risk information contained in SOFI. No information could be provided in relation to checks on consignments under customs transit procedure. A 100% physical check is carried out on unaccompanied baggage which is treated as freight and in this category products of animal origin are found declared often as personal effects. At the other BIP-airport-entry-point no information was provided as to the frequency of checks on freight by Customs and as to how often veterinary goods were detected but not declared as such. However, 11,403 kg of product of animal origin were detected in the unaccompanied baggage subject to 100% checking. At the BIP-port-entry-points: there are various information systems (PROTIS, GEMINI and ADEMAR) which contain the summary declarations of all arriving consignments. These systems are used by customs in addition to SOFI to target their activities. Details regarding the frequencies of checks and the results of checks were not provided to the mission team for all entry-points. In one BIP-port-entry-point details of customs checks carried out show that, in 2004, out of 1500 infringements detected, 47 related to veterinary consignments. In anther BIP- port-entry-point approximately 20 % of consignments declared for importation underwent a physical check. At present there is one functional scanner for containers which is used on a targeted basis. In another port-entry-point, while a scanner has been installed, it is not currently operational.

Import of post consignments Although a point of entry for parcel post was not visited, Customs provided some information as to the checks carried out. Live animals cannot to be sent by mail under the "Postal Convention" but for products of animal origin may be sent. Regarding mail, according to customs 5-15% of parcels are subject to a physical check Selection is on the basis of origin, value, available resources and other customs general criteria. 10 No specific instructions regarding the requirements in relation to products of animal origin have been provided to Customs staff. At the express freight centre visited selected consignments were checked by customs. Consignments for checking are selected on the basis of the information contained in the airway bill or in the manifest which are subject to 100% check by Customs. On the basis of this selection approximately 2% of consignments are checked physically by customs. There was no awareness of any products of animal origin being found in express freight during these checks and no statistics of seizures could be provided by the authorities on the spot. It was stated that one live animal (turtle) and some CITES products had been detected. 11 6. recommendations.text: The Central Competent Authority should ensure that the microbiological criteria for classification of production areas and lead and cadmium limits contained in the Order of 21 May 1999 are brought into line with those prescribed in Regulations (EC) No 854/2004 and 1881/2006, respectively.

The Central Competent Authority should ensure that the criteria for classification of live bivalve mollusc production areas comply fully with those mentioned in paragraphs 3, 4 and 5 of Part A of Chapter II of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 854/2004.

The Central Competent Authority should ensure that live bivalve molluscs from production areas classified as Class A and placed on the market meet the health standards for live bivalve molluscs laid down in Annex III, Section VII, Chapter V of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004, particularly those relating to microbiological quality (such as the limit of 230 MPN/100 g of intervalvular flesh and liquid).

The Central Competent Authority should ensure that plankton monitoring meets the requirements: of paragraph 4(a) of Part B of Chapter II of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 854/2004, particularly with regard to periodic sampling; paragraph 7 of Part B of Chapter II of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 854/2004, particularly with regard to information on the presence of toxic species.

The Central Competent Authority should ensure that purification centres meet the requirements set out in Part A of Chapter IV, Section VII of Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 853/2004, particularly paragraphs 3 to 5.

The Central Competent Authority should ensure that its decentralised services respect the instructions concerning the annual distribution of samples of live bivalve molluscs, as part of the monitoring/control plans (as in the case of oyster sampling).

The Central Competent Authority should ensure that all production areas are monitored at regular intervals, particularly to verify the possible presence of toxin-producing plankton in production waters and for biotoxins in live bivalve molluscs, in accordance with paragraph 1(c) of Part B of Chapter II of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 854/2004.

The Central Competent Authority should ensure that, when it considers the results of checks performed by food business operators (or organisations representing them) to decide on classification, opening or closing of production areas, sampling and analyses conducted by food business operators must be performed according to a protocol agreed between the competent authority and operators or organisation concerned in the food sector (in accordance with Part F of Chapter II of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 854/2004).

The Central Competent Authority should ensure that documents accompanying consignments of live bivalve molluscs are drafted correctly and that the information provided is in accordance with paragraph 4 of Chapter I, Section VII of Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 853/2004.

The Central Competent Authority should ensure that laboratories involved in official controls of live bivalve molluscs respect the number of individuals per sample for counting E. coli using the EU reference method, in accordance with section 1.25, Chapter I of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005. recommendations.text: To take measures to register transporters of ABP/DP and to ensure the updating of the lists of establishments, plants and operators as required by, respectively, Article 23 and Article 47 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. Recommendation based on conclusion 15. Associated findings: 9 and 10

citations.text: In France, official lists of approved and registered establishments are managed at regional level and are publicly available. Each region is responsible for updating their official lists on the basis of information provided by each relevant Département by using the national database of business operators (SIGAL). In 2012 an instruction was issued by DGAL highlighting the need to change the previous codification of establishments handling ABP/DP in order to bring it in line with the EU technical specifications for establishments and plants handling ABP. However, the audit team noted that a number of operators included in the SIGAL database did not appear in the official regional lists. This was also the case of a trader visited during the audit (see paragraph 20). According to representatives from DGAL this is due to the fact that the code-updating phase of registered and approved establishments is not completed yet. Moreover, an official in charge of updating the official lists stated not having time to do this task (see also paragraph 6). This is not in line with requirements laid down by Article 47(1) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009.

As regards registration of transporters and traders, a Ministerial Decree was issued in 2011 highlighting the obligation for these business operators to notify their activities to the departmental authorities and, in 2013, another instruction was issued to remind the local competent authorities to update the lists of establishment handling ABP/DP with registered transporters and traders. Moreover, according to representatives from DGAL, a meeting with various associations of business operators was held in 2011 where, among other things, this obligation was clarified. However, the audit team noted that in many cases, transporters and traders did not appear in the official regional lists or their number was very limited. Representatives from DGAL and business operators met by the audit team confirmed this is very likely an underestimation of the real situation. As a result, this is not fully in line with Articles 23 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. 5.2.3 Organisation and planning of official controls Findings

The system of official controls for the traceability of ABP/DP is negatively affected by an early stage of registration process of transporters of ABP/DP and by the unreliability of the relevant official lists of plants, establishments and operators involved in the chain of ABP/DP.

recommendations.text: To take account of the risk of diversion or misuse of ABP/DP in the organisation and implementation of official controls on the traceability of ABP/DP, including at the level of traders and transporters, as laid down by Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Recommendation based on conclusions 16 and 26. Associated findings: 11, 12, 13, 20 and 22.

citations.text: As indicated in the National Inspection Programme, the frequency of inspections of business operators handling ABP/DP is risk-based. It is determined by applying a formula which, among other things, takes into account the theoretical risk of the plant (on the basis of the nature of the activities and the products handled), the volume of the product placed in the market and the performance of the business operator (determined by the inspector in charge of the official controls). The resulting frequency of inspections may vary from once per year to once every four years. In the Départements visited, the audit team noted that Category 3 processing plants were inspected generally every three years and that the usual duration of an inspection is 2-3 hours. This level of official control does not allow to adequately take into account the risk of diversion or misuse of PAP (see also paragraph 13), therefore, this is not fully in line with Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

In the Départements visited, inspections were carried out at the planned frequencies and were largely in line with the frequency-criteria established by the National Inspection Programme. However, the audit team noted that the National Inspection Programme does 5 not include some registered business operators, namely transporters and traders handling ABP/DP, without any solid risk-based justifications being provided by the competent authorities and, as a result, these business operators are not subject to planned official controls (see also paragraph 20). This is not in line with requirements laid down by Article 3(3) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

A standard checklist is available for officials to carry out inspections in ABP plants. This checklist consists of a list of generic items applicable to all processing plants. In addition to that, a guide released in 2009 provides further details and legal clarifications. According to the competent authorities the checklist and the guide are going to be updated soon to take into account, among other things, the relevant changes in the legislation. The audit team noted that, although the current checklist (and the draft of the new one) is largely comprehensive, it contains only two-three generic items related to the traceability of ABP/DP. As a result, officials are only required to confirm, or not, if commercial documents and a traceability procedure are present (see paragraph 22) and this could lead to an oversight of the risk of misuse or diversion of ABP/DP. This is not fully in line with Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

The system of official controls covers a number of operators dealing with ABP/DP, however its effectiveness is negatively affected by the following: a) traders and transporters which are not subject to official controls without a risk based justification and, b) organisation of official controls which only allows superficial checks that cannot ensure enough attention to the risk of diversion or misuse of ABP/DP. 6 5.3 TRACEABILITY OF ABP/DP: OFFICIAL CONTROLS ON RELEVANT REQUIREMENTS Legal requirements Article 41, 43 and 48 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009; Articles 17(1), 25 and 32 of Regulation (EU) No 142/2011; Article 7 of Regulation (EC) No 999/2001; Article 8 of Directive 97/78/EC. 5.3.1 Imports, exports and intra-community trade of ABP/DP Findings

In a trader importing fishmeal visited, the audit team reviewed the documentation of three imported consignments of fishmeal in bulk and noted that for one of them no analysis showing the absence of unauthorised constituents of animal origin accompanied the consignment as required by Article 7 of Regulation (EC) No 999/2001 and set out in Section C, Chapter III of its Annex IV. The competent authorities stated that for such consignments of fishmeal, which had been released for free circulation, no analysis was available. The audit team noted that the competent authorities did not know this deficiency because the operator had never been inspected (see paragraph 12). 7 5.3.2 Operator obligations regarding identification, transport and traceability Findings

However, it was noted the following: a) the points related to the origin and the traceability of ABP/DP were not checked in a regular manner or, when checked, it was done in a superficial way. In particular, no checks were carried out which could identify discrepancies between the amounts of materials received and dispatched (e.g. checks on the patterns and congruence of incoming and outgoing material) and only one or two commercial documents were reviewed per inspection. Relevant inspectors stated this was mainly due to lack of time since the inspections usually last 2-3 hours (see paragraph 6); and furthermore in all establishments visited inspectors did not pay attention to the registration of the transporters, partly due to the lack of reliable lists of such business operators (see paragraph 10).

Official controls on ABP/DP are carried out in accordance with the national plan and using a standard checklist but, the fact that there is a very limited confirmation of arrival of consignments of ABP/DP traded from other Member States and that checks on traceability requirements are often carried out in a superficial manner or not at all, negatively affects the ability of the competent authorities to detect any diversion or misuse of ABP/DP (see conclusion 16). 5.4 INFORMATION ON THE CHAIN OF PAP TO BE USED IN AQUACULTURE FEED

The only controls carried out are during a routine inspection (see section 5.2.3) when a number of consignments may be checked. recommendations.text: To carry out the necessary checks to ensure that the sourcing and the transport of ABP and PAP for the manufacturing of feed for aquaculture take place under the conditions laid down by Article 7 and Annex IV to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001. Recommendation based on conclusions 52. Associated findings: 44 and 48

citations.text: However, the audit team noted that official controls paid limited attention to ensure the actual implementation and effectiveness of the business operator's control systems (see paragraph 22) and transporters and traders of ABP/DP are not subject to planned official controls (see paragraph 10). As an example, one Category 3 processing plant visited consisted of two units, including one handling multi-species ABP (comprising ruminants) which had been authorised in 2012 by the local competent authority to produce bloodmeal for aquaculture. It was noted that in 2012 an inspection took place but during this inspection no specific checks were carried out regarding the traceability, the handling of the products and the risk of cross-contamination, as the plant was not operating at the time and, afterwards, no further inspections were carried out, apart from an official sample to detect the presence of ruminant DNA, taken a few weeks before the audit. This is not in line with the conditions laid down by Article 7 and Annex IV to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001. 5.6.2 Use of PAP for producing compound feed Findings

However, although the inspectors explained that the new requirements for the use of PAP for aquaculture are indirectly taken into account in the context of the review of the Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points (HACCP) plan, the checklists used do not contain specific points on these provisions (see also paragraph 36). In particular, the audit team noted that these checklists do not contain specific items on transport and were not regularly checked despite this being identified as a potentially important issue in the follow-up of non-compliances (see paragraph 51). As an example, in one feed manufacturer, the audit team noted that one of the previous loads of a lorry carrying PAP in bulk from another Member State consisted of PAP of ruminant origin (lamb). After this load, a cleaning operation was recorded but the inspector in charge was not in a position to confirm neither if this cleaning was based on a documented procedure that had been given prior authorisation by a competent authority nor whether this cleaning would be accepted on the basis of the fact that France does not avail of derogations for transporters (see paragraph 34). This is not fully in line with the conditions laid down by Article 7 and Section B, Chapter V of Annex IV to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001.

Although the restricted scale of production and use of PAP for the production of feed for aquaculture animals (which is mainly traded to other Member States) and the good own- control systems of business operators lower the risk of diversion or misuse of PAP containing proteins of ruminant origin, during inspections, officials generally pay limited attention to the measures implemented by the business operators, in particular in relation to the sourcing of ABP/PAP and their transport. This limits the capability of the competent authorities to ensure that PAP destined to aquaculture does not contain proteins of ruminant origin. 5.7 FOLLOW-UP OF RELEVANT RECOMMENDATIONS ON ABP MADE IN PREVIOUS FVO REPORTS (DG SANCO/2013-6898) The table below summarises the follow-up to a part of the relevant recommendation made in report DG SANCO/2013-6898. This is because: a) the limited priority given to the risk of diversion or misuse of these products resulting in the planning and the carrying out of superficial checks on the traceability requirements that operators should fulfil, and b) the exclusion of traders and transporters from official controls without a risk-based justification. The production and use of PAP for aquaculture is limited in France and this type of feed is produced mainly for use in other Member States. The feed manufacturers and processing plants involved appear to have robust own-check programmes in place and the competent authorities have put in place some measures to ensure that only eligible PAP are used in the aquaculture sector. However, the reliability of these measures is weakened by the limited attention paid during inspections to the new requirements concerning the feed ban. This pertains in particular to the sourcing and transport of ABP and PAP. 15 7 CLOSING MEETING A closing meeting was held on 28 November 2014 with the representatives of DGAL and DGCCRF. At this meeting, the main findings and preliminary conclusions were presented by the audit team. The authorities did not express disagreement and stated that they would take the actions deemed necessary in order to address any weaknesses in the system identified during the audit. 8 RECOMMENDATIONS The competent authorities are invited to provide details of the actions taken and planned, including deadlines for their completion ('action plan'), aimed at addressing the recommendations set out below, within 25 working days of receipt of this audit report. To ensure that appropriate actions are taken to correct the deficiencies detected at BIP Lyon airport in order to ensure that the BIP complies with approval requirements of Annex II to Council Directive 91/496/EC. Recommendation based on conclusion: 19. Associated findings 11, 12, 13 and 14.

citations.text: The BIP has a sufficiently large changing room and washbasin with cold and hot water at the disposal of staff responsible for carrying out veterinary checks of live animals. However, a shower is not available in the BIP facilities for live animals contrary to the requirements of point 4 of Annex A to Directive 91/496/EEC. 3

The unloading area is adequate for the animal species expected, as required by point 2 of Annex A to Directive 91/496/EEC. Horses are transported to the BIP in boxes which are placed on the platforms pulled by the airport trailer. The equipment for the unloading (step-down) of horses from the above-mentioned platforms onto the rubber floor was not available, and needs to be procured. The airport operator provided assurances that the unloading equipment will be provided within the month after the audit.

The inspection area is suitable for carrying out the checks required. However, it is not fully equipped with the necessary tools that would allow staff to perform identity and physical checks (e.g. equipment to restrain, thermometer), contrary to the requirements laid down in Articles 3 and 4, and Annex II (parts I and II) to Decision 97/794/EC. The microchip reader was available during the audit. The competent authority informed that sampling for registered horses will be carried out only in suspicious cases following the derogation foreseen in Annex II (part III.1) to Decision 97/794/EC.

The animals' housing and isolation facilities are easy to clean and disinfect. However, the walls in the isolation facilities had gaps in them allowing communication with the outside that impedes the correct isolation of animals, when necessary.

In general the BIP facilities are ready for receiving and checking consignments of live animals. However, the facilities proposed do not fully ensure the standards for animal welfare during unloading and for isolation, whenever such need arises. In addition, a shower for the BIP staff should be made available. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS The proposed BIP is integrated into the existing national import control system. Allocation of tasks, responsibilities and duties, training, instructions and the cooperation agreement with Customs will support the correct implementation of the official import controls. At the time of the audit, facilities were ready to use but several shortcomings were noted with regard to the facilities and equipment. The shortcomings are minor, so that they can be rectified and appropriate equipment can be obtained before the actual listing of BIP Lyon airport in Commission Decision 2009/821/EC for the category for live animals (E). 7 CLOSING MEETING A closing meeting was held on the same day with representatives from the central and local competent authority and the airport operator. At this meeting, the main findings and the preliminary conclusions of the audit were presented by the auditor. The authorities did not express disagreement with the shortcomings identified during the audit. The competent authorities and the airport operator confirmed that the deficiencies of the facilities will be rectified and appropriate equipment will be provided before the actual listing of BIP Lyon airport in Commission Decision 2009/821/EC for the category for live animals (E). 5 8 RECOMMENDATIONS No. Recommendation 1.
