recommendations.text: Ensure that monitoring for Xyllela fastidiosa in the buffer zones in Corsica and PACA is implemented in line with Article 6(7) of Decision 2015/789/EU. The recommendation is based on conclusions No. 81 and 82. Associated findings No. 64, 65 and 66.

citations.text: The audit team noted that due to sampling and laboratory capacity problems, especially immediately after the first outbreaks, it was not possible to sample and analyse all the specified plants in the 100m area around the IZ. Instead, the area of 15m around each IZ was prioritised. In this area the specified plants were sampled and tested in line with provisions of the Decision.

In PACA the majority of the outbreaks were discovered in the last months of 2015 or in 2016, therefore no surveys had been carried out in the BZs at the time of the audit, which is not in line with the provisions of the Decision. In Corsica, due to the numerous recent outbreaks, the CA stated that it was not in a position to carry out surveys in line with the provisions of the Decision (i.e. visual inspections and sampling of plants with 18 symptoms based on a 100m x 100m grid). At the time of the audit, the entire BZ area was 380,100 ha; therefore the same number of visual inspections would be required annually to fulfil the requirements of the Decision.

The audit team was informed that visual inspections were and will be carried out in the BZs based on a grid split into 1km x 1km squares. The CAs noted that the proper implementation of the plan could be hindered by the inaccessibility of some areas. 5.3.4 Tracing back and forward of infection sources

No surveys were carried out in 2015 in the BZs in PACA. In Corsica the intensity of the surveys in the BZs is lower than that required by Article 6(7) of Decision 2015/789/EU. As a result there is no comprehensive information available about the infection status of the BZs.

The sampling and testing practice within a radius of 100m around the infected plants is not in line with the provisions of Article 6(3) of Decision 2015/789/EU. Therefore, the real extent of the spread of infection is not known in each outbreak site.

recommendations.text: Ensure that eradication measures are implemented following the confirmation of the presence of Xylella fastidiosa in line with Article 6(2) and 6(3) of Decision 2015/789/EU in particular concerning the removal of all host plants and the required testing of specified plants. The recommendation is based on conclusion No. 80. Associated findings No. 63 and 77.

citations.text: In the case of the first three outbreaks in Corsica it was assumed that the infection was caused by Xf subsp. pauca, therefore in the 100m area around the IZ, hosts plants of that subspecies and all symptomatic plants of other species were removed. Later, based on the assumption that Pm was the prominent source of infection, each plant of this species was removed. The audit team noted that due to capacity problems, Corsica SRAL could not return to all the outbreak sites where removal had been completed, to check for the presence and order the removal of plants of newly identified host species. For all outbreaks in PACA, immediate removal of host plants (known to be hosts at the time that the infected plants were detected) was ordered in the 100m zone and this had been implemented at the time of audit. 5.3.3 Surveys for Xf in the DAs

The audit team visited nurseries in the DAs in Corsica and PACA, to whom derogation B had been granted and noted: They keep records on entries and sales. In the case of private clients the name, address and telephone number is recorded; Plants are treated with pesticides at least once a month; They are inspected by the SRAL regularly; In the nursery in Corsica, host plants (Lavandula sp.) were present, although this species was not considered as a host plant at the time of the demarcation. SRAL informed the audit team that the lot was put on hold and sampled, and that destruction was planned in the case of positive results; 5.3.6 Other measures to prevent the spread of Xf

The measures taken in the DAs show the commitment of the French CAs to eradicating Xf, in order to protect major crops and environmentally and economically important areas. Specific efforts were made to implement appropriate measures. The demarcation of the affected areas, the eradication of infected plants and hosts (known at the time of detection) in the 100m radius and the trace back and forward of the infections was carried out in line with the provisions of Decision 2015/789/EU. However, as outbreak sites where eradication activity had been completed were not revisited after new hosts were identified, there is a risk that infected plants remain in those areas.

recommendations.text: Ensure that the movement out of a demarcated area of specified plants which have been grown for at least part of their life in that area, is only allowed when the plants have been grown in a site which meets all the requirements of Article 9(2) of Decision 2015/789/EU. The recommendation is based on conclusion No. 83. Associated findings No. 72, 73, 74, 76 and 77.

citations.text: DGAL stated that it interprets the provisions of Article 9 of Decision 2015/789/EU as providing the possibility to grant three different types of derogations to nurseries in the DAs. SRAL authorises the movement of host and specified plants within and outside of the DAs according to the scheme outlined in paragraphs 72-75 below. In general, the applicable derogation depends on the type of plants and the length of time they spend in the DA. Derogation A is applied to nurseries who deal with marketing of plants which are in pots or containers and the premises are not considered as growing fields (i.e. plants are not multiplied and kept on solid surface). It is granted for non-host specified plants which were in stock in the nursery at the time of demarcation; Derogation B is applied for the same type of nurseries as derogation A. It is granted for non-host specified plants, which enter the nursery from outside the DAs after demarcation and which do not spend more than one vegetation period at the premises; Derogation C is applied to nurseries which deal with host plants or propagate and/or keep stocks of specified plants at the premises, in containers or on the open field longer than one vegetation period.

Derogation A is granted if the nursery Carries out an inventory on the stocks; Carries out permanent insecticide treatment of the plants against insect vectors; Keeps a record on sales and keeps a register of observations any disease symptoms; Receives prior authorisation of the stocks from SRAL; Subscribes for the BSV and follows training on Xf organised by an expert body.

Derogation B is granted if the nursery Keeps a record on entries (date, supplier, quantities) per plant species; Carries out permanent insecticide treatment of the plants against insect vectors and keeps a record of the treatments; 20 Keeps a record on sales (date, client, quantities) per plant species and keeps a register of observations of any disease symptoms; Subscribes for the BSV and follows training on Xf organised by an expert body.

The audit team noted that derogations A and B are not in line with provisions of Decision 2015/789/EU. However, DGAL stated that based on the French language version of the Decision, it interprets that the movement ban of Article 9 refers to plants which have been cultivated in the DAs and does not include those that are kept on premises for wholesale and retail purposes only. The CA considers that the measures, linked to derogation A and B provide the necessary guarantees of not distributing the pest through sales of planting material. The CA has also emphasised that the approach was developed based on the need to allow trade of planting material without pronounced risk while taking efforts to prevent the spread of Xf.

The audit team visited nurseries in the DAs in Corsica and PACA, to whom derogation B had been granted and noted: They keep records on entries and sales. In the case of private clients the name, address and telephone number is recorded; Plants are treated with pesticides at least once a month; They are inspected by the SRAL regularly; In the nursery in Corsica, host plants (Lavandula sp.) were present, although this species was not considered as a host plant at the time of the demarcation. SRAL informed the audit team that the lot was put on hold and sampled, and that destruction was planned in the case of positive results; 5.3.6 Other measures to prevent the spread of Xf

Nurseries located in DAs are allowed to move non-host specified plants outside their DA without fulfilling all requirements of Article 9(2) of Decision 2015/789/EU. It creates a potentially high risk as the plants spend time in the nursery, surrounded by potentially infected plants without any protection against transmission by vectors.

recommendations.text: Ensure that surveys in and outside the demarcated area take into consideration the presence and biology of the specified plants as required by Article 3 of Decision 2015/789/EU, in particular relating to the accessibility of hosts in private gardens and in remote areas. The recommendation is based on conclusion No. 58. Associated findings No. 50, 51 and 66.

citations.text: Outside the DAs, surveys in the two regions targeted nurseries and public places, where there were reports about the presence of Pm plants or symptomatic plants. The audit team was informed that in both regions, there are numerous private properties where Pm and other host plants are present. Accessing these properties for surveillance purposes is very difficult. In Corsica many private properties are second homes of residents in continental France and the owners are not present for much of the year. Therefore in many cases it is difficult to obtain the consent of the owner/tenant for the survey.

In some areas, especially in Corsica, Pm has become part of the wild flora and is commonly found in scrublands (in French - maqui). The audit team was informed that there are signs that some of these wild plants exhibit symptoms of Xf. However, the majority of these plants are located in sites that are difficult to access in order to take samples and practically inaccessible for the implementation of eradication measures, if necessary. SRAL Corsica surveyed some scrublands with a drone and confirmed the presence of symptomatic Pm plants. SRAL intends to contact the National Botanical Conservatory of Corsica, who are involved in flora mapping of wild areas, in order to collect information about the spread of Pm and to involve them as appropriate in surveillance activity. 14

In 2015 France carried out a comprehensive and risk based Xf national survey as required by EU legislation. The surveys outside the DAs in Corsica took into consideration the new risk elements identified as a result of the outbreaks. In PACA, as the outbreaks were detected recently, there was no time for comprehensive surveys outside the DAs. In both regions, the limited accessibility of private properties, scrublands or other natural sites compromise the surveys. The lack of movement controls of specified plants beyond the controls related to the implementation of the plant passport system outside the DAs does not increase the risk of spread substantially as there is limited trade of plants outside those areas.

The audit team was informed that visual inspections were and will be carried out in the BZs based on a grid split into 1km x 1km squares. The CAs noted that the proper implementation of the plan could be hindered by the inaccessibility of some areas. 5.3.4 Tracing back and forward of infection sources

recommendations.text: For those audit activities that have not been subject to independent scrutiny, suitable arrangements for such scrutiny should be put in place in order to comply with the requirements of Article 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. The recommendation is based on conclusion No. 51 Associated findings No. 48 and 49

citations.text: For DGCCRF, even if some potential mechanisms exist (the Ministerial Audit Committee) that could be suitable to undertake independent scrutiny of the audit processes, these mechanisms are not being used for this purpose at present.
At the time of the DG SANTE audit, no decisions had been taken as to when and how independent scrutiny of the DGCCRF internal audit processes would be achieved. Conclusions

For DGCCRF, independent scrutiny of the current audit processes has not yet been carried out. This is contrary to the requirements of Article 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. 5.2.3 Auditor competence 5.2.3.1 Legal requirements Articles 2(6) and 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 do not lay down specific requirements regarding the competence of auditors. Article 6 of the same Regulation requires that staff performing official controls "receive, for their area of competence, appropriate training enabling them to undertake their duties competently" and "keep up-to-date in their area of competence and receive regular additional training as necessary" Section 6.6 of the Annex of Commission Decision 2006/677 provides guidance on auditor competence: "Auditor competence and selection criteria should be defined under the following headings: -- generic knowledge and skills -- audit principles, procedures and techniques; management/organisational skills, 14 -- specific technical knowledge and skills, -- personal attributes, -- education, -- work experience, -- auditor training and experience. It is essential to put a mechanism in place to ensure auditors are consistent and their competencies are maintained. Competencies required by audit teams will vary depending on the area they are auditing within the control or supervision systems. As regards the technical knowledge and skills required by auditors, the training requirements for staff performing official controls (Chapter 1 of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 882/2004) should also be considered." 5.2.3.2 Findings

recommendations.text: To ensure that samples of food of non-animal origin are handled and labelled in such a way as to guarantee both their legal and analytical validity, as required in Article 11(7) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Recommendation based on conclusion 37. Associated finding: 33.

citations.text: In relation to the handling of samples: a. In Le Havre and Marseille BIPs, officials used tamper-proof seals and the samples were transported under the responsibility of the competent authority. This was different in BIP Roissy-CDG, where the bags for the samples were not closed with a tamper-proof seal5. This was already noted during the previous audit DG(SANCO) 2010-8554. 4 In their comments to the draft report, the competent authorities noted that, after satisfactory documentary checks, the second consignment was released. 5 Immediately after the audit, the SIVEP informed the audit team of the corrective actions implemented to eliminate this shortcoming: the "Inspection Guide" has been amended requiring, amongst others, the use of tamper-proof bags individually identified and sufficient communication to the laboratory so that the integrity of the sample can be verified at arrival. The expected date for implementation was end of May 2016. 9 b. DGCCRF closes the samples with commercial adhesive tape and attaches the sampling document with an aluminium seal. This procedure does not render the sample tamper-proof. In addition, the operator is responsible for the transport of the sample to the laboratory. The practice of using non tamper-proof samples coupled with the circumstance that the operator himself transports the sample for analysis does not guarantee the legal validity of the sample required by Article 11(7) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

Enhanced controls are implemented when necessary on the consignments presented at the borders. Sampling procedures are correctly implemented by the two sanitary authorities. The sealing and handling of samples, when the competent authority does not maintain the chain of custody, cannot ensure their legal and analytical validity for laboratory testing. 10 5.3.2 Decision on the consignments and enforcement measures Legal requirements Article 5 of Directive 97/78/EC. Article 8(3) of Regulation No 885/2014. Article 8(2)(a) of and Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 669/2009 Article 9(6) of Regulation (EC) No 884/2014. Article 12 of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) No 322/2014. Articles 19(2) and 24 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Findings

recommendations.text: To ensure that physical checks in all designated points of entry are carried out only in the premises of food businesses subject to the hygiene requirements laid down in Regulation (EC) No 852/2004, so that food of non-animal origin can be handled hygienically, in line with Article 16(3) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Recommendation based on conclusion 19. Associated findings: 14 and 15.

citations.text: DGAL uses BIP facilities for the controls under their responsibility (products of animal origin and feed). For the controls on food of non-animal origin, identity and physical checks are implemented in interim storage facilities operating under Customs supervision. The importers propose on a case-by-case basis the storage facility, chosen amongst any operator (not necessarily food or feed operator) functioning in the area2. The competent authority underlined that this practice is not a use of the derogation provided under Article 19 of Regulation (EC) 669/2009. They also stated that they are satisfied with the guarantees provided by the current arrangements.

The system described in the previous paragraph does not ensure that the facilities used for identity and physical checks are hygienically adequate to store food. The registration as food operators of these interim storages is not a pre-requisite, so operators are not necessarily subject to the obligations laid down in Regulation (EC) No 852/2004. Verification of the hygiene conditions is done when the officials go on-the-spot to implement the import controls. This arrangement does not ensure that products are always handled hygienically (which is required by Article 16(3) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004). 5.1.3 Fees

Controls on food of non-animal origin, under the responsibility of DGCCRF, are performed in temporary storage facilities where hygiene conditions are only verified after the goods arrive. This arrangement does not ensure that goods are handled hygienically.

recommendations.text: To ensure, in accordance with Article 27(4) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, and with the criteria laid down in Annex VI to Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, the collection of fees occasioned by the increased level of controls provided for in Article 14 of Regulation (EC) No 884/2014, Article 13 of Regulation (EC) No 885/2014 and Article 13 of Regulation (EC) No 2015/175. Recommendation based on conclusion 18. Associated findings: 16 and 17.

citations.text: In response to the recommendation of the audit DG(SANCO) 2010-8596 on the fees borne by the operators, DGCCRF introduced the Statutory Order of 16 August 2013, 2 In their response to the draft report, the competent authority noted that currently there is no specific registration system for bonded warehouses where food of non-animal origin can be presented for checks and stored while awaiting the result of the testing. If the premises have a food storage activity, they are registered in the food sector and subject as such to hygiene rules. There is currently no link between the enhanced import controls and the hygiene controls in these establishments. 5 setting the amounts of the fee for import checks on the food of non-animal origin referred to in Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 669/2009.

Regarding emergency measures taken under Article 53 of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002, the French authorities amended the Customs Code in 2014 to provide a national legal basis for charging operators the costs of import controls. Nevertheless, the implementing decree has not been drafted yet, and the requirements of Article 14 of Regulation (EC) No 884/2014, Article 13 of Regulation (EC) No 885/2014 and Article 13 of Regulation (EC) No 2015/175 are not complied with (all costs resulting from the official controls including sampling, analysis, storage and any measures taken following non- compliance, shall be borne by the feed or food business operators). Conclusions on the general requirements regarding the official controls system

In compliance with the EU legal requirements, staff are appropriately qualified to perform their job, and instructions are available. The communication between and within the competent authorities functions well, which contributes to the effectiveness of the controls.

recommendations.text: To have mechanisms in place to ensure that in the BIP Roissy-CDG, all products of animal origin entering the Community undergo veterinary checks by gathering all pertinent intelligence, and in particular the information on manifests, as required in Article 6(b) of Regulation (EC) No 136/2004. Recommendation based on conclusion 25. Associated finding: 22.

citations.text: At the BIP Roissy-CDG, staff from SIVEP explained that manifest checks have not been carried out since 2013. The competent authority explained that (a) the resources required for manifest checks are disproportionate to the number of undeclared consignments detected, (b) the non-declared consignment ­ if any ­ would have left the airport by the time staff has time to check the manifests, and (c) data in the manifests are often difficult to interpret. This position does not comply with the requirements laid down in Article 6(b) of Regulation (EC) No 136/2004, to gather all pertinent intelligence for the purpose of detecting consignments not presented for controls3.

The cooperation between Customs and the two sanitary authorities ensures that the relevant consignments are presented for sanitary controls. For products of animal origin, the lack of manifest checks at the BIP Roissy-CDG opens the possibility that mis- declared or non-declared consignments enter the Union without the prescribed controls. 5.3 IMPLEMENTATION OF THE IMPORT CONTROLS Legal requirements Article 1(1) of Regulation (EC) No 136/2004. Article 8(1)(b) and 9(2) of Regulation (EC) No 669/2009. Articles 3(1), 11(7), 16(2)(c) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Article 4(3) of Directive 97/78/EC. Commission Regulation (EC) No 401/2006. Article 8 of Regulation (EC) No 884/2014. Findings 5.3.1 Implementation of the documentary, identity and physical checks

recommendations.text: To ensure that the system of checks before long journeys is implemented as described in the official control procedures, in line with Article 8(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, to verify that the journey logs submitted by the organiser are realistic and indicate compliance with Regulation (EC) No 1/2005, as required by its Article 14(1). Recommendation based on conclusion 28.

citations.text: Although the procedures and instructions provide the necessary support for effective checks on journey planning, the fact that districts do not implement some of the requirements mean that the approved planning to provide feed, water and rest to the animals is not assured. For exports going into Turkey by road, this absence of assurance together with the lack of awareness of the operating hours of the Turkish border controls and of the time needed to go through at district level, create a risk for unnecessary suffering to animals.

recommendations.text: To ensure that appropriate checks at any stage of a long journey are in place, and performed, to verify that declared journey times are realistic and that the journey complies with Regulation (EC) No 1/2005, as required by its Article Recommendation based on conclusions 18, 28 and 29. Associated findings: 14, 23, 24, and 25.

citations.text: The DGAL procedure covering all the checks related to the journey logs (see also paragraph 9) also refers to checks at time of loading during which the handling of the animals and vehicle conditions could be verified in line with requirements (Article 15(1) and Annex I, Chapters III and VI of Reg. 1/2005). However, it does not require the performance of checks at time of loading. In this regard: 6 DGAL informed the audit team that checks at the moment of loading is something that is under study as there are difficulties with having official staff available to perform them; For 2016 two of the districts met had not planned nor performed any such check and were the departure point for a total of 69 export consignments; Another district, departure point for 55 export consignments, programmed and performed one check at time of loading in 2016. This check was of a multi-vehicle consignment and reported compliance of vehicles and of handling of the animals but detected that the journey time that had been indicated by the organiser in the journey plan was underestimated. This occurred because after loading the first vehicle the driver waited for the other vehicles to also load, in order to travel together, and these loading and waiting times had not been included in the journey planning. The consignment left with the journey plans, submitted to and already stamped by the district, unchanged, contrary to the requirements of Art. 14(1)(b) of Reg. 1/2005. The district sent a formal notification to the transporter informing them about the results of the check and indicating corrective action required for future journeys.

The absence of checks at the moment of loading prevent the competent authorities from having adequate confirmation of the handling at loading and maintenance conditions of vehicles leaving from France for export. 5.3 RESTING Legal requirements Articles 14, 15 and Chapter V, Annex I of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005. Findings

Regarding retrospective checks to verify the travelling and resting times to provide water, feed and rest to the animals (Art. 15 of Reg. 1/2005): Two of the districts met informed the audit team that they had performed the required 5% minimum retrospective checks of journey logs but could not provide the corresponding records. The other district informed that because of lack of human resources it had been unable to carry out these checks in due time; The three districts stated that it was difficult to obtain the return of journey logs from the transporters and that up to 2016 no system was in place to attempt to ensure this return. For 2017 a system to obtain the journey logs was being designed and would be implemented; Two districts informed the audit team that when attempting in 2017 (in preparation for this audit) to obtain satellite navigation data and temperature registers for consignments exported to Turkey during 2016 almost none had been received. One district stated that it received one set of satellite navigation for a consignment but that the data provided was impossible to analyse; In 2016 one animal died during the journey in each of four consignments leaving from France for export. None of the districts from which the consignments originated had targeted these as journey logs to be investigated; Until October 2017 two of districts met had not yet implemented a system with identified criteria to select the journeys to be targeted for retrospective checks and the other district was in the initial stages of implementing such a system.

Although the procedures indicate the type and frequency of checks on planning of journeys and on returned journey logs they do not include any reference to checks of journeys' satellite navigation data. DGAL stated that the checks on satellite navigation data are planned to be included as part of the revision and update of the extensive 2011 procedure (see also paragraph 9).

The districts met had not implemented some requirements from DGAL procedures that had already been in place for between one to six years. Namely: Journey planning to be provided to district authorities two working days prior to the intended departure date (Annex II, (3)(b) of Reg. 1/2005); Checks on contingency plans (Articles 14(1) and 11(1)(b)(iv) of Reg. 1/2005); Proof of reservations at control post(s) to unload and rest the animals; 9 Put in place a system to ensure transporters return the completed journey logs (Annex II, (8) of Reg. 1/2005); Perform at least 5% retrospective checks of journey logs and keep the corresponding records.

Although the procedures and instructions provide the necessary support for effective checks on journey planning, the fact that districts do not implement some of the requirements mean that the approved planning to provide feed, water and rest to the animals is not assured. For exports going into Turkey by road, this absence of assurance together with the lack of awareness of the operating hours of the Turkish border controls and of the time needed to go through at district level, create a risk for unnecessary suffering to animals.
The system of retrospective checks does not provide satisfactory assurances for detecting if journey times were realistic and for its compliance with legal requirements.

Associated finding: 25, 26 and 27.

citations.text: The districts met had not implemented some requirements from DGAL procedures that had already been in place for between one to six years. Namely: Journey planning to be provided to district authorities two working days prior to the intended departure date (Annex II, (3)(b) of Reg. 1/2005); Checks on contingency plans (Articles 14(1) and 11(1)(b)(iv) of Reg. 1/2005); Proof of reservations at control post(s) to unload and rest the animals; 9 Put in place a system to ensure transporters return the completed journey logs (Annex II, (8) of Reg. 1/2005); Perform at least 5% retrospective checks of journey logs and keep the corresponding records.

Most of these shortcomings had not been detected by the system for supervision and verification of official controls. However, when preparing for this audit the districts met reviewed their performances in this area detected some of them and are taking steps to address these (see also the 2nd and 5th bullets of paragraph 23).
France had a higher percentage of cattle consignments exported in 2016 with animal welfare non-compliances (12.6%) than the EU average for that same period (8.3%). Conclusions on resting

The fact that different levels of supervision fail to detect existing shortcomings and the higher percentage of animal welfare non-compliances in consignments leaving from France indicate that the current system of supervision is not achieving its objectives of ensuring correct performance of tasks in the area of animal welfare during transport. 5.4 UNEXPECTED DELAYS AT THE BORDER Legal requirements Article 11 of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005. Articles 3, 4, and 5 of Directive 96/93/EC. Findings

recommendations.text: To ensure that contingency plans of transporters exporting live animals are checked and include measures to meet the animals' needs for bedding, feed and water in the eventuality of unexpected long delays at the EU border as required by Articles 3(a) and 11(1)(b)(iv) of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005. Recommendation based on conclusion 37.

citations.text: As the prescribed check on contingency plans are not properly implemented, there is no assurance that in the eventuality of unexpected long delays at the border the needs of animals blocked at the border can be met, and that these animals are not caused unnecessary suffering. 11 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS The measures in place do not provide satisfactory assurances that exports of live animals operate smoothly and that these journeys are correctly planned and carried out in line with animal welfare requirements to prevent causing unnecessary pain, suffering or injury to the animals. The existing procedures and instructions do provide the necessary support for effective checks on journey planning. Nevertheless, the districts' lack of implementation of some requirements means that the approved planning to provide feed, water and rest is not guaranteed to prevent unnecessary suffering to animals during long distance transport by road. This is of particular relevance for exports to Turkey due to the districts' lack of awareness of the operating hours of the Turkish border controls and of the time needed to go through. In addition, the lack of implementation of checks on contingency plans means that there are inadequate assurances that in the eventuality of unexpected long delays at the border the needs of animals blocked at the border can be met, and that these animals are not caused unnecessary suffering. Given that currently there are no exports by road from France to Turkey the impact of both the above-mentioned non-implementations on the welfare of animals is restricted to exports to other destinations, which in general have much faster and less problematic border checks. The system of retrospective checks is not being fully implemented, and contains a few gaps, and therefore does not provide satisfactory assurances that the verifications made will detect if journey times were realistic and if journeys complied with the Regulation 1/2005 and prevented unnecessary suffering to the animals. The current system of supervision on the correct performance of tasks is not achieving its objectives in the area of animal welfare during transport. This was demonstrated by the fact that the shortcomings noted were not detected by that supervision, and also by the high percentage of animal welfare non-compliances in consignments leaving from France as compared with the EU average. The system in place to issue animal health certificates prevents problems occurring with certificates, which could cause rejections or delays in entering non-EU countries, thereby helping live animal exports to operate smoothly. 7 CLOSING MEETING A closing meeting was held on 13 October 2017 with representatives of the competent authorities, at which the main findings and preliminary conclusions of the audit were presented by the audit team. 12 8 RECOMMENDATIONS The competent authorities are invited to provide, within 25 working days of receipt of the report, an action plan containing details of the actions taken and planned, including deadlines for their completion, aimed at addressing the recommendations set out below: No. Recommendation 1. Recommendation based on conclusion 28. Associated findings: 21, 25. 2. Recommendation based on conclusions 18, 28 and 29. Associated findings: 14, 23, 24, and 25. 3. To ensure that verification of the effectiveness of district level work in the area of anima

recommendations.text: Ensure that monitoring of Xylella fastidiosa in the buffer zones is implemented in line with Article 6(7) of Decision 2015/789/EU in particular that it is based on a grid split into 100m x 100m squares. The recommendation is based on conclusion No. 55. Associated findings No. 43, 45, 46, 47, 48 and 49.

citations.text: In 2016, the surveillance in the BZs started in August and the activity was carried out according to a protocol, developed by DGAL. The audit team noted that: There were over 300 BZs in Corsica, the majority of which consisted of natural scrubland and/or mountainous area with difficult access; The 20 BZs in PACA were mainly situated in urban areas with numerous private properties and not always easily accessible. Taking into consideration these and the available resources France applied a specific system in 2016 as follows. In PACA a survey grid of 100m x 100m was used in the inner 1 km part of each BZ, while in the 1km ­ 10km part a grid of 1km x 1km was applied; In Corsica a grid of 1km x 1km was used in the BZs situated in the northern part of the island (17 outbreaks). In South Corsica, until August 2016, the 324, largely overlapping BZs were surveyed based on a 5km x 5km grid. Thereafter, in the light of a possible establishment of a BZ between a future eradication zone in the northern part of the island and a containment zone in the southern part, the CA started surveying the outer parts of the BZs in South Corsica, based on a 1km x 1km grid.

In each grid square, two observation points were designated. The surveillance team checked the vicinity of the observation point for the presence of specified plants and took samples in the case of the presence of symptoms or any suspicion. The plants were sampled individually, composite samples were not collected. The CA informed the audit team that for better coverage of the areas, in the future new observation points will be selected each year. The audit team noted that in 2016 only a proportion of the grids, identified by France were actually checked. The proportion varied in the different BZ. The audit team observed surveys, carried out by FREDON agents in the BZs of PACA and Corsica and noted that the agents: Were well trained and experienced and were fully familiar with the details of the DGAL and FREDON inspection and sampling protocols; Possessed all necessary equipment for the visual surveys and sampling, including the recording of the outcome; Located the pre-defined observation points with the help of maps, aerial photos and GPS devices. As the observation points were selected based on spatial information, it was necessary to adjust them to the actual conditions (visibility, accessibility) of the site; Did a 360o visual survey at each point and searched for specified plants with visible or suspicious symptoms and tried to link these to the possible bacterial infection (as opposed to mechanical damage); It was also noted that only plants in the close vicinity (maximum 50m) of the observation point were checked. The survey protocol did not require agents to search a larger area and in many cases, access was very difficult; Individual samples were taken from symptomatic and suspicious specified plants. These were packed, duly labelled, transferred, in cool boxes and sent to the laboratory by express mail, ensuring the arrival the following day. The exact GPS position of each individual plant was recorded and the plants were clearly labelled for future identification in the field; After each inspection, a standard report was prepared using a computer tablet. After each working day these reports were uploaded to the central database.

The audit team noted that the use of grids larger than 100m x 100m, in combination with the applied survey method, which does not include entering private gardens and natural areas difficult to access, was not suitable to obtain comprehensive information about the infection status of the area. The visual checks in the randomly selected observation points provided information only about a small part of a grid which was not representative and the vast majority of the area remained unchecked. Such surveillance is also not in compliance with the requirements of the Decision, which requires, in the BZ, that the surveyed area be based on a grid split into 100m x 100m squares.

Recommendation No 1 of the 2016 audit report recommends France to ensure that the monitoring in the BZs is implemented in line with Article 6(7) of the Decision. This recommendation has not been addressed. 15

Recommendation No 4 of the 2016 audit report recommended France to ensure that surveys in the DAs take into consideration the presence and biology of the specified plants, and in particular the accessibility of hosts in private gardens and in remote areas. The audit team noted that due to climatic conditions and composition of the flora in the BZs in Corsica and PACA, the survey period of August-December 2016 was suitable as practically all host plants of Xf subspecies multiplex and the vast majority of specified plants could be visually checked (being in full vegetation with leaves) and duly sampled. However, as it is explained above (see paragraph no. 45) there were no attempts made to access host plants in private gardens and remote areas. Therefore, recommendation No. 4 of the 2016 audit report remains only partly addressed. 5.2.3 Surveys in the Infected Zones

The survey system, applied by France in the BZs is not in line with the provisions of the Decision. It does not provide the required level of meticulousness and territorial coverage and therefore, the information collected about the infection status of BZs is inadequate and unreliable.

recommendations.text: Ensure that eradication measures are implemented following the confirmation of the presence of Xylella fastidiosa in line with Article 6(2) and 6(3) of Decision 2015/789/EU in particular concerning the immediate removal of all host plants found to be susceptible in the EU territory of the subspecies of the pathogen identified in the particular infected zones. The recommendation is based on conclusions No.73 and 74. Associated findings No. 60, 61, 62, 63, 64, 66, 67 and 68.

citations.text: The outbreak in Menton was treated as a special case for the DRAAF/SRAL for the following reasons: The first laboratory tests in 2015 identified the presence of Xf subspecies multiplex on some Polygala myrtifolia plants, which were removed and destroyed already in 2015; EU host plants of the subspecies multiplex known at that time, were also removed and destroyed; During the first laboratory test, a PCR method (Hernandez-Martinez et al., 2006) was used which could not detect Xf subspecies pauca; After the recent version of the EPPO Xf diagnostic protocol was published, the DNA extract of the positive sample was re-tested with a different method (Pooler and Hartung, 1995) and found positive for Xf subspecies pauca; After the new test result was confirmed, DRAAF/SRAL inspectors revisited the IZ and carried out an inventory to identify the presence of plants, which were hosts of the subspecies pauca in the EU; The Xf subspecies pauca hosts and other specified plants in the close vicinity of the Polygala myrtifolia plants, removed in 2015 were sampled and tested again, individually. All results were negative; The newly identified hosts (Dodonaea viscosa, Laurus nobilis, Nerium oleander, Olea europea, Westringia fruticosa) were then marked, treated and removed in line with the provisions of the Decision; 18 However, the CA decided against the removal of sixteen 300-400 year old Olea europea (olive) trees. These plants did not show any symptoms and repeatedly tested negative during 2016-2017; DRAAF/SRAL decided to protect these olive trees with insect-proof nets. The plants were heavily pruned and the upper part of the trunk and remaining branches of the canopy were wrapped with these net. The audit team noted that protecting the trees with netting is not in line with the Decision and its efficacy against the further spread of the pest is not yet established.

The audit team noted that eradication measures in PACA, in particular the removal of host plants in the IZ, were generally in line with the provisions of the Decision, except for: Delays in removal and destruction of the host plants due to problems with identification and notification of the land owners and The non-removal of olive trees in the Menton IZ.

In Corsica, eradication measures, fully in line with provisions of the Decision were implemented only in the case of the first outbreaks, identified in 2015. The audit team noted: The number of outbreaks is very high; 237 were identified until February 2016 and a further 104 in the period February 2016 ­ March 2017; The number of host species, found positive increased rapidly and at the time of the audit there were 36; A part of the IZs are located in areas with difficult access where the removal of any plant is sometimes very difficult; A considerable part of the IZs cover natural land or abandoned agricultural land, where, after the removal of the hosts, no agricultural activity is expected. Therefore the CA has concerns regarding possible soil erosion. The CA also fears that the areas where the host plants were removed will be recolonised by invasive plants species from the surrounding areas, which may change the flora substantially.

Due to the above mentioned concerns and due to the limited accessibility, in newly established IZs in Corsica removal and destruction of all host plants is not carried out. The following plants present in the IZ are removed and destroyed: Until May 2016: plants which were tested positive or showing symptoms and all the Polygala myrtifolia plants, regardless of their health; Since May 2016 in addition all plants of the species, which tested positive, are also eradicated.

The audit team was informed by the CA that although numerous new host species were identified in Corsica in 2016, only about 25% of the IZs, established in 2015 and about 75 % of the IZs established in 2016 were revisited. During these inspections over 1,000 samples were taken and about 0.6% of these tested positive.
The CA stated that the immediate removal and destruction of the host plants in Corsica was not possible due to the large number of outbreaks, in particular in South Corsica. 19
On the basis of the above the audit team noted that in Corsica, the eradication measures were not in line with the Decision and therefore there is a continuous presence of the bacterium in the IZs.

The audit team furthermore noted that although there is no comprehensive information available about the range of vectors and their transmission potential, related to Xf subspecies multiplex, results of insect collections showed the continuous and high presence of cicadas in the IZs of Corsica.

The eradication measures in PACA are largely in line with the provisions of the Decision. However, some delays in removal of the host plants in certain IZs and the non-removal of olive trees in the case of the Menton IZ compromise their efficiency. The use of protective netting is not in line with the Decision.

The eradication measures in Corsica are not in line with the provisions of the Decision and do not ensure the elimination of the bacterium from the IZs. 20 5.4 Movement control of specified plants Legal requirements Article 6(8) (road signs), Article 9 (movement ban), Article 10 (traceability) and Article 11 (official checks) of the Decision. recommendations.text: Ensure that road signs are set up indicating the delimitation of the demarcated areas as required by Article 6(8) of Decision 2015/789/EU. The recommendation is based on conclusion No. 89. Associated finding No. 75.

citations.text: The CA informed the audit team that the DAs, established after the first outbreaks, detected in 2015 or early 2016 in Corsica were signposted. However, after the number of DAs increased exponentially, it was technically not possible to indicate the border of each. In PACA there are no road signs either. The majority of the DAs are located in highly populated urban areas, with numerous exiting roads. Therefore the CA informed the audit team that they considered that it was not feasible to apply road signs. The audit team noted that the current practice is not in line with Article 6(8) of the Decision. Notwithstanding the difficulty in applying road signs in urban areas the audit team is of opinion that the compliance with this provision of the Decision is necessary to facilitate controls of specified plants moving out of the DAs. 5.4.2 Movement ban of specified plants

Contrary to the requirements of the Decision, there are no road signs at the borders of the DAs. This reduces the level of general public awareness about the DAs and increases the risk of unintentional movement of specified plants out of them.

recommendations.text: Ensure that the movement out of the demarcated areas of specified plants which have been grown for at least part of their life in that area, is only allowed when the plants have been grown in a site which meets all the requirements of Article 9(2) of Decision 2015/789/EU. citations.text: The audit team visited several nurseries, both producers and traders with outlets in the BZs and noted that: The majority of the sales take place during the spring (February-May) and autumn (October-December) period. The retailers receive their stocks in containers or pots generally from outside the DAs. The plants are usually sold quickly, spending no more than 3-4 weeks at the premises. However, the ligneous plants could be kept for longer periods if not sold; The producer nurseries apply regular insect controls, however the retailers generally do not use any pesticides due to environmental and health protection reasons. The premises are not isolated and are usually surrounded by areas, where the insect vector of the bacterium is present; The audit team found evidence that one production nursery sells specified plants (young vegetable and herbaceous ornamental plants) outside the DA to professional clients and the CA did not apply any measure to stop this; The nurseries are generally cooperating with the CAs; 21 The nurseries are strongly concerned with the current economic impact of the control measures and in particular about the future as the possible extension of the Xf host range may affect other important plant species they produce or trade with; The nurseries often question the necessity of the measures and request the application of tailor-made actions based on the assessment of the risk related to their activity in the BZ; The nurseries are generally aware of the requirements; in particular they are familiar with the list of specified plants. They keep appropriate records on their production, incoming stocks and sales to professional clients regarding specified plants. The records include the name and address of the supplier/client, date, plant species, varieties and quantities; In the shops, usually at the cash registers, posters or information sheets are available about the specific measures introduced in the DAs, including the list of specified plants and maps showing the DA border; A MAAF note requires nurseries in the DAs to keep records of their private clients. The nurseries usually keep records of the sales of specified plants to private clients, but it is not integrated into their IT system Each nursery and shop visited asked for the postal code of the private client. In addition in Corsica the name and phone number of the buyer and destination address of the plants are requested; Due to legal reasons (personal rights, data protection) the information is only collected if the client agrees to provide it. The nurseries are not entitled to refuse the sales, if the postal code is outside the DA. It cannot be controlled either, whether the private clients actually plant or use the plants within or outside the DA.

The audit team found that the current system of official controls, as described in paragraphs 76-78, in particular in PACA, allows for the possibility that specified plants, which have been grown for at least part of their life in a DAs, move out of those areas, mainly through sale to private clients. Thus the provisions of Article 9(1) of the Decision are not implemented. 5.4.3 Application of the derogation provided by Article 9(2) of the Decision

The current system of movement controls cannot guarantee that specified plants, which have spent a part of their life in the DAs, do not leave those areas. Therefore a risk exists for Xf spread with human assistance. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS A centralised institutional structure with clear division of responsibilities is in place to deal with Xf outbreaks. The national contingency plan and the national action plan for controlling the disease provide a good basis for the implementation of the necessary measures. Despite of significant efforts, resources are not sufficient for the proper implementation of the Decision. A good laboratory network with appropriate testing facilities and quality control regimes ensures the proper analysis of the samples. However, due to weaknesses in performance of some laboratories, the 2016 test results could contain false-negatives. The ongoing lack of capability to identify the subspecies in each relevant case may compromise the application of the eradication measures laid down in the Decision. During the 2016 Xf surveys outside the DAs, a broad range of measures and information sources was used and the inspection sites were selected based on the identified risk(s). The survey system in the BZs is not in line with the provisions of the Decision. It does not provide the required level of meticulousness and territorial coverage and therefore, the information collected is inadequate and unreliable for the proper establishment of the infection status. The surveys in the IZs are only partly in line with the Decision and therefore they do not provide a fully comprehensive basis for the implementation of the eradication measures. France applies certain but not all eradication measures laid down in the Decision. However, they are only partly in line with the Decision in PACA, and largely not in line in Corsica. The current measures do not provide the required level of guarantees necessary to eradicate the pathogen. Although France applies certain movement controls, the current system cannot guarantee that specified plants, which have spent a part of their life in the buffer zones do not leave those areas. There is a significant risk of spread of Xf from the currently infected areas, especially from those areas in PACA. Eradication is perceived as impossible in the southern part of Corsica. However, in the northern part of the island and in PACA, eradication may still be possible, if the relevant provisions of the Decision are fully implemented. 24 7 CLOSING MEETING A closing meeting was held on 31 March 2017 at the headquarters of DGAL in Paris, during which the main findings and preliminary conclusions of the audit team were presented. The CA accepted the information provided by the audit team. During the closing meeting the CA generally accepted the findings and preliminary conclusions of the audit team concerning the non-compliances. However, they emphasised that the risk of spread is correctly managed. As proof they mentioned that their wide-ranging, risk based surveys in the other parts of France did not find any positive case. The CA recommended that the audit report should make practical, implementable recommendations, which are proportionate to the identified risk. Furthermore, France is of the opinion that the Commission should propose an amendment of the Decision, which should take into consideration the specific conditions of the outbreaks in different MSs. 8 RECOMMENDATIONS The NPPO of France is recommended to: No. Recommendation 1. 2. Ensure that monitoring of Xylella fastidiosa in the buffer zones is implemented in line with Article 6(7) of Decision 2015/789/EU in particular 3. that it is based on a grid split into 100m x 100m squares. 4. The recommendation is based on conclusion No. 55. Associated findings No. 43, 45, 46, 47, 48 and 49. 5. citations.text: There is a supervision system in place allowing different competent authorities involved in the implementation of surveillance and control programmes (including the AMR monitoring one) to monitor their progress. citations.text: Contrary to the requirements of point 2.3.2 of part A of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU, less than 170 of isolates from the SNCP were subject to AST in 2014 and 2016. citations.text: In contrast to the requirements laid down in point 2.3 of Decision 2013/652/EU, the collection of samples at the slaughterhouses was not representative enough due to the following: A lack of randomisation in the collection of samples. The work instructions drafted by DGAL for the years 2015-2017 stated that samples should preferably be taken on Mondays Tuesdays or Wednesdays. This is to allow the laboratories to complete their processing within the 5 working days of the week. In the slaughterhouses visited samples were mainly taken on Mondays and Tuesdays and in some cases only on Mondays. In addition, the batches to be sampled in the 6 slaughterhouse were not always chosen randomly. Different factors affected the choice of batch, such as the personnel available at the slaughterhouse or the size of the batch. The caecal samples gathered were not evenly distributed over each month of the year. Sampling started always either in February or March and finished occasionally in November. Furthermore, in some cases, samples were not taken in July or August due to staff taking leave over this period of time. According to officials met during the audit, the late start was mainly due to the drafting of the work instructions for a given year that were finalised late the previous year. recommendations.text: To put in place measures aimed at ensuring that planned official controls on operators along the chain of production of ABP and derived products are actually carried out in accordance with the planned arrangements, as required by Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Recommendation based on conclusion: 47 Associated finding: 31

citations.text: The implementation rate of the scheduled inspections of approved ABP operators was 62% in 2016 and 58% in 2017 (174 out of 298 scheduled controls was actually carried out). The competent authority explained this low implementation rate by the fact that there had been an increase in the request for approval of composting plants and biogas producers, due to a national programme in this sector, and therefore, 215 approval visits had to be carried out in 2017. As these approval visits have to be prioritised and are time-consuming, scheduled official controls often have to be postponed to the following year. As inspections of registered operators will have to be considered in the future planning, a further decline in the rate of implemented regular inspections is very likely to be expected (see also finding 15). 5.2.1 Hygiene requirements

The competent authority was unable to meet its planned targets for official controls in the ABP sector in 2016 and 2017 due to a spike in unscheduled approval visits and the limited time available to inspectors to carry out official controls. This indicates a weakness in the official control system given the resources available are insufficient to carry out the number of planned inspections and there is no built-in contingency to be able to absorb ad-hoc requests such as new establishment approvals. As official controls on registered operators will also have to be factored in from 2018 on, the implementation rate of inspections will almost certainly decrease further, weakening the system overall.

recommendations.text: To ensure that the commercial documents which accompany ABP and derived products during transport are issued in accordance with the requirements of Chapter III, Annex VIII of Regulation (EU) No 142/2011. Recommendation based on conclusion: 48 Associated finding: 35, 37, 39

citations.text: The audit team visited a storage plant which stored PAP on behalf of two processing plants. The establishment had been approved for the storage of PAP in big bags in 2016 and has never been inspected since. The audit team noted that the establishment has not been well maintained and at the time of the visit did not comply with legal requirements laid down in Section 1 of Chapter III, Annex IX to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011 anymore. The operator declared that they are currently planning a comprehensive refurbishment of the storage premises. Moreover, in addition to the storage of PAP in big bags for which it was approved, the establishment is storing also a liquid product (poultry fat) in tanks; however, this activity is not included in its approval document. The audit team reviewed several commercial documents for the consignments together with the inspector and found that several of them were incomplete and contained inaccuracies. 12

In general, checks on commercial documents accompanying consignments of derived products were regularly carried out during inspections and these checks were recorded in the relevant points of the checklist. The officials met were largely familiar with relevant requirements; however, some of them mentioned difficulties in assessing commercial documents as they were not familiar with the model for intra-EU trade. In France, for national trade, there is no specific form required, but any document is accepted which includes the relevant information, in line with point (4a), Chapter III, Annex VIII to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011. In all premises visited during the audit, the audit team checked a random sample of these documents and in most cases, these documents were not fully in line with the legal requirements (form, data missing such as approval/registration number, wrong place of loading, no indication of species etc.). Some of these non-compliances had already been spotted by inspectors during official controls, but the operators had not rectified these shortcomings (see finding 39). These shortcomings might also limit the ability of the competent authorities to ensure that certain ABP and PAP are eligible to be used in the production of feed for aquaculture.

The OF/SI manufacturer visited traded an amount of around 800 tonnes (3% of his production) in 2018 to other Member States, including consignments consisting of 100% PAP and/or MBM mix. Contrary to Article 48(3) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009, TRACES notifications relating to intra-EU trade were not made for these products. The competent authority stated that such notification is not required by the relevant internal instruction (see finding 21). The operator had not issued commercial documents for these consignments either, which had not been spotted during official controls. During an official control in 2017, the inspector had identified non-compliances as regards the accompanying commercial documents for the trade within France and had asked for an amendment, but the operator had yet to react up to the time of the audit. 13 5.2.3 Exports and imports of PAP

Routine official controls still need to be strengthened as they did not detect a number of shortcomings, in particular with regards to the issuing of commercial documents. Inaccuracies and information gaps in commercial documents used for domestic trade weaken the competent authority's ability to verify the traceability of certain ABP and PAP and to verify whether they are used in accordance with their intended purpose. The implementation of official controls in relation to hygiene requirements was in general satisfactory.

recommendations.text: To ensure that information about the arrival of consignments of processed animal protein is notified to the Member State of origin, by means of TRACES, as required by Article 48(3) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. Recommendation based on conclusion: 49 Associated finding: 21, 38

citations.text: In 2017, DGAL prepared two service notes (590 and 790) on the requirements of the national and intra-EU trade of ABPs and derived products, including PAP and MBM. The audit team reviewed the notes and determined that there is a detailed description of how the French competent authority has to notify the competent authority of origin via the Trade Control and Expert System (TRACES) about the arrival of the consignments as required by Article 48 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. In particular, note 590 is very detailed and includes also a comprehensive annex with a list of specific cases. However, OF/SI containing PAP and/or MBM are not listed as requiring notification. 8 This is not in line with the requirement of Article 48(3) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. Note 790 also provides for the possibility to delegate the required TRACES messages to the operator under certain conditions, where more than 30 consignments per year are dispatched or received. The competent authority has to verify annually a defined sample of TRACES notifications to see whether the operator is fulfilling the conditions for this derogation. This arrangement, however, has not had a notable impact on the rate of notifications of the arrival of PAP consignments (see finding 37).

The audit team noted that, although training and instructions had been provided (see findings 5, 7, 21), in the vast majority of cases arrivals of consignments of PAP were not confirmed by the French competent authorities to the competent authorities of the Member States of origin by means of TRACES, contrary to Article 48(3) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. In 2017, according to figures of the competent authorities, arrival of only 7.37% of such consignments was confirmed, and in 2018, 4.45%.

The audit team identified several shortcomings relating to TRACES notifications of intra-EU trade of PAP and OF/SI. For OF/SI, the competent authority had omitted to include a requirement for the operator to issue a TRACES notification, thereby undermining the traceability of the consignments. The percentage of PAP consignments arriving to France from other Member States which are notified back to the competent authorities in the Member State of origin is still wholly inadequate (approximately 4%), impacting on the fulfilment of traceability requirements in intra-EU trade.

recommendations.text: To ensure that the departure of consignments of organic fertilisers and soil improvers containing processed animal protein is notified in TRACES as required by Article 48(3) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. Recommendation based on conclusion: 49 Associated findings; 21, 39

citations.text: The audit team identified several shortcomings relating to TRACES notifications of intra-EU trade of PAP and OF/SI. For OF/SI, the competent authority had omitted to include a requirement for the operator to issue a TRACES notification, thereby undermining the traceability of the consignments. The percentage of PAP consignments arriving to France from other Member States which are notified back to the competent authorities in the Member State of origin is still wholly inadequate (approximately 4%), impacting on the fulfilment of traceability requirements in intra-EU trade.

recommendations.text: To ensure that the export of consignments of ruminant processed animal protein takes place in line with the requirements laid down in points 1(c) and (d), Section E, Chapter V, Annex IV to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001. Recommendation based on conclusion: 50 Associated findings: 40-44

citations.text: When, following the amendment of Regulation (EC) No 999/2001, exports of consignments of PAP derived from ruminants started in July 2017, the BIPs in France implemented the instruction communicated by SIVEP (see finding 22). In the BIP visited, the procedure for export checks established by the BIP included a verification of the arrival of the consignment in the port via an extract of the tracking application "AP+" including the seal number, which the operator has to provide as the BIP only has limited access to this application. In addition, a second extract from the application is required when the container has been loaded and the ship has left the port, which usually is sent seven days after the departure of the vessel. In order to record this check in TRACES, BIP staff entered the name of the official in charge and the port as the place of the official control in the control tab, but no box of a check carried out was ticked. 1

In this way, the BIP visited by the audit team verified the exit of all 24 consignments of PAP containing ruminant protein in 2017 and 43 in 2018 notified to them via TRACES, until the exit of consignments via this port stopped in February 2018. Since the SIVEP procedure TI 240 was issued only in March 2018 (see finding 23), no seal check was ever carried out at this BIP.

According to the evidence provided by the competent authority, in another BIP, through which the majority of consignments were exported from France, the information that the consignment actually left the EU was received in relation to around 99% of consignments in 2017 and around 94% in 2018 up to the time of the audit (for 2018: 1049 out of 1139 valid commercial documents). Around 70 consignments were still under verification at the time of the audit, as the departure of these containers had not yet been confirmed via the extract of the tracking application. Evidence was received after the audit that these 70 consignments had exited the EU. In some cases, the operators had created the commercial documents but not notified the BIP of the exit of the consignments. The BIP only verified the exit after the audit, in a few cases several months after the consignments had exited, despite the fact that the internal procedure sets a deadline of 15 days to react to non-confirmation of exit. The audit team was not provided with evidence of competent authority follow-up in cases where the operator had failed to notify the BIP of the arrival of the consignment at the port or indeed its exit from the EU. For 11 consignments, the BIP stated that they received a notification in TRACES much later than the creation of the commercial document, and in four cases, no notification was received at all, despite the creation of the commercial document in 1 In its response to the draft report, the competent authority noted that to demonstrate that the consignment of PAP has left the EU, an operator may be requested by a BIP, in addition to submitting information in the AP + software and in the commercial documents, to provide a delivery note for the consignment in question. Such requests may be ad hoc or systematic depending on the outcome of controls carried out in exporting establishments. If a BIP does not have access to the AP + software, it should put in place a procedure to verify the exit of the consignment from the territory of the EU. In such cases, the BIP may request that the operator provides a delivery note on a systematic basis. The competent authority stated that to date only the BIPs of Le Havre and Marseille-Fos are concerned by the export checks of PAP and these two border posts have access to the AP + software. 14 TRACES, which should have triggered such a notification. After the official instruction was issued by SIVEP in March 2018, around 2% of seal checks were carried out at this BIP, whereas 3% were required.

In another BIP however, no verification of whether the containers had exited, either following the procedure TI 240 (see finding 23) or their own procedure, was ever carried out; containers were neither tracked nor a seal check performed. This was the case for 270 consignments which were notified by operators via commercial documents in TRACES in 2017 and 653 consignments in 2018 up to the time of the audit. This is not in line with point 1(c), Section E, Chapter V, Annex IV of Regulation (EC) No 999/2001. Following the audit, the BIP confirmed the exit of the 653 consignments in 2018 by providing extracts of the tracking application "AP+". The audit team verified a random sample of these consignments in TRACES and found that in general, the basic data matched the data provided in the commercial documents although in several cases, the destination of the consignment according to the tracking was different (another non- EU country) from the destination stated in the commercial document.

All processing plants visited exported PAP to non-EU countries via the last mentioned port as the exiting point. The audit team noted that in several cases different points of exit were selected in the corresponding box in TRACES (the BIP, but also the port as designated point of entry for phytosanitary controls). Neither the operator, nor the competent authority could provide evidence that the seals of these export consignments had been checked at any BIP, contrary to the requirements of point 1(c), Section E, Chapter V, Annex IV of Regulation (EC) No 999/2001. In one case, the operator had asked for a visit in 2017 in order to prepare for the export of some consignments. recommendations.text: The authorities should ensure that the procedures implemented for the approval of establishments of a food business operator follow adequately the requirements of Article 2(1)(c) of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004, that each establishment (unit) has a unique approval number, to allow a correct implementation of Article 31 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 and Article 6(2) of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004. Recommendation based on conclusions Nos 31 and 32. Associated findings Nos 28 and 29.

citations.text: In the first case, during the approval procedure, the authorities approved as a single establishment and assigned a unique approval number to a set of four individual facilities located adjacently or near to each other. During the visit the audit team identified two different units (buildings adjacent and with a direct communication between them being considered one unit) physically separated, with independent entrances, different operational staff and, in one of them, performing different operations. These two units are located in a public common area which cannot be considered as a unique area under the full control of the food business operator. The authorities informed the audit team that in this particular case the food business operator registered the activity and the sites (geographically very close) under the same business registration and Siret number. Because the approval procedure is bound to the registration of the business activity and to the Siret number, the authorities had no other possibility than to grant a global approval for all units and assigning a unique approval number.

Therefore, the approval procedure implemented by the French authorities allows the existence of exceptional cases in which Article 2(1)(c) of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004 is not respected. As a result the requirements of Article 31 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 and Article 6(1) to (3) of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004 are not met.

In most of the cases, the approval procedures implemented, which commence after food business operators are registered with the National Institute of Statistics and Economic Studies (Siret number), are fit for purpose and in line with the EU rules.

However, there are exceptional circumstances where different units of a same business operator can have the same unique approval number. This is not in line with the requirements of Article 2(1)(c) of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004 which leads to the requirements of Article 31 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 and Article 6(2) of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004 not being met. 5.3 OFFICIAL CONTROLS 5.3.1 Official control of the production chain Legal requirements Article 17(2) of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002, Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 854/2004, Chapter I of Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 854/2004, Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. The audit team visited two freezer vessels outside metropolitan France and noted that they had been inspected by the relevant departments in accordance with the set procedures, although the minimum frequency of once every two years has not been followed.

The audit team visited eight processing establishments in five French departments and the authorities of those departments provided detailed information concerning the inspections of the approved establishments. During the visits the audit team noted that, with regard to the DGAL controls, the defined inspection frequencies (based on the risk category) were not respected in two out of six establishments (the remaining two establishments have been recently approved). These two establishments were located in two different departments. The audit team also noted that the frequencies for the inspections within the scope of DGCCRF were respected in the establishments visited.

The authorities of the two departments where the frequencies were not respected informed the audit team that another establishment also had not been inspected within the set frequencies. They attributed this to staff shortage (sick leave and transfer of staff), additional tasks acquired that were not initially foreseen (new approval, follow- ups, investigations of alerts) and increased export certification tasks.

The official control system in place covers completely the production chain of tuna fishery products and is globally implemented as planned. However, the audit team noted instances where the defined procedures were not adhered to, e.g. inspection frequencies for establishments on land and freezer vessels, and completion of the inspection within the defined timeframe.

Recommendation based on conclusion No 65. Associated findings Nos 59 and 60.

citations.text: However, in one establishment the audit team noted that the competent authorities approved a freezing process that is not in accordance with the EU requirements. The audit team noted that a part of a cold storage room had been dedicated to freeze fishery products and the duration of the freezing process was set at 72 hours. The audit team checked the relevant production records and noted that, at the start of the freezing process the products were at 2°C, after 48 hours were at -11.5°C and after 72 hours were at -18°C.

The competent authorities informed the audit team that this type of freezing, "static freezing", is allowed in France and is documented in the Technical Instruction DGAL/SDSSA/2015-807 of 12/11/2015 and provided the audit team with a copy. The audit team informed the French authorities that the practice and the instruction do not respect the EU rules, namely the requirements of Chapter I(I)(C)(1) of Section VIII of Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 853/2004.

In general the operations carried out by the operators were broadly in line with the EU rules with the exception of the freezing process in one establishment on land ("static freezing") and in one freezer vessel (double step freezing). citations.text: The plans mentioned above generally cover the requirements of Regulation (EC) No 854/2004 in relation to environmental contaminants and parasites. However, they do not include testing of relevant fishery products for tin. Additionally, sampling for histamine carried out for product in the internal market, which only covers the retail level, is not implemented as required by Chapter II(C) of Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 854/2004 and by Chapter 1(1.26) of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 ­ random testing, which if it is carried out outside retail would require nine sample units.

In 2017 fishery products were sampled (one sample unit and usually at retail level) to determine the levels of additives and in 2018 two specific tasks targeting tuna were executed. One (TN 273 KA) focused on the use of vegetable extracts and the other (TN 273 KH) on tuna loins (chilled/fresh). According to the authorities 64 samples were taken in tuna loins and 24 of these showed abnormal results for ascorbic acid (22 samples with values ranging 351 mg/kg to 3 500 mg/kg) and nitrates/nitrites (two confirmed cases with nitrosylated pigments). Non-conform results for histamine were not detected. Following the non-compliant results the authorities issued warning letters and, in some cases, administrative sanctions.

However, those controls are not fully in line with Chapter II(C) of Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 854/2004 and Chapter 1(1.26) of Annex I to Regulation (EC) no 2073/2005 because samples are only taken at retail level (not random).
