recommendations.text: To ensure that the official control staff receive the necessary additional training and support, in line with the provisions of Article 6(b) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, for carrying out their control duties in establishments producing RTE food in relation to the different applicable areas of the legislation, in accordance to their individual needs. Recommendation based on conclusion: 20, 31, 100 Associated findings: 11, 13, 14, 25 to 28, 58 to 69 and 88 to 93

citations.text: Both administrations have systems to ensure officials have access to training, amongst other, on relevant RTE topics. a. DGAL training includes food technology, inspection of food safety management systems, HACCP based procedures, microbiological criteria, alerts and outbreaks management and auditing. In this regard the audit team noted that while the training for most of the above technical topics was delivered to a large number of officials, this was not the case for audit training, although national control procedures require local CAs to carry out audits or to use auditing techniques routinely in their controls in RTE producing establishments. b. DGCCRF training includes Hygiene Package provisions, HACCP and alert management. According to the local officials, HACCP is covered to a limited extent in the induction training provided. In recent years more HACCP training started to be offered by DGCCRF and 35 of the 543 officials involved in the official controls have participated to it. No DGCCRF staff in the DD(CS)PP visited by the audit team participated to it. Training on microbiological criteria/Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 or specific to RTE sector is not available to DGCCRF officials. This does not support them in the related official controls (see paragraphs 58 to 61, 63, 68 and 69). 5 In their comments to the draft report the CA noted that DGCCRF is unsure what constitutes `high risk' and, in the absence of a definition, believes that there is no need to differentiate between `ready-to-eat food' and `high-risk ready-to-eat food'. 7

Both DGAL and DGCCRF staff have access to the "Better Training for Safer Food" (BTSF) initiative and the "resource persons" met participated in BTSF sessions. The official control staff met was in general experienced and knowledgeable for their work. Some support/training needs were identified during the audit, mainly in relation to: a. CAs' assessments and audits of good hygiene practices and HACCP, grading of non-compliances and enforcement and follow-up action (see paragraphs 11, 58-62 and 88 - 93). b. approval of establishments and keeping it under review (see paragraphs 25 to 28) linked mainly to the staff understanding of the rules. c. CA's controls over sampling and testing procedures linked to a lack of understanding of some of the applicable requirements (see paragraphs 11b, 63 to 69).

This suggests that the official control staff is not adequately kept up-to date in their area of competence as required by Article 6(b) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 for the areas highlighted above. The audit team did not note any problems related to facilities and equipment for the performance of official controls.

The challenges identified, mainly in relation to aspects of training, may have an impact on the controls over the production of RTE food, if not adequately addressed. 4.3 REGISTRATION/APPROVAL OF FBOS Legal requirements Article 6 of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004, Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004, Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 854/2004 and Article 31 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Findings

DGAL's had recently updated the approval procedures. The general inspection handbook instructs inspectors to check that the activities carried out by the establishment correspond to those covered by the approval. The FBOs visited by the audit team were in most cases approved for the activities they carried out. However, the audit team noted in four of the six approved establishments visited instances on non-compliance with the provisions of Article 31(2) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 and/or the national procedures explained by the CCA as local staff's apparent lack of awareness of the rules.

The comprehensive approval procedure supports official control staff in their work and several elements of it are implemented satisfactorily. Nevertheless, staff's lack of correct understanding of certain provisions thereof as well as the less strict national rules do not ensure that compliance with the EU legislation is routinely achieved. 4.4 OFFICIAL CONTROLS OF FBOS PRODUCING RTE FOODS 4.4.1 Organisation and implementation of Official Controls Legal requirements Article 17 of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002, Articles 3, 4(2)c, 8, 9, 10, 11 and 12 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, Article 5 of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004, Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 854/2004, Articles 1 and 5 of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 Findings 4.4.1.1 Risk based official controls 11

The differences in the development of the control systems for the different sectors suggest a missed opportunity for sharing good practices and exploiting synergies within and between DGCCRF and DGAL with a view to providing comparable support for staff carrying out controls in establishments with similar risks, further strengthening the control systems and their consistencies as well as ensuring a uniform control approach towards all FBOs. 4.4.3 Challenges encountered by the CA in the organisation and performance of controls over the production of RTE foods

recommendations.text: To finalise the review of the system for organising risk based official controls in establishments producing RTE food and adopt the required provisions that adequately reflect the risks associated with the food and the use of the food as required by Article

(1)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Recommendation based on conclusions: 30, 95 Associated findings:21 to 24, 32 to 39 3. To bring the current national measures and control procedures in place in line with the EU requirements in particular as regards: - FBOs' demonstration of compliance with the food safety criteria Listeria monocytogenes as required by Article 3(1)(b) of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005; - FBOs' testing for Staphylococcal enterotoxins in all cases required by Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005; - the derogation from the freezing treatment of farmed fishery products as required by Regulation (EC) No 853/2004, Annex III, Section VIII, Chapter III, Point D3(d). - the approval of establishments to ensure compliance with the definition of establishment in Article 2(1)(c) Regulation (EC) No 852/2004, Recommendation based on conclusion: 31, 95 Associated findings: 27, 28, 47 to 50, 62

citations.text: All FBOs are required to register with the Business Formalities Centres to enable the company to be created and be assigned a SIREN (business) number and a SIRET6 number. The FBO declares the main activity performed in accordance with the French Administrative Nomenclature (NAF) codes drawn up by the National Institute of Statistics and Economic Studies (INSEE). The Business Formalities Centres are obliged 6 In their comments to the draft report, the CAs noted that a SIRET number is assigned to any primary or secondary establishment within the meaning of Article R123-40 of the Commercial Code, i.e. `any permanent establishment, distinct from the registered office or principal establishment and headed by the person required to be registered, an official or a person with the power to enter into legal relationships with third parties'. 9 to inform INSEE of any business creation, modification or cessation (Decree of 18 March 1981). The DGAL and DGCCRF databases are automatically updated through a link to this INSEE data.

Both CAs have procedures in place for registration of RTE producing establishments and in the case of DGAL also for approval. However, the registration system does not favour the correct identification of production activities, including ready-to-eat, for all types of establishments. This has an impact in the DGCCRF's ability to organise the related risk based official controls.

Each CA has put in place a system of routine risk based official controls over production of RTE foods, supported by comprehensive procedures and covering relevant aspects of the legislation. The procedures for organisation of controls are currently under review for further fine-tuning the risk determination for the RTE sector. While some of the national provisions and procedures provide clarification for aspects that go beyond the EU requirements, other are less strict and if applied as such may potentially provide a lower level of safety than the EU requirements, in particular as regards Listeria, Coagulase-positive Staphylococci and controls for parasites in fishery products.

recommendations.text: To strengthen, in particular in establishments producing composite products and establishments producing food involved in alerts, the CAs assessments of good hygiene practices and HACCP based procedures required by Article 10(2)(d) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 and the audits required by Article 4(3)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 854/2004, in particular when assessing compliance with Articles 4 and 5 of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004, in order to ensure that the measures required from FBOs are able to adequately address the potential for cross-contamination and the introduction of hazards. Recommendation based on conclusions: 6, 19, 96, 97, 100 Associated findings: 2b, 3, 4, 11a, 13a, 14, 17, 38, 41, 45, 58 to 61, 87 to 93

citations.text: In addition, there are different national rules addressed to CAs and FBOs that support a harmonised national approach for the RTE sector: a. National legislation applicable at retail, in particular for storage and transport temperatures for food of animal and non-animal origin. See also paragraphs 45, 46, 102 for additional support for the RTE sector and related controls available in ANSES opinions, guides, instructions and working procedures. The national federation for trade and distribution also adopted guidance on microbiological criteria applicable at retail. b. Industry guidance endorsed by the three administrations (DGAL, DGCCRF, DGS) which applies also to RTE meat products, dairy products and raw vegetables ready to be used have been issued and supports FBOs and CAs in their controls. This is not the case for the composite products sector or for raw products (e.g. tartare, carpaccio, sushi), highly popular according to ANSES (see last paragraph of chapter 3.1). Both FBOs and CAs met highlighted different challenges, in particular for the composite products sector (see paragraph 101). Support needs for the official controls in this sector were identified by the audit team (see paragraph 13, 14, 58 to 61) c. Pasteurisation of meat products is described in the industry guidance endorsed by DGAL and the related Fiche Technique of the Vademecum for DGAL official controls. Depending on the production method, type of meat products and validation outcome, a minimum core temperature of 55°C for more than 40 minutes may be efficient to destroy non-sporulated pathogen flora and reduce the total flora. The examples seen on the spot involved temperature of above 65°C for more than 50 minutes. d. Arrêté of 19 October 2006 on the use of processing aids in the production of foodstuffs allows washing with chlorine solution in a concentration of maximum 80 ppm, followed by rinsing, as decontamination method for fruits, vegetables and mushrooms ready to use under national rules. The same legal act allows the use of acetic acid solution with pH below 2.8, followed by rinsing, as processing aid for unprocessed trout and salmon to flocculate the surface mucus.

The lack of clarification on what constitutes RTE which takes account of national consumption habits and FBOs' approaches as well as the lack of guidance for the composite products RTE sector do not support the related official controls and uniformity thereof. 4.2 COMPETENT AUTHORITY Legal requirements Articles 4 and 6 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Findings
An array of sector specific support mechanisms and access to several technical training, aid the CAs in their controls on production of RTE food, but to lesser extent for composite products.

The controls on Hygiene Package requirements in establishments producing food of animal origin are well developed. This was noted to a lesser extent for establishments producing composite products in particular in the case of DGCCRF, with an unknown percentage of registered establishments not subject to such controls on a scheduled basis.

The controls cover satisfactorily a range of aspects of the Hygiene Package, with some areas for improvement in relation to FBO's measures for prevention of cross- contamination and sampling and testing procedures. The CAs' ability for detection of the 23 non-compliances and assessment of the impact thereof is sometimes hindered by the current system for targeting controls and the limited use of systematic reviews.

The differences in the development of the control systems for the different sectors suggest a missed opportunity for sharing good practices and exploiting synergies within and between DGCCRF and DGAL with a view to providing comparable support for staff carrying out controls in establishments with similar risks, further strengthening the control systems and their consistencies as well as ensuring a uniform control approach towards all FBOs. 4.4.3 Challenges encountered by the CA in the organisation and performance of controls over the production of RTE foods

citations.text: The official controls over FBOs compliance with the microbiological sampling and testing requirements of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 are limited. CAs are not 17 required to verify FBOs' sampling methods. In the case of alerts, CAs verify the testing method indicated in the laboratory test results. Nonetheless, official control decisions are taken on the basis of FBOs' test results. The CCA clarified that CAs have the option of taking official samples from time to time to provide clarification to the inspector, guide his/her work and determine the measures taken following the inspection.

The controls cover satisfactorily a range of aspects of the Hygiene Package, with some areas for improvement in relation to FBO's measures for prevention of cross- contamination and sampling and testing procedures. The CAs' ability for detection of the 23 non-compliances and assessment of the impact thereof is sometimes hindered by the current system for targeting controls and the limited use of systematic reviews.

recommendations.text: To ensure that the competent authority takes the required enforcement action when identifies non-compliances as required by Article 54 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, in particular in establishments producing food involved in alerts and for re-occurring deficiencies for which FBOs actions only address partially the non-compliance and do not adequately address the risk. Recommendation based on conclusions: 98 Associated findings: 52 to 56, 84 to 94

citations.text: The procedures also establish deadlines for finalising the controls, reporting and following-up of non-compliances. Within the current establishment rating system, these deadlines do not support swift FBO action to address non-compliances when such non 7 In their comments to draft report, the CCA noted that the threshold of 1 000 cfu/g was set instead of 10 000 cfu/g for the other products to be consumed cooked, in order to take into account the risk of minced or thinly sliced products being insufficiently cooked through. In some cases, products labelled as `to be cooked' have been considered `ready-to-eat', either because the instructions on the label were not specific enough for the consumer, or because, given eating habits, the product could be consumed without first being cooked or reheated. 15 compliances do not impact on the overall rating for the establishment.

The effectiveness of the control and enforcement system is also weakened by the fact that some long-standing deficiencies detected and classified by the CAs as medium or major ones are not adequately followed­up and enforced by the CAs to ensure the FBOs swiftly remedy the situation.

recommendations.text: To review the official sampling strategy for products of animal origin pre-packed by the manufacturer, intended to be subject to testing for Listeria and ensure it is not discriminatory as required by Article 3(4) and (6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Recommendation based on conclusions: 99 Associated findings: 75 to 80 29

citations.text: Between 2013 and 2017 DGAL took 2167 RTE samples. From 2013 to 2016 the sampled matrixes only included unpasteurised dairy products and sausages while in 19 2017 sliced pig meat products were targeted. During this period the testing focussed on Salmonella and Listeria testing (STEC in 2014). Sampling of RTE for microbiological criteria does not take place every year at production level. The non-compliance rates identified range from zero in 2017 for Listeria in sliced meat products to 2.25% in 2016 for Listeria in unpasteurised dairy.

Official sampling and testing of RTE food is in place. Official laboratories are accredited and subject to NRL coordination. The organisation of the official sampling for RTE food of animal origin prepacked by the producers, with a view to testing for Listeria, suggests a discriminatory approach focusing more on RTE food produced in other countries, including other MS.

recommendations.text: Ensure that decree No 15-580 of 30 April 2015 of the Prefect is brought in line with provisions of Article 19 of Decision (EU) 2015/789, in particular concerning the removal of restrictions and administrative requirements related to the movement of specified plants from the EU to the territory of Corsica. The recommendation is based on conclusion No. 29. Associated finding No. 6.

citations.text: In Corsica, Decree No 15-580 of 30 April 2015 of the Préfet (as amended), allowing import of specified plants from non-EU countries and entry from EU territory outside the DAs to Corsica only by professionals and only following a detailed request, is still in force. The competent authorities of Corsica do not authorise any entry of Xf host plants from infected EU Member States, such as Italy and from the Alicante Province of Spain to the island. The audit team noted that the restrictions implemented by the Decree of the Préfet are not in line with Article 19 of the Decision which requires Member States to repeal or amend measures they have adopted to protect themselves against the introduction and spread of Xf. 5.1.3 Service notes, work instructions

A centralised institutional structure with clear division of responsibilities is in place to deal with Xf outbreaks. National and regional legislation, DGAL service notes and work instructions ensure and facilitate the direct application of provision of the Decision. However, Decree No 15-580 of 30 April 2015 of the Préfet is not in line with Article 19 of the Decision as it implements additional protection measures and trade restrictions which are not justified by the existing plant health risk.

recommendations.text: Ensure that the annual monitoring of the presence of Xylella fastidiosa in the buffer zones is carried out in line with provisions of Article 6(7) of Decision (EU) 2015/789 in particular that it covers the territory of the buffer zones, that samples are taken from asymptomatic plants in the vicinity of symptomatic plants and that requirements of Article 3(1) of the same Decision are also observed. The recommendation is based on conclusion No. 62. Associated findings No. 48, 49, 51 and 52.

citations.text: In the PACA region, in the period April-October 2018, FREDON carried out monitoring in the circles of 5km radius around the established IZs according to the DGAL work instructions (see blue circles in Figure IV). In line with provisions of Article 6(7) of the Decision a grid split into 100m x 100m squares within a zone of a width of 1 km surrounding the IZs and a grid split into 1km x 1km squares within the 1-5 km part of the BZs was applied. However, no surveillance was carried out beyond 5km radius in the remaining territory of the 44 municipalities, declared as BZ (see chapter 5.3.1). Therefore the presence of Xf was not checked in some parts of the BZs, which is not in line with Article 6(7) of the Decision.

The audit team was informed that the monitoring protocol requires the pre-definition of two observation points in each grid square from which the presence of symptomatic specified plants needs to be checked visually. Each identified symptomatic specified plant must be sampled for laboratory tests.

The audit team observed a monitoring, carried out by FREDON in a BZ, and noted that the agents: Carried out the grid-based monitoring in line with DGAL work instructions; Were well trained and experienced and possessed all necessary equipment for the visual surveys and sampling; Selected two observation points in each square then located those points with the help of maps, aerial photos and a GPS device; Carried out a 360o visual check from each observation point, checked the vicinity for the presence of specified plants with visible or suspicious symptoms and took samples only from symptomatic plants; The exact GPS position of each sampled plant was recorded and the plants were labelled. The packing, labelling and mailing method ensured the full traceability and conservation of the samples; After each inspection, a standard report was prepared electronically, which was uploaded to the central database after the field inspection was finished.

The audit team noted that: The applied practice of visual checks from two observation points, in particular for the grids squares of 1km x 1km, and in the grids of 100m x 100m in urban/semi- urban areas with scattered vegetation and restricted view, does not ensure that specified plants present in the grid are visually inspected taking into account the available technical evidence. Consequently symptomatic specified plants could be overlooked and not sampled. This is not in line with Article 6(7) of the Decision; In the BZs laboratory samples are taken only from the symptomatic plants, while Article 6(7) of the Decision also requires sampling of asymptomatic plants in the vicinity of the symptomatic ones.

The 2018 annual monitoring in the BZs was partly in line with provisions of Article 6(7) of the Decision as certain parts of of the BZs were not checked and the applied system of two observation points does not ensure that specified plants present in each grid are visually inspected. Therefore symptomatic plants could be overlooked and not sampled. Consequently the monitoring cannot fully confirm the status of Xf in those areas.

audits.title: Animal welfare - tail-biting and tail-docking of pigs

recommendations.text: To finalise the provision to farmers and inspectors of clear compliance criteria so that farmers have a clear indication of what is required and inspectors can more effectively enforce the legal requirements of Council Directive 2008/120/EC and Council Directive 98/58/EC that are related to risk factors for tail biti based on conclusions 35, 36, 37, 39, 60, 63, 64 and 65. Associated findings 16, 17, 20, 47, 48, 49, 50, 51 55 and audit findings in Annex II.

citations.text: The relatively high levels of lesions detected during a survey in two slaughterhouses indicate serious animal welfare problems in a significant number of French farms and a need for an enforcement strategy aiming at improved compliance with minimum requirements as well as serious improvement measures to reduce the incidence of tail biting.

The sector has started to record evidence of tail/ear biting lesions. However, procedures for the assessment of lesions are incomplete. Farm risk assessment tools are still being developed and there is no robust framework in the Action Plan for improvement measures or when farms should transition to rearing pigs with intact tails. These last three components need to be put in place quickly in order to start making tangible progress to improve compliance with the Directive. In addition, the extended CA deadlines (end 2022 to 2024) mean that without a focus on shortening deadlines and sufficient priority, full compliance with legal requirements will not be reached within the next four years.

An error in the interpretation of legal requirements in official guidance and inspection checklists means that the legal requirement for all categories of pigs to have access to enrichment materials is not being enforced.
There are no specific programmes in France for animal welfare measures on pig farms currently financed or co-financed by the European Union Fund for Rural Development (EUFRD).

Official controls have not yet started to enforce compliance criteria for legislative requirements related to risks for tail biting though this is planned for 2020 once guidance is revised. Whilst the premises visited complied with the existing vademecum, they did not comply with existing legislative requirements on enrichment material and the requirements prohibiting routine tail docking.

Mistakes in the interpretation of legal requirements for enrichment material and interpretation of requirements on mutilations mean that animal welfare and cross compliance inspections massively underreport the high rates of non-compliance for these two items with serious implications for cross compliance payments.
The provision of water through liquid feeding systems does not ensure that all pigs over two weeks of age have permanent access to a sufficient quantity of fresh water.

It is unlikely that corridors can provide suitable accommodation for sick and injured pigs in most building and management scenarios. Blanket acceptance of the use of corridors by the CA without strict conditions and a case-by-case assessment intended to ensure that these areas are suitable for all the objectives specified in the relevant legislation is not in accordance with these legal requirements.

responses.response: conformité clairs sur chacun des points réglementaires relatifs à des facteurs de risque de la caudophagie. recommendations.text: To provide inspectors with instructions and guidance which enable them to enforce the provision on the prevention of tail biting and avoidance of routine tail docking, as laid down in the second paragraph of point 8 of Chapter I of Annex I of Council Directive 2008/120/EC, in particular: how they should assess the evidence of tail and ear lesions on farm; at what point farmers should start trialling batches of pigs with intact tails; what constitutes sufficient measures by farmers to change inadequate environmental conditions or management systems before resorting to tail docking of pigs. Recommendation based on conclusions 34, 35, 36, and 38. Associated findings 9, 23, 24, 27, 29, 31, 48, 49 and audit findings in Annex II.

citations.text: The central competent authority estimates that the incidence of tail docking in France is over 99%. This is routine tail docking. The CA does not yet enforce the legal requirements in Point 8 of Chapter I, Annex I, of the Pig Directive to take measures to prevent tail-biting and other vices by improving inadequate environmental conditions or management systems.

DGAL and INAPORC have funded a French version of the German SchwIP tail-biting intervention programme (Schwanzbeiß Interventions Programm) which will be available to veterinarians and technicians by end 2019. The programme is not intended for routine use on farms but to help identify risks for tail-biting in problematic farms. It is not clear how the tool will be utilised: by whom (5), and at what frequency, nor how farms are defined as "problematic" or by whom. The sector wish to collate data on the outcomes to gain an overview of the common problems/solutions found. Recording of ear/tail lesions on farm

The pig sector distributed in May 2019 a sheet for recording evidence of tail and ear lesions on farms which requires farmers to record incidence and severity of bites in one house for each category of pigs throughout the rearing period. It includes space to record any changes to environmental conditions on farm. Whilst this is progress, registering data from only one house in farms that have two or more houses would not provide an overview of the farm situation in relation to evidence of tail biting. This would not satisfy the requirement for evidence described in paragraph two of Point 8 of Chapter I, Annex I, of the Pig Directive. Monitoring sheets can be easily integrated into basic farm management procedures as every house already has a management/health monitoring sheet. This would give a representative picture of the situation on holdings, where biting problems may vary from location, or type of housing/ climate, over the whole premises within the different categories. Actions involving private veterinarians

There are CA proposals to fund health visits in 2022 to 2023 by veterinary practitioners to review implementation of training, risk factors and monitoring tools and by 2024 that individual farm plans will be used by the CA in the context of official controls. However, there are at present no proposals in the Action Plan for farmers to implement the legal requirement of paragraph 2 Point 8 of Chapter I of Annex I to the Pig Directive relating to improvement measures in a coherent and consistent way. Enforcement through official controls See section on official controls. Additional findings on the Action Plan

There are no intervention levels for tail biting defined to establish when farmers should/can start trials on keeping pigs with intact tails. It is notable that some Member States have already set intervention levels for when these should start. The only mention of rearing small groups of pigs with intact tails as "control groups" within existing premises is one sentence in the fiche for recording evidence of tail/ear biting which states: "If few bites have been observed for six months, have you thought of contacting your technician or veterinarian in order to set up a `whole tail' trial?". As there is no definition of what is "few bites" and no threshold has been set for any move to rearing pigs with intact tails, this will at present only be on a voluntary basis whereas the legal requirements of paragraph 2 Point 8 of Chapter I of Annex I to the Pig Directive clearly state that routine tail docking is prohibited. The staff working document accompanying Commission Recommendation (EU) 336/2016 also states in Point 9 that "When tail-biting has stopped, then some batches (1-2 litters) of undocked tails should be trialled ­ with a view to stopping the docking of tails."

There are no proposals for dealing with the trade in tail docked pigs, including from other Member States. Some Member States are working together to draft proposals to deal with this issue which will require close cooperation to ensure the provisions of the Directive are complied with.

DGAL has worked with stakeholders to implement an Action Plan on tail docking as part of the overall animal welfare strategy. It has taken actions to develop criteria for certain legal requirements that are related to tail biting risk factors on tail docking of pigs to enable inspectors and farmers to make a judgement on whether individual farms comply with EU requirements but these have not yet been implemented. Tail docking is still routinely carried out and the CA is not yet enforcing the corresponding legal requirements.

The relatively high levels of lesions detected during a survey in two slaughterhouses indicate serious animal welfare problems in a significant number of French farms and a need for an enforcement strategy aiming at improved compliance with minimum requirements as well as serious improvement measures to reduce the incidence of tail biting.

The sector has started to record evidence of tail/ear biting lesions. However, procedures for the assessment of lesions are incomplete. Farm risk assessment tools are still being developed and there is no robust framework in the Action Plan for improvement measures or when farms should transition to rearing pigs with intact tails. These last three components need to be put in place quickly in order to start making tangible progress to improve compliance with the Directive. In addition, the extended CA deadlines (end 2022 to 2024) mean that without a focus on shortening deadlines and sufficient priority, full compliance with legal requirements will not be reached within the next four years.

Docked pigs received from other farms may present a challenge for the competent authorities to change management practices on the farms receiving these animals which is not addressed in the Action Plan. 8 5.2 ECONOMIC FACTORS Legal requirements Article 33 of Regulation (EU) No 1305/2013 (6) Findings European and National Funding Measures in the Pig Sector

The planning, execution and follow up of official controls were carried out according to the existing procedures in place. However: DGAL and the local CA acknowledge that the existing guidance for legal requirements relating to risks for tail biting to official veterinarians (OVs) to carry out and report the results of inspections consistently is not fully satisfactory but is a work in progress. In addition there has been no training on the implementation of the new guidance and 10 checklists given to official veterinarians at District level although all those met were aware of the Action Plan and the ongoing developments related to it; Article 3 (2) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 requires that official controls should be unannounced. Official controls on pig farms are not routinely unannounced in all regions of France; Existing procedures do not include: defined criteria for certain legal requirements relating to tail biting risks to enable inspectors to assess farmers' compliance; nor do they contain any framework or instructions for assessing the evidence of tail/ear lesions and improvement measures in farms that rear docked pigs; The vademecum cites Council Directive 91/630/EEC as the main legal base for inspection requirements. This directive has been amended a number of times and superseded by the Pig Directive; The legal requirements on the prohibition of tail docking are being incorrectly assessed by inspectors as compliant: even when routine tail docking is practised on almost all farms, the recording of evidence of tail/ear injuries has only recently started, and farms are not required to put in place improvement measures to improve environmental conditions in order to prevent tail biting; There are serious implications for cross compliance payments as the question on mutilations (PB 3 of the cross compliance inspection form) is being interpreted only in relation to whether tail docking itself was performed in a satisfactory way, and not whether it was legally justified to tail dock on the farm. A non-compliance rate averaging 4% was recorded during 2014 to 2018 when the true situation is actually nearer to 100% according to DGAL and the pig sector. Due to a mistake in interpretation of the Pig Directive, point D0303 of the inspection vademecum and the related animal welfare inspection checklist report (Protection animale en élevage grill d'inspection l'élevage de porcs) only require the provision of enrichment material to pigs in groups, and sows and gilts in groups of more than 10 animals. Point PB7 of the cross compliance checklist indicates that the requirements for enrichment material are not applicable to sows and gilts in stalls.

DGAL intends to: Intensify official controls on pig farms at the end of 2019 once the inspection vademecum has been updated, including increasing unannounced inspections and incorporating improved enforcement and follow up procedures trialled in the largest pig producing area to improve the consistency of controls and their impact in 2020; Hold specific animal welfare training in 2020 for official vets dealing with pigs, including on the updated inspection vademecum and in the Districts to organise trainings for farmer groups based on non-compliances detected in local farms; Work on incorporating/using the results of risk assessment tools in the framework of their controls; Take phased enforcement measures to rectify the mistakes in the transposition of requirements for all pigs to receive enrichment material. DGAL informed the sector that 11 in June 2019 that all pigs must receive enrichment materials not only those kept in groups. However, there is no timeframe for these actions defined and until this issue is addressed the sector will not be in compliance with the requirements of point 4 of Chapter I, Annex I of the Pig Directive.

recommendations.text: To ensure that inspections are carried out without prior warning as required by Article 3(2) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Recommendation based on conclusion: 34. Associated findings: 22.

citations.text: The audit team noted that in the vast majority of the cases observed, a warning had been given to the FeBOs (2-14 days in advance) on the visits by the authorities (both from the DGAL and the DGCCRF side). Both authorities confirmed this practice and explained that prior notification was given to ensure the availability of the necessary staff and access to relevant documentation. The audit team pointed out that while such an approach can be justified in rare cases (remote locations, irregular working hours, etc.), providing the FeBOs with prior notice is not in line with the requirements laid down by Article 3(2) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

The system of planning of inspections is based on appropriate risk-related factors and thus ensures that the official controls are carried out regularly, on a risk-basis and with appropriate frequency. Verification of the correctness of labelling is adequate to ensure that labelling requirements have been met by the operators. The effectiveness of the inspections is however weakened by several elements including the giving of prior notice to establishments prior the inspections, deficient assessment of operators' HACCP-plans, and incomplete verification of the appropriateness of the operators' retained samples. 5.2.2 Sampling 5.2.2.1 PLANNING OF OFFICIAL SAMPLING

recommendations.text: To ensure that official controls are capable of verifying that feed business operators meet the requirements on hazard analysis and critical control points (HACCP) in accordance with Articles 6 and 7 of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005, and that the effectiveness of such controls is guaranteed, as required by Article 4(2(a)) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Recommendation based on conclusion: 34. Associated findings: 23. 12

citations.text: In every establishment visited, the audit team checked the DGAL feed inspectors' assessment of the operators' hazard analysis and critical control points (HACCP) plans. In many cases, the inspectors' assessment was sufficient. However, in 5 of the 11 establishments visited, the audit team noted shortcomings in relation to the adequacy of the risk assessment for some ingredients used for the production of feed additives, and for some of the feed additives themselves (predominantly contaminants of chemical origin, e.g., heavy metals, dioxins/polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs), etc.). The failure of the operators to identify relevant hazards, as required by Article 6(2)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005, was neither spotted by the inspectors met during the audit nor had been identified in any of the previous inspection reports. In one case, there was no adequate HACCP plan in place at the time of the visit.

Verification of the correctness of labelling is adequate to ensure that labelling requirements have been met by the operators. The effectiveness of the inspections is however weakened by several elements including the giving of prior notice to establishments prior the inspections, deficient assessment of operators' HACCP-plans, and incomplete verification of the appropriateness of the operators' retained samples. 5.2.2 Sampling 5.2.2.1 PLANNING OF OFFICIAL SAMPLING

recommendations.text: To ensure that staff carrying out official sampling follow the sampling requirements laid down by Article 1 and Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 152/2009. Recommendation based on conclusion: 44. Associated findings: 43.

citations.text: A systemic shortcoming was noted by the audit team in terms of the preparation of final samples from the aggregate ones for control of substances where non-uniform distribution of the analyte/substance is presumed. The inspectors would normally use simple manual mixing to ensure appropriate homogenisation rather than special equipment (e.g. mechanical or automatic dividers) which is required by part 9(4) of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 152/2009. For substances with a non-uniform 4 In their response to the draft report the competent authority noted that composition analyses to verify the correctness of declarations on the additives present and the concentrations thereof are also carried out at the request of investigators on feed sampled under the monitoring and control plan concerning undesirable and prohibited substances. 9 distribution, simple manual mixing alone cannot ensure complete homogenisation of the aggregate sample. Only in one case the inspector stated that there was one mechanical divider available. Conclusion on the planning and implementation of official sampling

The system in place for planning of official sampling is effective and risk-based. However, the effectiveness of the sampling is weakened by the fact that the representativeness of the sampling, and thus the samples' legal and analytical validity, is not ensured for controls on substances with a non-uniform distribution. 5.2.3 Actions taken on non-compliances

recommendations.text: To ensure that official controls are capable of verifying feed business operators' fulfilment of obligations on appropriateness of retained samples taken, as required by section on "Quality control" of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 183/2005. Recommendation based on conclusion: 34. Associated findings: 29.

citations.text: As for the operators' obligation to take samples of ingredients and of each batch of products manufactured and placed on the market, or of each specific portion of production (in the case of continuous production) in sufficient quantities using a procedure pre-established by the manufacturer (hereinafter: retained samples), the audit team checked several samples in all of the establishments visited. In the vast majority of cases they could not be considered as adequate due to the absence of a pre-established written procedure (on taking of retained samples) by the operators, absence of sealing, and/or insufficient quantity. This is not in line with the requirements laid down in the section "Quality control"(4) of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 183/2005. The audit team noted that the absence of sealing had not been identified as a non-compliance in the available inspection reports.

The system of planning of inspections is based on appropriate risk-related factors and thus ensures that the official controls are carried out regularly, on a risk-basis and with appropriate frequency. Verification of the correctness of labelling is adequate to ensure that labelling requirements have been met by the operators. The effectiveness of the inspections is however weakened by several elements including the giving of prior notice to establishments prior the inspections, deficient assessment of operators' HACCP-plans, and incomplete verification of the appropriateness of the operators' retained samples. 5.2.2 Sampling 5.2.2.1 PLANNING OF OFFICIAL SAMPLING

recommendations.text: To ensure that when official controls identify non-compliance, actions are taken to ensure that the operator remedies the situation as required by Article 54 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Recommendation based on conclusion: 49. Associated findings: 46 and 47.

citations.text: The audit team examined two RASFF notifications (one originated from France and one was sent to France due to the distribution of the affected product) and the actions taken by the relevant competent authorities (mainly by the DGCCRF through its Alert Unit). Whilst the immediate actions taken to ensure withdrawal of the products affected from the market were sufficient and timely, in one of the two notifications the return of the affected product to the country of origin was not verified and documented by the competent authority. This situation could not thus be considered as completely remedied as required by Article 54 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

In every establishment visited, the audit team studied non-compliances from previous inspections (if any had been identified). Examples included deficient labelling, HACCP- related deficiencies, etc.). The audit team noted that in many cases the inspection reports and communication with the FeBOs did not contain an unambiguous request for corrective action and consequently no timeframe was specified for the FeBO to remedy the deficiency(ies). Dedicated and comprehensive follow-ups were very rarely carried out. The inspectors met clarified that such follow-up(s) would be done during the next planned inspection. However, the audit team pointed out that in the vast majority of the cases the next planned inspection would be in four-five years' time and thus the timeliness and effectiveness of the corrective actions, if any, would not be verified within a reasonable period of time. The situation observed is not in line with the requirements laid down by Article 54 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

The fact that the competent authority does not specify timelines to operators to remedy non-compliances identified during official controls and it may be between 4 and 5 years before corrective actions are verified, weakens the effectiveness of the overall control system. 5.2.4 Establishments producing/trading non-authorised (in the EU) feed additives but are exporting or re-exporting them from the EU to a non-EU country

recommendations.text: To ensure that official controls are capable of verifying that feed business operators, exporting non-authorised (in the EU) feed additives/premixtures to third countries, meet the requirements laid down by Article 12 of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002. Recommendation based on conclusion: 12 and 53. Associated findings: 7 and 51.

citations.text: The audit team noted that provision of information on activities related to production for/trade with third countries of non-EU authorised feed additives/premixtures was not 3 Available at: http://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/country_profiles/details.cfm?co_id=FR 3 mandatory in the application form for registration/approval. This does not allow building knowledge on such activities and operators involved (see finding 51). The competent authorities clarified that the application forms and the registration process were being revised to better identify the precise activities of the FeBO.

There is a well-established system in place for the registration and approval of operators, which supports the planning of official controls. However, absence of verifiable information on production and trade of non-EU authorised feed additives/premixtures weakens the organisation of official controls on relevant establishments. 5.2 PLANNING AND IMPLEMENTATION OF OFFICIAL FEED CONTROLS 5.2.1 Inspections 5.2.1.1 PLANNING OF INSPECTIONS

The audit team observed that neither the DGAL nor the DGCRF possessed any list of the relevant establishments though they had a note from an industry association clearly identifying the number of non-EU authorised feed additives/preparations/premixtures and the trade of those with third countries by French operators.6 The competent authorities explained that they were experiencing difficulty in collating information on relevant activities and establishments since reporting of such activities was not compulsory, although strongly recommended. As a result, the relevant activities could be discovered only during an inspection. Under these circumstances it is clear that no official controls can be planned and carried out with the aim to verify that relevant FeBOs meet the requirements laid down by Article 12 of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002. The competent authorities informed the audit team that the current revision of the application forms and the registration process would rectify this issue (see finding 7). However, no information on the completion of that revision could be given.

The absence of information on relevant operators' activities precludes the organisation of official controls on establishments producing non-EU-authorised feed additives/preparations/premixtures and trading these with third countries. be taken on a case-by-case basis, since the measures will depend on the findings made in the case in question. 6 In their response to the draft report the competent authority noted that the information had been requested from the industry association, but the relevant authorities have not yet received it. The competent authorities explained to the audit team that the association had raised the issue of the identification of such products. 11 6 OVERALL CONCLUSION In France, the planning of official feed controls is risk-based with inspections being generally well performed and, for the most part, capable of adequately verifying operators' fulfilment of relevant legislative requirements. Weaknesses in the control system included the provision of prior notice to operators on upcoming inspections, inadequate verification of the suitability of operators' HACCP-plans, and some minor shortcomings in the preparation of final samples and retention of samples by operators. With regard to enforcement, the competent authority's actions following identification of non-compliances do not necessarily include active follow-up and verification that the identified deficiencies have been remedied by the operator. Finally, the authorities' lack of awareness on which operators are exporting non-EU-authorised feed additives/premixtures undermines the effectiveness of the system of official controls in this regard. 7 CLOSING MEETING A closing meeting was held on 5 April 2019 with the representatives of the DGAL and the DGCCRF. The main findings and preliminary conclusions of the audit were presented by the audit team. The authorities present did not indicate any major disagreement with these and provided further clarifications and presented comments on some of the findings and preliminary conclusions. 8 RECOMMENDATIONS The competent authorities are invited to provide details of the actions taken and planned, including deadlines for their completion ('action plan'), aimed at addressing the recommendations set out below, within 25 working days of receipt of this audit report. recommendations.text: To ensure that official checks on the validation process verify compliance with the requirements laid down in Section 2 of Chapter I to Annex XVI to Regulation (EC) No 142/2011, in particular, in points 1, 3(b) and 4 with respect to the critical parameters to be checked and monitored for the continuous process and to alterations made to the process. Recommendation based on conclusion: 23 Associated finding: 15

citations.text: The audit team noted that two of the operators visited had received approval for using processing method 7 in a continuous system, however: a. One operator, despite being approved for processing in a continuous system, had carried out validation for the processing method in a batch system with single loads of material ranging from 80 to 120 kg while the targeted operational capacity of the system was up to two tonnes per hour. This way of processing was neither reflected in the operators HACCP-based procedures nor in the approval document issued by the authority; b. Neither of the two operators explained in the validation file the way they measured the feeding rate to demonstrate the minimum transit time inside the entire relevant part of the continuous system to ensure sufficient exposure of the processed material to desirable processing parameters. Moreover, there were no critical control points (CCPs) established for the parameter(s) relevant for the continuous process, such as: (i) feed screw revolutions per minute, (ii) the electric power, (iii) the evaporation/condensation rate, or (iv) the number of pump strokes, if relevant, that would allow a correlation to be made between the exposure to processing parameters and the transit time; c. HACCP-based procedures, attached by both operators to the validation file, determined critical limits (values) in relation to temperature and processing time. 6 One operator, in its HACCP-based procedures had established a 30% tolerance for these limits. This would allow the processing of material below the critical limits though the audit team did not see any evidence that such a situation had arisen. The above points are not in compliance with the requirements laid down in points 1, 3(b) and 4 of Section 2 of Chapter I of Annex XVI to Regulation (EC) No 142/2011. They had not been detected or objected by the competent authority during the approval process.

The process for granting approval ensures that insect PAP placed on the market complies with microbiological safety criteria, but was insufficiently robust as regards the assessment of the validation of the processing method and of the HACCP-based procedures; this however did not affect the safety of the product.

Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 (since 14/12/2019 Article 9 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625), based upon which the frequency of the inspection of an establishment is established, are reliable and correctly reflect the real conditions of the inspected food producing establishments, by: envisaging the introduction in the formula of a "corrective factor" to take into account particular non-conformities identified during previous inspections; ensuring that the official veterinarians correctly evaluate any non- conformities and categorise them by relevance and gravity. Recommendation based on conclusion No 65. Associated findings Nos 43 and 60. The competent authority should ensure official controls identify relevant non-compliances and that the action plans presented by food business operators to correct any non-compliances are evaluated and verified within the specified deadlines, as required by Article 54 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 ( since 14/12/2019 Article 138 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625). Recommendation based on conclusions Nos 65 and 77. Associated findings Nos 5, 50, 51, 59, 63, 64, 73,74, 99 and 102. The competent authority should ensure that the definition and the production of mechanically separated meat is brought in line with that of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004, in its Section V to Annex III. Recommendation based on conclusions Nos 76 and 77. Associated findings Nos 69, 72, 73, 74 and 75. 4. The competent authority should ensure that approvals of food producing establishments are kept up to date and are reflected in the lists made publicly available by the central CA, as required by Article 31.2 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 (since 14/12/2019 Articles 10(2), 138(2)(j) and 148 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 and Article 45 of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1715). Recommendation based on conclusions Nos 40 and 41. Associated findings Nos 35, 37 and 39. 5. The competent authority should ensure that a system of supervision is established of the performance of official staff that are carrying out official controls, as required by Article 12.2 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Recommendation based on conclusion No 32. Associated findings Nos 27 and 29.

citations.text: Risk classification is determined by DGAL by the application of a formula which comprises the outcome of the last inspection and the volume, type and target of production; the reliability of the FBOs, in performing their own-checks and informing the CAs of any real or potential risk, is not weighted appropriately in this formula. It is noted that the highest risk class IV does not necessarily include insufficiently performing FBOs; FBOs with high volumes of production, or targeting highly sensible consumers, may also be included in this class. On the other hand, a very negative notation of one of the elements of the formula does not necessarily lead to an increase in the risk classification of the FBO. Consequently, the risk classification of establishments might not exactly reflect the situation seen by the DG Health and Food Safety audit team during visits to premises (see paragraph 63). Local CAs stated that they may update the risk classification given at central level (only up or down by one class), but this is rarely done.

After each inspection a report with the findings is created and signed by the official. The FBO receives the report with an accompanying letter containing the final decision, signed at Department level. The findings are recorded in the RESYTAL database and are scored, according to their seriousness, within the formula used for the risk classification of FBOs for the following year (see paragraph 43).

Official controls are planned on the basis of the risk categorisation of FBOs, which does not give the necessary weight to the key elements supporting the categorisation. As a consequence, the frequency of controls and follow-up of previously detected non- conformities may be not appropriate.

Article 62 of, and Annex X to Directive 2005/94/EC; Article 18 of Regulation (EC) No 1099/2009. Article 11 (1) to (3) of, and Annex X (points 3, 5, 6 and 7) to Directive 2005/94/EC. Based on conclusions (138) and (139), and associated findings (23), (49), (71), (76) and (124).

Articles 6, 7, 9, 10 (1) and (2), 11 (1) and (3), 16 (1) and (3), and 17 of, and Annex X (points 6 and 7) to Directive 2005/94/EC. Based on conclusion (32), and associated findings (20), (21), (30) and (45).

Article 11 (2) and (3) of, and point 6 of Annex X to Directive 2005/94/EC. Based on conclusion (85), and associated findings (71) and (82).

To ensure that the authorities will only authorise movements of live poultry from a protection zone to areas free from the disease after the animals have been tested and the presence of the disease have been excluded. Article 23 (1)(b) of Directive 2005/94/EC. Based on conclusion (68), and associated finding (56).

The competent authority should introduce appropriate safeguard mechanisms to mitigate any risks related to conflict of interest when a private veterinarian is appointed as an official veterinarian, since it is possible that the same private veterinarian can attest for the fitness of transport/emergency slaughter of a bovine animal under his/her private practice and afterwards carry out the ante- mortem or/and post-mortem inspection of that same animal. Recommendation based on conclusion No 45. Associated findings Nos 19 and 20.

citations.text: The CVI can be signed by the private veterinarian who also provides services to the farm. There are no safeguard measures in place to ensure that the same private veterinarian attesting the suitability of an injured bovine animal to be transferred to the slaughterhouse or for on-farm slaughter, is excluded from performing the AMI/PMI of the same animal as a private veterinarian under contract.

The veterinarian's fees and travel expenses for the initial examination of the animal outside a slaughterhouse and for the completion of the part of the CVI relating to the private veterinarian are borne by the applicant for the visit and are paid directly to veterinarian. 5.2.3. Staffing and equipment

There are procedures in place ensuring that private veterinarians when carrying out official tasks under contract are impartial and free of conflict of interest. Nonetheless, there are no safeguard mechanisms or measures in place to mitigate such risks when a CVI is issued. As a consequence, it is possible that the same private veterinarian can attest the fitness of transport or on-farm slaughter of a bovine animal under his/her care and subsequently carry out the AMI/PMI of the same animal when assigned to perform official control tasks. 14 5.3. Il s'applique à l'ensemble des agents de l'organisme DGAL, y compris les vétérinaires privés agissant en qualité de vétérinaire officiel. recommendations.text: The competent authority should allocate the necessary official staff to ensure that in the case of slaughterhouses of domestic ungulates all relevant official tasks, primarily the ante-mortem inspection and when required the post- mortem inspection (i.e. in slaughterhouses slaughtering more than 1000 livestock units per year) are carried out by or under the supervision of the official veterinarian in line with Article 18(2) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 and Article 7 of Regulation (EU) 2019/624. Recommendation based on conclusion No 128. Associated findings Nos 72, 73, 75, 85, 86 and 87.

citations.text: In the second slaughterhouse reviewed, also slaughtering over 1000 LVU per year it was explained that it is possible that on certain days, the OV is not permanently present throughout the day. Therefore, it is possible that the OA can carry out the AMI of bovine animals which do not present any abnormalities and those animals to be slaughtered. This is not in line with Article 3 of Regulation (EU) 2019/624 which requires that this task must be carried out under the supervision of the OV (that is, with the OV present in the premises). Animals presenting abnormalities are detained by the OA and undergo a second-level AMI, performed by the OV. This issue regarding the absence of the OV during AMI was identified during the 2019 internal audits, but no recommendations were made to address it.

It was also explained by the CAs that in the specific case where an animal is obviously in distress when the OV is not present at the premises, the OA informs the OV as quickly as possible and directly makes an appropriate decision, which may be: the immediate slaughter of the animals fit for human consumption (for example, an animal which has just been injured either in the lairage or during transport and is obviously in distress), retaining the carcase and offal for inspection by the OV. This practice is not in line is with Article 3 of Regulation (EU) 2019/624; the emergency killing of the animals unfit for human consumption (for example, a sick animal in obvious distress).

The audit team was informed that at local level, the local organisation and the priorities defined by the departmental authority may explain why the AMI might be carried out by 19 an OA under the responsibility and not under the supervision of the OV as required by Article 3(1) of Regulation 2019/624.

Based on the information provided by the CCA for bovine slaughterhouses, the staff of the VIS is systematically present during slaughter. The OV is present for decisions linked to the PMI and systematically validates this decision by signing the slaughterhouse seizure certificates. If the OV needs to be absent, including in slaughterhouses slaughtering over 1000 LVU per year, carcasses suspected of presenting abnormalities during the PMI are detained by the OA to be inspected at a later stage by the OV (see paragraph 87).

One OV in charge of a slaughterhouse slaughtering over 1000 LVU per year stated that it is possible that the OV might not be present at all times during slaughter since he/she might be assigned to other tasks elsewhere, during this period the OV can be reached by phone if needed. This is not in line with the requirements of Article 7 of Regulation (EU) 2019/624 that requires that PMI must be carried out under the supervision of the OV in slaughterhouses slaughtering over 1000 LVU.

The OV can carry out the PMI of slaughtered animals or entrust part of this task to one or more OAs under his supervision. If it is not the OV who directly performs the PMI, the OA performs the PMI of the animals after slaughter (first level of PMI). The OA sorts the animals depending on whether or not they present abnormalities. Animals presenting abnormalities are retained. The abnormalities might be pathological lesions, abnormalities requiring further investigations or inspection (e.g. identification or FCI issues, known health risks etc.) by the OV either on the same day or early the next day. 21 Due to the lack of continued presence of the OV highlighted in the paragraph above this procedure does not always ensure, in slaughterhouses slaughtering over 1000 LVU, that the PMI is carried out under the supervision of the OV as required by Article 7 of Regulation (EU) 2019/624. The issue regarding the absence of the OV during PMI was also identified during the 2019 internal audits.

The VIS perform various controls regarding bovine identification, checks on the FCI and on hygiene requirements during slaughter, including AMI/PMI and record their findings in the CA's information systems. Regarding the AMI of bovine animals, the implementation of the central level instructions does not ensure the required (supervisory) presence of OV in the slaughterhouses at all times required by EU legislation. Similarly, the PMI of bovine animals is not performed at all times under the OV supervision in slaughterhouses slaughtering more than 1000 LVU per year.

recommendations.text: The competent authority should take measures to ensure that only fit bovine animals accompanied by a Veterinary Certificate of Information are transported to slaughterhouses, as required by point 1 of Chapter I of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 1/2005. Recommendation based on conclusion No 129. Associated findings Nos 79 and 80.

citations.text: The following are (non-exhaustive) examples of animals considered unfit for transport: serious open wound; animal suffering from a severe prolapse; animal unable to move by itself without suffering (example: dairy cow with spread legs); newborn whose navel has not healed; calves less than 10 days old, transported over 100 km; pregnant female ready to give birth (more than 90% gestation)/or having given birth less than a week before transport.

It was evident from the documentation reviewed by the audit team that bovine animals that had suffered an accident (including a non-open fracture) or had a non-serious prolapse were transported to the slaughterhouses accompanied by a CVI document signed by a private veterinarian, provided that they were able to move independently/unassisted. In the CVI the private veterinarian attested their capability of transfer, the fulfilment of the requirements of Council Regulation (EC) No 1/2005 and indicated which additional measures should be taken in order to ensure that no additional suffering is caused during transport. This practice is permissible under DGAL's relevant guidance document contrary to point 2(a) of Chapter I of Annex I to Regulation (EC) 1/2005 which lays down that animals unable to move independently without pain or to 20 walk unassisted shall not be considered fit for transport. This has already been identified in a previous DG Health and Food Safety audit (ref. DG(SANTE) 2015-7427).

There are procedures and guidelines in place for official staff for the relevant controls, which provide guidance on how to act in different scenarios regarding the handling of cull cows (i.e. emergency slaughter, identification of unfit animals for transport and/or slaughter). The controls system identifies relevant non-compliances, which are followed up satisfactorily. Yet, as already identified in a previous DG Health and Food Safety audit, bovine animals that have suffered an accident are transported to the slaughterhouses accompanied by a CVI, without all EU requirements being met.

recommendations.text: The competent authority should allocate the necessary official staff to ensure, in the case of poultry slaughterhouses, that the requirements of Article 18(3) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 and those of the relevant Article 25(1) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627, are fully implemented; and that also primarily the ante-mortem inspection and when required the post-mortem inspection (i.e. in slaughterhouses slaughtering more than 150,000 poultry per year) are performed by or under the supervision of the official veterinarian in line with Article 18(2) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 and Articles 3(2) and 7(1)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2019/624. Recommendation based on conclusion No 130. Associated findings Nos 95, 96, 97 and 101.

citations.text: Similarly to domestic ungulates, there are no provisions in place to carry out AMI for poultry at the holding of provenance, therefore the AMI must be carried out at the slaughterhouse by or under the supervision of the OV, in line with Article 18(2) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The requirement that the OV is present during slaughter activities is implemented only in those poultry slaughterhouses slaughtering more than 15,000 tonnes per year (34 out of 914 slaughterhouses covering 70% of production).

In 17 slaughterhouses with an annual throughput between 10,000 and 15,000 tonnes the procedures in place require the permanent presence of at least one member of official staff (OV/OA) during slaughter activities with a daily supervisory visit by the OV in case not permanently present. In the remaining 78 slaughterhouses (with a capacity ranging from 300 to 10,000 tonnes per year), at least one member of official staff (OV/OA) is present for certain days each week. These arrangements in place do always ensure that the AMI/PMI is carried out under the supervision of the OV. Article 7(1)(a)(ii) of Regulation (EU) 2019/624 requires that PMI can only be performed by an OA under the responsibility of the OV in slaughterhouses slaughtering less than 150,000 poultry per year.

In the low-capacity slaughterhouses, the VIS is not present throughout the slaughter activities and only visits the slaughterhouses with a minimum frequency of two visits per year while the slaughterhouse is in operation. Besides the AMI issue highlighted in paragraph 95 the current arrangements are not in line with Article 18(3)(c) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 which allows slaughterhouse staff to assist in the performance of official control tasks in poultry and lagomorphs slaughterhouses when the task is carried out in the presence of the OV or the OA and following their instructions.

When permanently present at the slaughterhouse or during visits/inspections, the OV or OA carries out a PMI, which includes an inspection of the viscera and body cavities of a representative sample of each flock and an inspection of the poultry declared unfit for consumption by the slaughterhouse staff. The latter is not in line with Article 25(1)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627 according to which the OV/OA shall inspect the viscera and body cavities of a representative sample of each flock, on a daily basis. In France, the derogation of Article 25(2) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627 has not been applied to date.

The number of available official staff and the procedures in place for their deployment while on operation do not ensure in 880 poultry slaughterhouses (30 % of total national production) compliance with the requirements of Article 18(3) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627 regarding the presence of official staff, of Article 25(1) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627 regarding the practical arrangements of the PMI of poultry and the supervision requirements of Article 18(2) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 and of Articles 3(2) and 7(1)(a)(ii) of Regulation (EU) 2019/624. 5.5. OVERALL CONCLUSION DGAL is the central supervisory authority with responsibility over the animal health, welfare and animal identification. National legislation, procedures and guidelines for official controls are in place. BDNI provides detailed information of all bovines and their holdings, and is used to target controls. The official staff perform controls including their follow-up and take enforcement action where needed. Regarding AMI/PMI of bovine animals, the arrangements in place do not ensure the presence of an OV in the slaughterhouse at all times. As a consequence, and contrary to Regulation (EU) 2019/624 the following tasks may be carried out by the OA under the responsibility, rather than under the supervision (i.e. present on the slaughterhouse premises) of the OV: a) the AMI carried out in absence of AMI by an OV in the holding of provenance, and b) the PMI in slaughterhouses slaughtering over 1000 LVU per year. The slaughter of dangerous domestic ungulates on-farm is allowed and is considered as emergency slaughter. The information provided to the audit team indicates that, official veterinarians at the slaughterhouses accept bovine animals that have suffered an accident, including fracture, as being fit for transport if certain criteria established in a specific guidance are fulfilled. This is not in line with EU requirements since it cannot be precluded that the journey does not cause additional suffering to these animals. Furthermore, the CAs have not introduced any specific safeguard measures to ensure that private veterinarians act independently and are free from any conflict of interest when performing their official duties. In relation to the official controls applied in poultry slaughterhouses, and despite efforts made in recruiting new staff, a considerable number of these establishments continue not to operate in line with the EU requirements regarding the presence of official staff. The data 29 available suggest that this concerns 880 poultry slaughterhouses, responsible for 30 % of total national production. The arrangements in place do not ensure that the requirements of Regulation (EU) 2019/624 are complied with as the AMI/PMI in slaughterhouses slaughtering over 150,000 poultry per year do not systematically take place under the supervision of the OV. In addition, in slaughterhouses slaughtering less than 150,000 poultry per year, the AMI is not carried out under the supervision of the OV and, where the PMI takes place under the responsibility of the OV, the presence of the OA is not ensured.
