audits.title: animal welfare - transport by livestock vessel to non-EU countries

recommendations.text: The competent authority should update documented procedures to provide sufficient information and instructions for staff, as required by Article 12(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, to carry out official controls at the port, including inspections carried out according to Articles 19 and 20 of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005. Recommendation based on conclusions: 40 and 42. Associated findings: 3, 4, 33 and 38.

citations.text: For many of the specific technical requirements, included under Section 1 of Chapter IV of Annex I to the Regulation, to be checked when approving a vessel and which are not of a veterinary nature the Vade Mecum: in some instances (ventilation air exchanges and backup water pumping system) indicates that only "the classification society referred to in Chapter IV, Section 1, Point 1 of the Regulation, is competent to" test/verify/certify the requirements, thus implying that the competent authority officials working at the port of exit (hereafter "port inspectors") do not have the skills to verify these requirements; in other instances (fire-fighting and power supply systems, all monitoring and alarm systems) indicates that is not the responsibility of the port inspectors, but must be certified in the ship's safety certificates issued by a classification society; does not provide sufficient instructions on how to verify the suitability of the drainage system including its tanks and pumping and backup pumping systems; instructs the port inspectors to verify these requirements by checking certificates issued by a classification society. According to Section F2102 of the Vade Mecum, checks on these certificates consist in a verification that they are still valid. The DGAL acknowledged that certificates issued by classification societies do not certify compliance with the technical animal welfare requirements listed in Section 1 of Chapter IV of Annex I to the Regulation.

In addition, for pre-loading controls, the Vade Mecum only indicates that the presence of the equipment listed in Section 1 of Chapter IV of Annex I to the Regulation must be checked but not that these are in good working order (water and drainage pumps and backup pumps, alarm systems, firefighting equipment and power generation devices). This is not in accordance with Article 20(1)(c) of the Regulation.

Due to the nature of the audit, it was not possible to attend a physical inspection of a livestock vessel. Concerning an inspection for approval: the Vade Mecum does not explain how to verify compliance with the specific technical requirements of the vessel (see also paragraph 3); port inspectors indicated they check ventilation systems by asking the operator to turn them on and verifying that air is exiting the vents, as instructed by the Vade Mecum. This type of check however does not confirm that the ventilation systems are providing the minimum required air changes per hour on each deck (Point 2 of Section 1 of Chapter IV of Annex I to the Regulation). According to the Vade Mecum, only a classification society can verify this (see also paragraph 32). according to the Vade Mecum, port inspectors should verify compliance with the requirement for alarm systems only by consulting classification society certificates, as it is not their competence to verify the presence of such devices. The port inspectors however indicated that they ask the ship's captain to run a mock emergency to check the alarm systems. According to inspection reports examined by the audit team, the port inspectors were requesting this mock test already in 2017, although not for all the alarm systems included in Point 8 of Section 1 of Chapter IV of Annex I to the Regulation. port inspectors were capable of explaining the layout of a vessel's drainage system from its plan. In the example used, drainage would be flowing in the corridors before reaching the drains leading to the pumps in the lower floors. Feed is given to the animals on these same corridors, meaning that it will be contaminated during the journey, contrarily to the requirement of Point 1.3 of Chapter VI of Annex I to the Regulation.

In the pre-loading checklists, port inspectors confirm that the equipment listed in Section 1 of Chapter IV of Annex I to the Regulation was present. There is no indication that they verify that this equipment is in good working order, although this is required by Article 20 of the Regulation (see also paragraph 4).

Documented procedures do not provide the necessary instructions for port inspectors on how to verify all the relevant legal requirements as part of a practical official control of a livestock vessel. In particular, these instructions are generally inadequate to support the port inspectors in verifying compliance with the specific technical requirements of the Regulation during official controls for approval of livestock vessels.

The effectiveness of controls of livestock vessels is dependent on the experience of the port inspectors. For some of the requirements, the port inspectors go beyond what the procedures indicate. Nonetheless, official controls are not adequately verifying all the requirements, and this could have implications for animal welfare during sea journeys. Controls carried out on vessels loading in France and during the French approval procedure for livestock vessels are inadequate to minimise the animal welfare risks linked to most specific technical equipment on board.

recommendations.text: The competent authority should take measures to ensure that they have access to suitably qualified staff, as required by Article 5(1)(e) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, when carrying out inspections according to Articles 19 and 20 of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005, in particular on the technical requirements listed in Section I of Chapter IV of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 1/2005. Recommendation based on conclusion: 41. Associated findings: 3, 27, 32, 33 and 38.

citations.text: For many of the specific technical requirements, included under Section 1 of Chapter IV of Annex I to the Regulation, to be checked when approving a vessel and which are not of a veterinary nature the Vade Mecum: in some instances (ventilation air exchanges and backup water pumping system) indicates that only "the classification society referred to in Chapter IV, Section 1, Point 1 of the Regulation, is competent to" test/verify/certify the requirements, thus implying that the competent authority officials working at the port of exit (hereafter "port inspectors") do not have the skills to verify these requirements; in other instances (fire-fighting and power supply systems, all monitoring and alarm systems) indicates that is not the responsibility of the port inspectors, but must be certified in the ship's safety certificates issued by a classification society; does not provide sufficient instructions on how to verify the suitability of the drainage system including its tanks and pumping and backup pumping systems; instructs the port inspectors to verify these requirements by checking certificates issued by a classification society. According to Section F2102 of the Vade Mecum, checks on these certificates consist in a verification that they are still valid. The DGAL acknowledged that certificates issued by classification societies do not certify compliance with the technical animal welfare requirements listed in Section 1 of Chapter IV of Annex I to the Regulation.

Port inspectors are responsible for inspecting and approving livestock vessels (Article 19 of the Regulation) but they do not have the technical knowledge to verify compliance with the specific technical requirements of Section 1 Chapter IV Annex I of the Regulation (Article 5(1)(e) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625).

Documents submitted with the application include classification society certificates, deck plans and a contingency plan: The application files reviewed by the audit team had these supporting documents. The deck plans illustrate the layout of the livestock area, and watering, drainage, ventilation, lighting and fire-fighting systems. According to the Vade Mecum, when carrying out the physical inspection, the port inspectors must verify that these systems are laid out according to the plans. The port inspectors are accepting certificates issued by any classification society as proof of compliance with most of the technical requirements found in Section 1 of Chapter IV of Annex I to the Regulation (see also paragraph 3). Verification of these technical requirements is an official control task, and can therefore only be performed by a competent authority or a person or body to which this task has been delegated (Article 2(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625). The port inspectors also indicated that, apart from the validity, there was nothing else they could check in the classification society certificates. Contingency plans provide instructions to care for sick or injured animals during the sea journey. They do not provide guidance for other possible emergencies that may arise at sea, such as fire outbreaks or engine failures leaving the vessel adrift at sea. 9

Due to the nature of the audit, it was not possible to attend a physical inspection of a livestock vessel. Concerning an inspection for approval: the Vade Mecum does not explain how to verify compliance with the specific technical requirements of the vessel (see also paragraph 3); port inspectors indicated they check ventilation systems by asking the operator to turn them on and verifying that air is exiting the vents, as instructed by the Vade Mecum. This type of check however does not confirm that the ventilation systems are providing the minimum required air changes per hour on each deck (Point 2 of Section 1 of Chapter IV of Annex I to the Regulation). According to the Vade Mecum, only a classification society can verify this (see also paragraph 32). according to the Vade Mecum, port inspectors should verify compliance with the requirement for alarm systems only by consulting classification society certificates, as it is not their competence to verify the presence of such devices. The port inspectors however indicated that they ask the ship's captain to run a mock emergency to check the alarm systems. According to inspection reports examined by the audit team, the port inspectors were requesting this mock test already in 2017, although not for all the alarm systems included in Point 8 of Section 1 of Chapter IV of Annex I to the Regulation. port inspectors were capable of explaining the layout of a vessel's drainage system from its plan. In the example used, drainage would be flowing in the corridors before reaching the drains leading to the pumps in the lower floors. Feed is given to the animals on these same corridors, meaning that it will be contaminated during the journey, contrarily to the requirement of Point 1.3 of Chapter VI of Annex I to the Regulation.

In the pre-loading checklists, port inspectors confirm that the equipment listed in Section 1 of Chapter IV of Annex I to the Regulation was present. There is no indication that they verify that this equipment is in good working order, although this is required by Article 20 of the Regulation (see also paragraph 4).

This, together with the absence of suitably qualified staff for assessing specific technical requirements for livestock vessels translates into a poor evaluation of these requirements (such as air changes per hour on each deck of a livestock vessel, and the equipment used for watering and drainage systems on board a livestock vessel) during the approval and pre-loading inspections.

citations.text: The DGAL informed the audit team that BCP staff have access to guidance documents and instructions via its quality assurance intranet websites. The documents include three vade mecums respectively for import controls on animals, goods of animal origin and feed of non-animal origin. The DGAL staff also have access to the IMPADON database for further information to support documentary checks. With the exception of the vade mecum for live animals, the guidance documents and instructions have yet to be updated in order to take account of EU legislation which entered in force as of 14 December 2019.

The DGAL "guide d'inspection" contains general instructions for the performance of official controls at BCPs by its staff. It includes measures to be taken in the case of non- compliant consignments, in particular, destruction, redispatch and special treatment. This guide has also yet to be updated to take account of the measures provided for in Articles 65, 66 and 67 of the OCR.

The DGAL stated that the reasons for not having updated these instructions were due the prioritisation of staff resources in the preparations for the withdrawal of United Kingdom from the EU and the management of business continuity during the Covid-19 pandemic. The DGAL confirmed they would update the documented procedures in the period 2022-2023.

The competent authorities have documented procedures and guidance for the performance of official controls on consignments of animals and goods entering the EU, 8 in line with Article 12(1) of the OCR. However these have not been updated as appropriate, which is not in line with Article 12(3)(b) of that Regulation.

However, the lack of recent internal audits of the system of official controls on imports of animals and goods, including verification of compliance of the BCPs with minimum requirements, has had an adverse impact on the effectiveness of implementation of official import controls, and on the competent authorities' obligation to ensure the availability of suitable border control facilities (see section 5.3.), in particular for checks on goods of animal origin and feed of non-animal origin. This is, in part, further aggravated by the lack of updated documented procedures. 5.2 IMPLEMENTATION OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS ON IMPORTS/TRANSITS OF ANIMALS AND GOODS

citations.text: The audit team noted that, for consignments of animals and goods of animal origin intended for transhipment within the transhipment period, the DGAL stated that it requires TRACES-NT to be used for the notification of such consignments, in line with Article 16(1) of Regulation (EU) 2019/2124. The DGAL further stated that each BCP must set up a local procedure to monitor the notified information before the transhipment period expires. The DGAL informed the audit team however that, in practice, the BCPs do not have systematic access to customs declarations or manifest data (other than roll- on roll-off ferry manifests). As a consequence, the BCP staff can only rely on operators' notifications (see section 5.2.2).

However, the lack of recent internal audits of the system of official controls on imports of animals and goods, including verification of compliance of the BCPs with minimum requirements, has had an adverse impact on the effectiveness of implementation of official import controls, and on the competent authorities' obligation to ensure the availability of suitable border control facilities (see section 5.3.), in particular for checks on goods of animal origin and feed of non-animal origin. This is, in part, further aggravated by the lack of updated documented procedures. 5.2 IMPLEMENTATION OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS ON IMPORTS/TRANSITS OF ANIMALS AND GOODS

The audit team evaluated one CHED-P authorised for transhipment at a port BCP. For this consignment, there was a five-month delay in notification of the arrival. The CHED- P for this consignment was, following a documentary check only, finalised as a transhipment to a third country. In reality, this consignment was stored for at least five months at the terminal. The competent authority, although having a transhipment procedure in place, was not aware of this consignment until its notification in TRACES.

All consignments notified at an airport BCP were subjected to at least a documentary check and an identity check, even in cases where the transhipment period was not exceeded. However, for 19 of these consignments, no date of departure was indicated in part I of the CHED-P, thus not allowing calculation of the transhipment period. In 17 of 21 cases where a physical check was not done, it was stated that the reason for not performing the physical check was `reduced checks'. For three of the five consignments 14 on which physical checks were performed, the transhipment period had not been exceeded.

The DGAL technical instruction for transhipped consignments does not require any pre- notification or checks other than in cases where the transhipment period has been exceeded. In such cases, those consignments should be subject to a documentary check, and with an identity and physical check only in cases of suspicion of non-compliance.

The DGAL could not provide evidence that the BCPs of transhipment acted in line with their instruction. In addition, as noted in section 5.1.5, BCPs do not have systematic access to customs declarations or manifest data, and as a consequence, BCPs only rely on the operator's notification of transhipment.

The audit team noted that the procedure in place does not ensure that, in the event that a transhipment takes place, it is done in line with Articles 13 and 16 of Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/2124. 5.2.3 Transit and ship supply procedures

However, a number of shortcomings were noted in the implementation of official controls. They concerned, for example, prior notification of arrival of consignments, documentary checks, transhipment and transit, and decisions on consignments and, in addition, the performance of documentary checks for food of non-animal origin other than upon arrival of the consignment at designated BCPs. These shortcomings collectively undermine the effectiveness and appropriateness of official controls to ensure that only compliant consignments of animals and goods enter the Union. 5.3 MINIMUM REQUIREMENTS FOR BORDER CONTROL POSTS

citations.text: During the current audit cycle, five audits were planned in 2017, whereas six were carried out, and in 2018, three out of six planned audits were carried out. No audits took place between 2019 and 2021, with none planned for the remainder of 2021. The DGAL explained that during this period, audits could not be carried out for resource reasons, activities related to the preparedness for the withdrawal of United Kingdom from the EU and the COVID-19 pandemic.

The audits are concluded with individual audit reports, detailing the objectives, scope, findings and conclusions, and recommendations if applicable. Follow-up of previous audit recommendations is carried out by desk-based assessment or during the subsequent on-the-spot audit. As no audits have taken place since 2018 for above-mentioned reasons, follow-up on the 2018 audits is still outstanding.

The General Inspectorate of Services of the DGCCRF also carries out internal audits and verification checks. The prioritisation of these internal audits is based on an analysis of risk factors which leads to the establishment of a multi-year program for 2016-2020. The audit of official controls on imports of food of non-animal origin and food contact materials, which was scheduled for 2020, did not take place. The DGCCRF stated that this was due in part to the COVID-19 pandemic and the transfer of responsibilities to the DGDDI).

The DGCCRF stated that the multiannual audit programme is currently being revised, but that there are no plans to integrate import control audits in view of the transfer (see section 5.1.1). The DGDDI stated that it did not yet plan any audits for the same reason.

The audit team noted that the competent authorities have procedures in place to verify the effectiveness of their controls and carry out internal audits in line with Articles 5(1)(a), 6(1) and 12(2) of the OCR. However, there has been a shortfall in its implementation as no such internal audits have been carried since 2018, prior to the entry into force of the OCR. citations.text: The audit team noted discrepancies in the relevant boxes of part I of the CHED-As evaluated, which were either not fully or correctly completed. Examination of the documentary checks showed that the discrepancies in part I were either not detected or corrected, and that the outcome of those checks had been recorded as satisfactory. These CHEDs had subsequently been validated and the corresponding consignments accepted for entry into the EU, which is not in line with Article 2(3) of Regulation (EU) 2019/2130.

All but three consignments of goods of animal origin intended for import, evaluated by the audit team, were subject to documentary checks and identity checks. Identity checks were either full identity checks or checks on seals in accordance with Article 3 of Regulation (EU) 2019/2130. With the three exceptions (see section 5.2.5), the frequency 16 rate for identity checks was in line with the baseline frequency rate set out in Article 5 and Annex I to Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/2129.

The audit team noted discrepancies in the relevant parts of the CHED-Ps evaluated, which were either not fully or correctly completed, and that the information included in part I of the evaluated CHED-Ps did not match the information in the accompanying certificates or attestations in 10 out of 28 CHED-Ps verified, which is not in line with Article 2(3) of Regulation (EU) 2019/2130. However, the CHED-Ps were subsequently finalised and the corresponding consignments accepted for entry into the EU, which is not in line with Article 55 of the OCR.

For one consignment re-imported, the DGAL did not provide evidence that the consignment was accompanied by an official declaration of the competent authority or of public authorities as regards handling, unloading storage and reloading of the consignment in the third country, which is not in line with the requirements laid down in Article 3(2)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2019/2074. However the other requirements of Article 3 of said Regulation were met, including the monitoring of the transport and arrival at the place of destination.

However, a number of shortcomings were noted in the implementation of official controls. They concerned, for example, prior notification of arrival of consignments, documentary checks, transhipment and transit, and decisions on consignments and, in addition, the performance of documentary checks for food of non-animal origin other than upon arrival of the consignment at designated BCPs. These shortcomings collectively undermine the effectiveness and appropriateness of official controls to ensure that only compliant consignments of animals and goods enter the Union. 5.3 MINIMUM REQUIREMENTS FOR BORDER CONTROL POSTS

citations.text: The audit team evaluated four CHED-Ps authorised for transit. Two of the four consignments concerned imports rather than transit, including one with a destination in Switzerland.

Out of the eight CHEDs verified, there were two cases of animals being introduced followed by a quarantine period; however the details of the controlled destination (quarantine) were not completed in part II of the CHED for both cases. The DGAL clarified that for both cases, this decision was made in error.

The audit team noted that in two cases, details on the total number of animals checked were either not completed, or indicated that no animals were checked, in part II of the CHED-A. This did not enable verification that a clinical examination had been carried out on the animals concerned in line with Article 4(3) and paragraphs 2, 5 and 6, as applicable, of Part II of Annex I to Regulation (EU) 2019/2130.

The audit team noted discrepancies in the relevant boxes of part I of the CHED-As evaluated, which were either not fully or correctly completed. Examination of the documentary checks showed that the discrepancies in part I were either not detected or corrected, and that the outcome of those checks had been recorded as satisfactory. These CHEDs had subsequently been validated and the corresponding consignments accepted for entry into the EU, which is not in line with Article 2(3) of Regulation (EU) 2019/2130.

In addition in four out of the eight CHED-As evaluated, the impact of the transport on animals was not completed in part II, which is not in line with Article 56(3)(b) of the OCR and Article 40(2) of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1715.

All but three consignments of goods of animal origin intended for import, evaluated by the audit team, were subject to documentary checks and identity checks. Identity checks were either full identity checks or checks on seals in accordance with Article 3 of Regulation (EU) 2019/2130. With the three exceptions (see section 5.2.5), the frequency 16 rate for identity checks was in line with the baseline frequency rate set out in Article 5 and Annex I to Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/2129.

The audit team noted discrepancies in the relevant parts of the CHED-Ps evaluated, which were either not fully or correctly completed, and that the information included in part I of the evaluated CHED-Ps did not match the information in the accompanying certificates or attestations in 10 out of 28 CHED-Ps verified, which is not in line with Article 2(3) of Regulation (EU) 2019/2130. However, the CHED-Ps were subsequently finalised and the corresponding consignments accepted for entry into the EU, which is not in line with Article 55 of the OCR.

Following their evaluation of examples of imports of consignments of food of non- animal origin subject to a temporary increase of official controls or emergency measures, the audit team noted that the laboratory results had been delivered in a timely manner in line with Article 37(4)(d) of the OCR. The audit team noted however that, in three out of six cases, the inspector's conclusion of the laboratory tests was not recorded in TRACES-NT, which is not in line with Article 56(3)(b) of the OCR and Article 40(2)(b) of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1715. In the remaining cases, the details of the analyses, such as for example, the test method and detailed results, were not fully completed. The DGCCRF explained that, in accordance with its instructions, it does not require BCP staff to enter such results. 17 5.2.5 Decisions on consignments and follow-up

The audit team found that, in the case of a consignment of fishery products where the cold chain was not maintained, the competent authority at the BCP permitted the operator to subject the consignment to special treatment to alter the best before date of the goods by reducing it by six months to 18 months. This neither ensured compliance with the rules referred to in Article 1(2) of the OCR, nor was in line with the DGAL procedures.

The audit team noted, that a consignment of meat products, which was notified by the operator at the BCP of entry, was refused for reasons of a missing health certificate without being subjected to a documentary, identity or physical check. The health certificate was, however, uploaded in TRACES-NT. At the same BCP, but without being sent to the dedicated inspection centre used for controls of fishery products, the inspectors at this centre refused for similar reasons two consignments of fishery products without subjecting them to mandatory controls. The DGAL explained that the three consignments formed part of a `groupage' load. The operator did not present a health certificate for two consignments of composite products which also formed part of the load and following this finding the BCP staff also rejected all other consignments of animal origin previously mentioned which formed part of the load.

The audit team found that the decisions on these three consignments were not taken following the performance of official controls, including documentary checks and, where necessary, identity checks and physical checks, indicating whether the consignment is in compliance with the rules referred to in Article 1(2) of the OCR, which 18 is not in line with Article 55 of the said Regulation. The DGAL informed the team that it had since taken corrective action to ensure that consignments are only refused following the performance of official controls which indicate that the consignment is not in compliance with the applicable rules.

The audit team found that decisions on consignments were not always taken in line with Article 55 of the OCR. Conclusions on the implementation of official controls on imports/transits of animals and goods

However, a number of shortcomings were noted in the implementation of official controls. They concerned, for example, prior notification of arrival of consignments, documentary checks, transhipment and transit, and decisions on consignments and, in addition, the performance of documentary checks for food of non-animal origin other than upon arrival of the consignment at designated BCPs. These shortcomings collectively undermine the effectiveness and appropriateness of official controls to ensure that only compliant consignments of animals and goods enter the Union. 5.3 MINIMUM REQUIREMENTS FOR BORDER CONTROL POSTS

citations.text: However, the lack of recent internal audits of the system of official controls on imports of animals and goods, including verification of compliance of the BCPs with minimum requirements, has had an adverse impact on the effectiveness of implementation of official import controls, and on the competent authorities' obligation to ensure the availability of suitable border control facilities (see section 5.3.), in particular for checks on goods of animal origin and feed of non-animal origin. This is, in part, further aggravated by the lack of updated documented procedures. 5.2 IMPLEMENTATION OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS ON IMPORTS/TRANSITS OF ANIMALS AND GOODS

The audit team found that none of the evaluated BCPs met the minimum and detailed rules on minimum requirements for BCPs laid down in article 64 of the OCR and Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1014.

In the case of the selected BCPs which are designated for products of non-animal origin, categories PNAO-HC(food) and PNAO-NHC(feed), none had the pre-requisite areas or rooms for unloading, inspection or storage of goods, which is not in line with Article 3(1) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014.

However, the audit team found that the proposed commercial storage facility did not meet the minimum requirements for BCPs, which is not in line with Article 3(1) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014. The audit team made the following main observations: a. the flow of goods did not facilitate their proper handling and prevention of risks which may result from cross contamination; 20 b. the dedicated inspection areas did not have a supply of hot and cold running water or facilities for washing and drying of hands, which is not in line with Article 3(1)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014; and c. the ambient storage facilities were not appropriate to the categories of food of non- animal origin for which the BCPs were designated, i.e. the scope of designation was not limited to goods for which no temperature requirements apply.

Regarding the BCP Nantes Saint-Nazaire designated for goods of animal origin, the audit team found, inter alia, that appropriate arrangements were not in place for the proper handling of packed and unpacked goods and to prevent risks which may result from cross contamination. This is not in line with Article 64(3)(h) of the OCR and Article 3(9)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014.

The audit team found that, inter alia, in respect of the inspection centre Fécamp at BCP Le Havre which is listed for liquid fish oils and fats only, there was no procedure in place for cleaning and disinfection of the special pipes used for the unloading of bulk liquids of animal origin. This is not in line with Article 64(3)(h) and (i) of the OCR. In addition, the specification in the list of BCPs did not limit the use of this inspection centre for liquid in bulk only, despite the inspection centre availing of derogations laid down in Article 3(5) and 6(4) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014 for such goods.

Regarding the selected airport BCP for live animals (categories LA-E, LA-U and LA- O), the audit team observed that the changing room with shower facilities, unloading, inspection and housing facilities for other live animals, category LA-O, do not constitute one integrated and whole working unit, which is not in line with the minimum requirement laid down in Article 5(3) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014.

In addition, the audit team found that the facilities for categories LA-E and LA-U do not have restraining equipment in place for equidae, and that the restraining equipment for ungulates other than equidae are stored in a separate room to the inspection area, which is not in line with Article 5(1)(f) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014.

For BCPs Port de Saint-Nazaire Montoire, Nantes Saint-Nazaire and inspection centre Fécamp, the DGAL and the DGCCRF did not provide information on suitable 21 arrangements in place at all of the BCPs to ensure the smooth operation of official controls and to apply measures as provided for by Articles 65, 66 and 67 of the OCR, which is not in line with Article 64(3)(e) of that Regulation. Conclusions on minimum requirements for border control posts

None of the BCPs evaluated are fully compliant with the minimum requirements for BCPs for the categories of animals and goods for which they have been designated. Consequently the French authorities cannot guarantee the appropriate handling of animals and goods, the proper verification of compliance of those animals and goods and the prevention of the risk of cross contamination in these facilities. However, the competent authority has already initiated corrective actions in the BCPs concerned during this audit which, when completed, should go some way to achieving compliance in these BCPs. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS There is a system of official controls in place for animals and goods of animal and non-animal origin entering the Union though BCPs in France. These controls are implemented by well- trained officials, supported by documented procedures (albeit with some of these being out of date), and were generally implemented in line with those documented procedures and relevant Union legislation. However, shortcomings in both the organisation and implementation of official controls, and in the compliance of the facilities with minimum legal requirements, collectively weaken the effectiveness of the control system for entry of animals and goods into the Union. 7 CLOSING MEETING A closing meeting was held on 5 November 2021 by videoconference with the representatives of the central competent authorities during which, the main findings and preliminary conclusions of the audit were presented by the audit team. This meeting was followed by further clarification meetings and a final meeting on 19 November 2021. 8 RECOMMENDATIONS The competent authorities are invited to provide details of the actions taken and planned, including deadlines for their completion ('action plan'), aimed at addressing the recommendations set out below, within 25 working days of receipt of this audit report. citations.text: According to their reports, officials seem well able to identify existing non- compliances. Regarding their follow-up of deficiencies, the picture is mixed. The audit team saw examples of excellent follow-up (e.g. in one poultry slaughterhouse, the official veterinarian carried out all inspections according to the established frequency, systematically requested an action plan to the operator, consistently sent written warnings for non-compliances, additional timely follow-up visits, initiated an infringement procedure for repeated non-compliance, managed to bring the slaughterhouse in compliance with Annex 2 to the Regulation). There were also many cases with repeated reporting of non-compliances over several years, just in the inspection report without further measures taken, relying on a "good cooperation" with the operator, and therefore several cases of year-long delays in operators taking appropriate corrective actions. Conclusions on official controls

The inconsistent follow up of non-compliances leads to some deficiencies remaining for unacceptably long periods in the establishments that competent authorities are not addressing in an effective, dissuasive and proportionate manner. This undermines the purposes of the official controls to ensure compliance and spare any avoidable pain, distress or suffering to the animals at the time of killing. 7 5.2 LAYOUT, CONSTRUCTION, EQUIPMENT AND APPROVAL OF SLAUGHTERHOUSES Legal requirements Articles 8, 14 and 29 of Regulation (EC) No 1099/2009 Article 148 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 Findings

citations.text: The authorities included a note in the relevant vademecums and in the slaughterhouse newsletter to remind official staff of the deadline (December 2019) for the transitional period for requirements on layout, construction and equipment in slaughterhouses that were in operation before 1 January 2013. They did not issue dedicated information or reminders about the deadline to operators and there was no evidence of any coordinated official pressure on the operators to meet the deadline.

The audit team found evidence that the authorities only identified and communicated non-compliances in the establishments after the transitional period expired. They did not ensure that operators used the transitional period to bring their establishments in compliance with relevant requirements of Annex 2 to the Regulation. Therefore, when the transitional period finished, there were non-compliant establishments with regards to structure (e.g. passage ways which shall be designed to allow the animals to move freely; design of entry pathways/entry into gas stunning equipment) and equipment 8 (e.g. no installed device in the stunning equipment to continuously record stunning parameters, no alarms).

The actions of the authorities increased the awareness of official staff about structural requirements, but failed to ensure compliance of existing slaughterhouses by the end of the transitional period. The remaining structural non-compliances will create animal welfare risks until their correction and the absence of stunning equipment without recording will make it difficult for the authorities to audit operator's compliance that animals were stunned effectively in a continuous way.

recommendations.text: Ensure that CBs are accredited before being approved by the CA as established in Article 29(b)(iv) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 and Article 27(5)(c) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. Recommendation is based upon conclusions No 3 and 29 Associated findings No 2 and 20

citations.text: There are national provisions that are not in line with EU legislation. These are related to the procedure for approval of CBs, the granting of certain exceptional production rules (derogations) and the exchange of information between the CBs and the CAs in case of non-compliances (See relevant sections of this report). Conclusions on relevant national legislation and provisions

The INAO is responsible for the suspension/withdrawal of approval of CBs. The approval procedure is described in INAO-DIR-CAC-5-Rev. 4. CBs are approved by the INAO before they are formally accredited, on the condition that accreditation to ISO/IEC 17065:2012 is obtained within one year. This does require that the INAO receives from the COFRAC the operational admissibility of the CB's files, which is issued after the COFRAC has carried out a documentary check of all documents in the accreditation file. To obtain such operational admissibility from the COFRAC, the CB must have a control plan approved by the INAO. The COFRAC explained to the audit team that for them it is not acceptable to grant accreditation to a CB that has no real activity and for which it cannot be checked how inspections are carried out in practice. Nevertheless, once the CBs are approved by the INAO and have some real activities, COFRAC can grant accreditation if CB activities are carried out in line with ISO 17065. This practice is not in line with Article 29(b)(iv) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 and Article 27(5)(c) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007, as the CBs are approved before being accredited.

recommendations.text: Ensure that the supervision of INAO over CBs is effective and that in particular: 23 · the INAO takes into account the accreditation reports when supervising the CBs in line with Article 92c (1) of Regulation (EC) 889/2008; · the risk assessment carried out by CBs follows the INAO Directive INAO-DIR-CAC-3 Rev.11; · the INAO verifies that the selection of operators for sampling is properly based on risk. Recommendation is based upon conclusion No 28 Associated findings No 24 and 27

citations.text: The INAO provided to the audit team the most recent supervision reports for four CBs. The team noted that the instructions and the provisions in place for supervision of CBs were followed. In all cases, the report template was used. However, in two of the reports reviewed, there was no evidence that the inspectors had checked that the risk-based selection of operators for sampling was properly carried out by the CBs. As mentioned in chapter 5.2.4 below, the audit team found for the two CBs involved in the audit that the selection of operators for sampling and additional visits was not fully in line with the EU organic regulations, including for one of them that the risk assessment did not take into account the volume of production (see chapter 5.2.4 below). This had not been detected and recorded in the supervision reports. In addition, in the case of one CB, the supervision report did not make any reference to the number of samples planned for 2020, the treatment of positive results, the number and outcome of investigations, etc.

The INAO did not take into account COFRAC's accreditation reports when supervising the CBs, which is not in line with Article 92c (1) of Regulation (EC) 889/2008. Conclusions on approval, supervision and withdrawal of CBs

recommendations.text: Ensure that risk assessment procedures of CBs takes in to account the quantity of production and that the operators selected for sampling are the ones with the higher risk as established in Article 65(2) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Recommendation is based upon conclusions No 50 and 51 Associated findings No 43 and 45

citations.text: In addition, the two CBs visited have risk analysis procedures in place to select operators for additional visits. The CBs have a mixed risk assessment based on quantitative and qualitative factors. However, one CB did not have the volume of production as a risk factor in its procedure, which is not in line with Article 65(4) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 and the INAO Directive.

The two CBs also have procedures for sampling based on risk. The audit team noted that even if most of the operators selected for sampling are based on risk there is also an important number of operators that are randomly selected by the inspectors. Therefore, it 10 is very difficult for the CBs to have an overview to ensure that operators selected for sampling in the end are those posing the highest risk. In one CB, around 30 % and 40% operators classified as low risk were selected for sampling in 2019 and 2020 respectively. This is not in line with Article 65(2) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008.

recommendations.text: Ensure the effectiveness of the controls carried out by the CBs as required by Article 27(9)(b) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. In particular, that the inspection reports provide adequate information (including traceability exercises) on the type of verifications carried out by the inspectors and there are supporting documents attached to them. Recommendation is based upon conclusion No 59 Associated findings No 54, 55 and 56

citations.text: At the beginning of the year, inspectors are given an indicative annual plan of inspections with the operators to inspect and, in the CB's database, inspectors have online access to all necessary information concerning previous controls of the operators, and any pending non-compliances. However, the two CBs could not provide evidence that inspectors have the information the operator must submit to the CB when engaged in organic production in line with Article 63 of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 (a full description of the unit and of the precautionary measures).

The reports issued by the CB inspectors lack detail on how verification takes place, with no objective evidence attached to the reports. The reports consist of a template where inspectors tick off the aspects verified with little or no further description of, or references made, to the documents or records checked or any explanation to provide evidence that the item checked was in line with requirements.

For example, the audit team reviewed a report of an inspection carried out at an operator who has plant and livestock production. The inspector stated that the density of animals was in line with the requirements as were the records of veterinarian medicines and the 12 consumption of feed. The inspector also stated that the purchase and use of inputs and the quantity of feed produced and used was in line with requirements. However, these statements were not supported by evidence as the reports lack details on how the checks had been made. This lack of detail prevents effective supervision, as there is no evidence that can be objectively assessed. Nevertheless, in some instances, for example, when inspectors carry out an exercise to verify the balance between input and output, they attach to the report the sheet with all data collected, including references to the batches, processing sheet, invoices of purchases and sales and all quantities involved.

citations.text: The audit team reviewed several files related to detection of non-authorised substances at the two CBs involved in the audit. Both CBs initiate an investigation when there is a detection of non-authorised product or substance. However, the investigation is actually a form completed by the operators concerned and none of them declared any wrongdoing on their part in any of the cases examined by the audit team. The interpretation of the analytical report by one CB was not in line with the INAO decision. The CB only carries out an investigation and blocks the product when the laboratory analytical report indicated that the substance is detected above 0.02 mg/kg. If the quantity detected is below 0.02mg/kg no actions are taken and the product is considered organic. Furthermore, this CB has established thresholds above 0.02mg/kg for specific substances and applied concentration factors for some processing products like dried products. This is not in line with the organic rules (see paragraph 101 below).

The audit team reviewed several cases of non-compliances identified at operator level by the CBs visited and notified to the CAs. In all cases, the CB imposed sanctions on the operators in line with the catalogue of measures. However, deadlines for the investigation are not defined so it could take up to several months from the identification of the irregularity to resolve the case. The CB only notified the CAs of the irregularities at the end of the process when the CB certification committee has taken a formal decision. This is not in line with Articles 27(5)(d) and 30(2) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 and Article 20 92(4) of Regulation (EC) 889/2008 which require immediate notification of irregularities or the likely occurrence of irregularities.

In one particular case of Ethylene oxide contamination in sesame seeds originating in India, the CB only decided to take measures after a substantial delay even though the level of contamination was far above the maximum residue level. In addition, the CB informed the INAO about the case around 40 days after the detection of the substance. This constitutes significant misconduct on the part of the CB given there is an ongoing alert about Ethylene oxide contamination of sesame seeds and other products from India and there should be immediate exchange of information between the CBs and the CAs in order to enable the CAs to notify the Commission and other Member States through OFIS.

The audit team reviewed four cases related to OFIS notifications. There is a procedure to deal with notifications in OFIS. In the four cases investigated, the INAO and the CBs carried out investigations to identify the source of contamination. The CBs involved carried out inspection visits to the relevant operators and took samples. Other CBs involved were also informed. In two of the cases, the CB concluded that the contamination was accidental without providing robust evidence of that. The INAO provided information in OFIS respecting the established deadlines. citations.text: Representatives of CB2 stated that the ODGs carry out internal checks, which include organoleptic and if necessary, analytical testing of all batches of PDO/PGI wines prior to packaging, whilst official external checks take place only after their packaging by organoleptic testing of all wine batches of circa 5% of operators. The same procedure is followed when different batches of PDO wines are destined for blending.

For CB1 and CB2, the official organoleptic and analytical testing is triggered by declarations of packaging and carried out only on wine that has already been packaged (bottled or bag in box). Either no official testing is carried out by these CBs on wines prior to their marketing in bulk or it is carried out only upon request of the operator, e.g. if he disagrees with non-compliances identified by the ODGs. INAO stated that the official organoleptic and analytical testing of the PDO/PGI wines is carried out after packaging to be as close as possible to the final product sold.

However, as the operators may continue their routine activities during official inspections carried out by the CBs, these batches can potentially already be on the market using the PDO/PGI designation, without having been blocked until the results of the official testing confirm that they comply with the conditions in the specification and possess all the appropriate characteristics of the PDO/PGI designation. This is not in line with point 4(a) of Article 19 of Regulation 2019/34, which requires that a product cannot use the PDO/PGI designation relating to it unless the results of the official organoleptic and analytical testing prove that the product in question complies with the conditions in the product specification and possesses all the appropriate characteristics of the PDO/PGI designation concerned.

citations.text: The DGCCRF controls carried out by the regional BEVS on PDO/PGI wines during the 2020-2021 vinification periods revealed that the average level of non-compliant operators found was circa 30%. Of the 205 samples tested in 2020 and the 295 samples tested in 2021, 61 (or 30% in 2020) and 119 (or 41% in 2021) were found to be non- compliant. The regional BEVS met by the audit team stated that the main reasons for non-compliance are labelling problems, no indication of batch number, excessive sugar and sulphites content, rate of volatile acidity or enrichment higher than the maximum allowed for the PDO/PGI designation. The audit team noted that the frequency of non- compliance found by the CBs earlier in the production chain was much lower (see also paragraph 67 above). Although the regional BEVS results are not fully representative of the entire control system, since the sampling is based on risk analysis and notifications of non-compliances or fraud suspicion, the audit team considered that the high rates of non-compliance identified by the BEVS indicate that there may be shortcomings upstream in the control system. The DGCCRF controls carried out by the regional BEVS at wine distributors (see also paragraph 49) during the 2020-2021 vinification periods revealed high non-compliance levels similar to those referred to in paragraph 70 above. Thus, the average level of non-compliances found was circa 35%. PDO/PGI wines are also sampled by DGCCRF for official organoleptic and analytical testing during the marketing of wines. Of the 83 samples tested in 2020 and the 75 samples tested in 2021, circa 45% were found on average to be non-compliant.

citations.text: The audit team noted that: The planning of the RIBESS+ surveys was in line with requirements of Regulation (EU) 2020/1201; The central identification of the squares to be inspected does not consider the risk factors which are known or identified regionally (e.g., patterns in the spread of the disease, presence and dominance of sensitive plants); In many cases, the entire territory of the square cannot be accessed for inspection (e.g., private properties in urban areas, mountainous terrain, impenetrable natural or semi natural vegetation) which compromises the assessment of the plant health status and sampling; The inspection and sampling were carried out according to DGAL technical instructions. Symptomatic plants were prioritised for sampling and their geo-coordinates were sufficiently recorded for any possible follow-up. 5.5.3 Annual surveys of plants in the infected zones

The positives detected during the risk-based surveys carried out in the vicinity of the DAs in 2021 and 2022 indicate that the current DAs do no not reflect the full extent of Xf presence in the region. Therefore, the continuation of the delimiting surveys is essential.

During the 2021 BZ surveys, 81 samples tested positive, i.e., 5.5% of the totals. The positive rate was particularly high in Zone B and relatively low in Zone C. 80% of the positives were collected from the 400m parts of the BZs, while 70% of the positives originated from urban 20 epidemiological units. Table III summarises the result. In addition to the RIBESS+ findings 16 positives were detected in the BZs during the follow up actions of notifications from the public. Table III. Associated findings Nos 46 to 48, 73 and 74.

citations.text: In relation to the plant removals in the Region Occitanie, the SRAL stated that: The works are generally completed with steps in the following order: delimitation of the IZ, identification and notification of the owner of the positive plant, removal of the positive plant, prioritisation of the IZs for the removal of specified plants according to the identified risk (e.g. nurseries, sensitive agricultural crops in the proximity) and due to practical issues, inventory for specified plants, identification and notification of the owners of plants to be removed, completion of the removals; As much as possible, until they are removed, the positive tested plants are covered with insect-proof nets; For plant removals, a two-step approach was introduced, as any positive tested plant means a proven plant health risk. The identification and notification of the owner and the plant removal can be arranged more quickly than for all the other plants in the IZ subject to felling; The land register in the region contains up-to-date information about the owners; most of them can be readily identified and notified quickly; After the inventory of an IZ for specified plants is completed, the owners (typically 5 to 20) need to be identified and notified, which means a significant administrative burden; The owners have 10 days to submit their observations, after which the company awarded the public contract may intervene for private individuals. For communities and farm owners, a time limit of the order of one month is assigned for the destruction of plants; There were few appeals against the notifications, mainly due to the incorrect addressee in the documents. Thanks to the awareness raising activities of the municipalities and the CAs, the landowners generally accept the necessity of the measures; The plant parts removed by the company awarded the public contract are either incinerated at a safe site close to the IZ or shredded on-site, which is the common practice in natural and semi-natural areas; The large diversity in the accessibility of the sites and environmental concerns hindered the completion of the plant removals. If the number of positives increases, some additional measures are planned (e.g., automatic issuance of the notifications). After the outbreak is completely delimited, the IZs closest to the outer limit of the DAs are intended to be prioritised for plant removals.

The removal of plants was carried out with substantial delays in most of the IZs as the necessary capacities were established recently, which caused favourable conditions for the spread of the disease. The eradication impact of plant removals by shredding is strongly compromised by the massive aftergrowth in the semi natural and natural areas.

Although there were notable improvements since the 2021 audit in the number of IZs with completed eradication activities, the removal of plants including the positive tested and the potentially infected ones was carried out with substantial delays in most of the IZs, facilitating the spread of the disease.

recommendations.text: Consider continuing the delimiting surveys with extended and risk-based inspections and sampling, especially in Department Aude of the Region Occitanie, to obtain a comprehensive picture about the actual spread of Xf, for the appropriate establishment of the infected and buffer zones, in relation to the provisions of Article 4 of Regulation (EU) 2020/1201. The recommendation is based on conclusion No 55 and 56. Associated findings Nos 36 to 40.

citations.text: For the 2021 surveillance of the BZs, the RIBESS+ model was applied with the minimum criteria set by Article 10 of Regulation (EU) 2020/1201 (level of confidence ­ 90%, design (target) prevalence ­ 1% and the first 400m surrounding the IZ considered as higher risk). Seven epidemiological units (urban, semi-natural, fruit trees, extensive agriculture, alfalfa, vines, other) were established for the DAs. The entire territory of the BZs was divided into 100m x 100m squares. Each square was attributed to an epidemiological unit, based on the registered land use data. The two-step approach, in line with the relevant guidance document of the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA), was used for the determination of the sample numbers for the epidemiological units. The size of the host plant population was established 13 based on the agricultural production statistics, but also comprehensive botanical inventories carried out at the end of 2020 in the demarcated areas. Epidemiological estimations were made for the non-agricultural areas.

Although the surveys in the DAs were designed in line with EU requirements, not all relevant risk factors were taken into consideration during their implementation, which may have resulted in not detecting all positives present at the selected survey sites.

The high number of IZs, the proportion of positives in the samples from the BZs and the presence of insect vectors carrying the bacterium indicate that Xf is present in all epidemiological units of the BZs. Consequently, the extent of the infection in the BZs cannot be comprehensively identified with the applied statistical methods, and the established IZs only partially reflect the current spread.

citations.text: The felling of specified plants within a radius of 100 m around the infested plants was not complete. Felling of four taxa (Acer spp., Corylus spp., Citrus spp., Rosa spp.) out of the 20 specified by Article 1(a) of Decision (EU) 2012/138 has been ordered by the CA. The CA explained the reason for selecting these taxa was that only maple and hazelnut plants 8 had been found infested, citrus plants are the main hosts of the pest, and the inspection of roses is very difficult. The CA justifies the reduction of felled taxa with the general heritage status of the district, however this differs from the AVAP Decision No 19.130 which specifies the individual trees and plantations of protected trees (see also finding 26). There was no official assessment and written conclusion by the CA on record that the felling of any specified plant was inappropriate. At the time of the audit, 685 specified plants were located within 100 m from the infested plants and almost 500 of them were on private premises. The list of these plants contains the explanation that the difficulties related to felling are due to the change of owners of properties and the lack of access to private premises. The audit team noted the presence of a Prunus laurocerasus bush right beside the initially infested plant and a short Lagerstroemia plant close to the infested hazelnut.

The incomplete felling of specified plants within a radius of 100 m around infested trees does not comply with Annex II section 3 (1)(a) of Decision (EU) 2012/138, which allows the CA not to perform such felling only in exceptional cases, where the responsible official body concludes that it is inappropriate. 5.5.3 Destruction of plants

The delivery of official controls is adequate in preventing bovine animals unfit for (slaughter for) human consumption from entering the food chain. Nonetheless, the continued performance of AMI and PMI by OA without the presence of the OV in the slaughterhouse is contrary to EU requirements (except for PMI in low throughput slaughterhouses). The same applies to the absence of visual inspection of udders and its lymph nodes and the visual inspection of the gastro-intestinal tract and palpation of the gastric and mesenteric lymph nodes. It is necessary that the official controls verify that operators follow their existing procedures on dirty animals and carcases and that those are fit for purpose especially in the steps preceding PMI.
