audits.title: evaluate the application of measures for the prevention and control of avian influenza

recommendations.text: To design and implement surveillance for HPAI in wild birds and domestic poultry in a way that is appropriate and proportionate to their respective objectives, to act as an early warning system for the possible incursion of the disease in the French territory and to ensure its early detection in poultry. Article 26(2) and (4), and 27 of Regulation (EU) 2016/429. Articles 3(1)(a) and (b)(i), 4(1)(a) and (b)(i), and 10(2) of, and Annex II to Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/689. Based on conclusion 43 and associated findings14, 15 and 17 to 23.

citations.text: Surveillance for wild birds is regularly adapted according to the perceived risk of introduction of HPAI, and is enhanced in all territories where the level of risk increases, and in restricted zones around outbreaks. This resulted in a significantly higher number of samples taken from wild birds once the first outbreaks were confirmed, as that was considered a period with increased risk. However, at the time when the first few index outbreaks were detected in poultry in 2020, for which the authorities determined that introduction of the HPAI virus by wildlife was the most likely cause, the circulation of that HPAI virus had not yet been detected in wild birds in the affected areas.

The inability of the surveillance to detect promptly the virus in wild birds contrasts with the fact that the authorities considered circulation of the virus in them as the main cause for most of the initial outbreaks in the region. The NRL confirmed this a posteriori by virus phylogenetic studies. That sub-optimal effectiveness of the early warning system in wild birds cannot be considered in line with provisions laid down in Articles 26(2) and (4) and 27 of Regulation (EU) 2016/429, on the need to design and apply surveillance in a way that is appropriate and proportionate to the objectives pursued and to the risk factors involved in order to ensure the timely detection of the presence of the targeted disease. In doing that, the competent authority shall as well comply with EU requirements establishing the Union surveillance programme for HPAI, as laid down in Articles 3(1)(a) and (b)(i), 4(1)(b)(i) and 10(2) of, and Annex II to Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/689.

ANSES experts pointed out that passive surveillance alone had been sometimes ineffective to detect some of the outbreaks, due to a longer incubation period with excretion of virus for several days prior to the clinical stage of the disease. In areas with 9 a high density of poultry, this probably led to fast undetected spread of infection and an immediate overflow of cases that surpassed the disease management and control capacity.

Although the authorities have made efforts to increase the sensitivity of surveillance for HPAI in both wild birds and domestic poultry, neither component was effective as an early warning system to better prevent the evolution of both epizootics. The authorities are aware of it and, in particular for domestic poultry, they are working on further strengthening that surveillance.

recommendations.text: To ensure that operators fulfil their responsibilities to immediately notify the competent authority where there is any reason to suspect the presence in the poultry they keep of HPAI. Article 18(1)(a) and (c) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429. Based on conclusion 42 and associated finding 24.

citations.text: The audit team reviewed files related to HPAI suspicions. In most cases, business operators and private veterinarians had notified quickly to the authority abnormal mortality rates and clinical signs. However, the audit team noted on two visited establishments, unnecessary delays, of three and one day, respectively. In second instance, although the establishment immediately notified a suspicion to a private veterinarian, he suspected bacteriological infection and only on following day he took correct decision to notify the suspicion to the authority. This delay occurred in the area with a high density of poultry during ongoing epizootic. That is not in line with requirements laid down in Article 18(1)(a) and (c) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429.

Despite raised and maintained public awareness, the delayed notification of suspect cases by certain operators, as noted on the establishments visited by the audit team, likely contributed to the spread of the disease in areas with a high density of poultry.

recommendations.text: To take appropriate action to improve the effectiveness of the biosecurity measures applied by operators of poultry establishments, by: a) evaluating their suitability to mitigate the prevailing risk factors involved in the areas where they are situated according to the local circumstances and practices, and b) applying official controls to verify their proper application. Thus, they will be able to prevent the introduction and minimise the spread of HPAI, in particular in areas with a high risk of incursion of the disease via migratory wild birds. Articles 10(1)(a)(iii), (b) and (c), (4) and (5), and 11(1)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429. Article 5(1)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Based on conclusions 44, 46, 104 and 141, and associated findings 5 to 11, 33, 103 and 119. 35

citations.text: It was only in September 2021 when the DGAL defined high-risk areas for the likely dissemination of HPAI after introduction of the disease by wild birds (areas at risk of virus spread), taking into account the density of poultry establishments and some other risk factors, mainly related to the presence of domestic waterfowl (see map 5 in Annex 2). In those areas, additional enhanced biosecurity and surveillance measures apply in instances of moderate and high risk of HPAI introduction. The delayed definition of those areas was not in line with Article 3 of Commission implementing Decision (EU) 2018/1136, that was adopted in August 2018 and applicable until 20 April 2021.

Despite plenty of evidence on the inappropriate application of, and insufficient compliance with national requirements on biosecurity in poultry establishments in the areas affected by both HPAI epizootics, the competent authorities failed to correct those shortcomings (already noted in the previous report) and enforce those requirements before they started. This played a major role in facilitating the introduction of the disease and its further spread. The authorities only recently linked 14 the payment of compensation to compliance with biosecurity requirements, acknowledging that before the recent epizootics they had lost an opportunity to incentivise that compliance and to make HPAI preventive measures more effective

The recently published ANSES analysis of the epidemiological information obtained from the recent HPAI epizootics helps the authorities to understand the main risk factors present in the affected areas that contributed to the introduction and spread of the disease. The authorities have now sufficient information to tailor more effective risk-mitigating practices to better prevent the occurrence of HPAI epizootics in the future.

The authorities allowed repopulation of establishments affected by outbreaks of HPAI only after verifying properly that there was no risk of residual infection. This contributed to prevent the resurgence of the disease in those establishments. However, as regards compliance with biosecurity measures to prevent reoccurrence of the disease, the authorities did not verify that lower biosecurity levels, often identified in epidemiological enquires as the most likely source of introduction and spread of the infection, were adequately addressed and strengthened. 5.2 OPERATION OF THE ANIMAL HEALTH EMERGENCY PREPAREDNESS SYSTEM ­ APPLICATION OF THE SPECIFIC CONTINGENCY PLAN 5.2.1 Contingency plan ­ Availability, drawing up and regular updating

The authorities have repeatedly underlined the significant risk that the very high density of poultry represents for the areas affected by the two recent HPAI epizootics, but they have not acted accordingly to reduce it. This, coupled with the sub-optimal application of biosecurity measures to mitigate the prevailing risks of HPAI introduction and spread, raises concerns about their capability to prevent and control new HPAI epizootics.

recommendations.text: To make appropriate arrangements to perform adequate epidemiological enquiries and accelerate the analysis of their results in case of suspicion and confirmation of HPAI so that the competent authorities can take well informed decisions on the application of temporary restrictions before the disease is confirmed, as well as on the establishment and boundaries of, and prioritisation of disease control measures in restricted zones. Articles 55(1)(e) and (f), 56(a)(ii), 57(1) and (2), 62(1) and 64(1)(f) and (2) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429, and Articles 8(3), 9, 21(1)(c) and 23(a) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/687. Based on conclusion 45 and 139, and associated findings29 to 32, 41 and 107.

citations.text: Similar to what happened in previous HPAI epizootics, due to the sudden increase in the number of outbreaks, the departmental authorities were able to carry out complete epidemiological enquires, mostly, only at the beginning of the two recent epizootics. The audit team estimated that in 70-80% of the cases, they did not carry out an in-depth 11 enquiry. In the most affected département in the south-west region (Landes), the departmental authorities conducted complete enquires for the first eight outbreaks. Later on, they carried out enquires on some additional outbreaks, adding up to 20 in total (there were 341 confirmed outbreaks in this area). A similar situation was noted in the Pays de la Loire region (département Vendée), where the departmental authorities performed a limited number of in-depth enquiries only at the beginning of the 2021/22 HPAI epizootic.

During the two recent HPAI epizootics, the low number of epidemiological investigations and their varying quality precluded the authorities from obtaining fundamental information to understand the likely spread of the disease and to identify contact establishments. Hence, they could not take the right decisions to rapidly contain the spread of the disease.

Despite the efforts of the disease control centres established during the epizootics at national and regional level to coordinate the application of the main control measures in the affected areas, they lacked adequate timely expertise, epidemiological analytical capacity and up-to-date knowledge about available resources, to take certain important decisions at critical times. Thus, they could not provide adequate and rapid advice to the departmental authorities in those areas so that they could prioritise their actions to contain and prevent the spread of HPAI effectively.

recommendations.text: To take adequate administrative steps and make the necessary logistical arrangements to ensure sufficient capacity to apply killing of animals for disease control purposes and safe collection and disposal of the carcases of dead and killed poultry and of other contaminated products in establishments where the presence of HPAI is confirmed and where preventive killing needs to be applied as a control measure. Articles 13(1)(a), 43(2)(c)(i) and (iii), and 61(1)(b) and (c) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429 ­ on the responsibilities of the competent authorities to have access to adequate facilities and equipment and to have an effective organisation to be capable to take the necessary disease control measures. Articles 12(1) and 22(2) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/687 ­ on the disease control measures that the competent authority shall apply immediately upon confirmation of an outbreak of HPAI, and on preventive killing. Based on conclusions 47, 77, 89 and 138, and associated findings 37, 60, 61, 62, 85, 86, 87 and 107. 36

citations.text: During both recent epizootics, as the number of new outbreaks sharply increased, the resources available for killing and disposal of carcasses were quickly depleted. Some establishments could only be culled three to four days after confirmation, even up to seven days at some stages in 2022 during the 2021/22 epizootic (see chart 4 in Annex 2). For example, in one of the establishments visited by the audit team, a prolonged keeping of live infected animals potentially shedding the virus, facilitated infection spread and caused some secondary outbreaks. In addition, due to high mortality and delays in killing, when killing started many birds had already died. These shortcomings are not in compliance with EU requirements laid down in Article 61(1)(b) and (c) of Regulation 13 (EU) 2016/429 and Article 12(1) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/687.

The significant delays in the killing and disposal of animals and of other products that could be contaminated with the HPAI virus undermined the effectiveness of other containment measures and likely contributed to the further spread of the disease during the worst of both epizootics. 5.1.2 Diagnosis of HPAI

However, in both epizootics, a large proportion of the flocks subject to pre-emptive culling were already infected, indicating that this culling arrived late. In the most affected département (Landes), during the 2020/21 HPAI epizootic, out of 160 depopulated establishments, 70 were already positive for HPAI.

The exponential increase in the number of outbreaks in the 2021/22 HPAI epizootic, and the subsequent overflow of carcasses to be disposed of, exceeded the available 17 processing capacity and made preventive killing no longer feasible, as noted in the most affected département in the Pays de la Loire region (Vendée).

The shortcomings mentioned in the previous points did not allow the competent authorities to accelerate the killing of susceptible poultry within the restricted zone when the epidemiological situation so required. The actions were not in line with provisions of Article 61(1)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429 and Article 22(2) of Regulation (EU) 2020/687.

The shortage of capacity to depopulate (including for preventive killing) animals, to dispose of their carcases and to quickly visit establishments within restricted zones, undermined the effectiveness of the control measures to contain the disease.

However, due to the rapid increase in the number of affected establishments and poultry in the Pays de la Loire region, the capacity of rendering plants in the area was quickly exceeded. This slowed down the killing process and postponed some of the activities until the accumulated amount of killed animals could be disposed of safely. To cope with the lack of capacity and to prevent further delays in killing of poultry, the authorities opted for burial on site of carcasses, which they did at purposely-made landfills in some of the establishments affected. They also stored ABP temporarily in some affected establishments and other designated sites. Representatives of the authorities met conceded that they should have explored those alternatives in peacetime, to know their limitations beforehand and to negotiate feasible arrangements for their use.

At the time of the audit the departmental contingency plans had not yet been updated to anticipate and deal with such exceptional situations. They had not included details and pre-arrangements on the alternative methods of disposal of carcasses that can be used locally, e.g., a list of sites selected and authorised for storage or burial on site of carcasses.

The shortcomings highlighted in the previous points are not in line with requirements of Articles 13(1)(a), 43(2)(c)(i) and (iii), and 61(1)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429, on the responsibilities of the competent authorities to have access to adequate facilities to take the necessary disease control measures, including disposal of animals that may contribute to the spread of the disease, in the event of an animal health crisis. Conclusions on animal depopulation for the purpose of disease control

Since the previous Commission audit in 2019 the authorities had not taken adequate steps and had not made the necessary logistical arrangements to ensure sufficient capacity to collect and dispose safely of the carcases in establishments where the presence of HPAI was confirmed or as a preventive measure in areas affected by the disease. This caused significant delays in the depopulation of establishments and accumulation of carcases, which significantly undermined the effectiveness of other measures to contain the spread of the disease. 5.1.5 Cleaning and disinfection

In general, the departmental Plans for Sanitary Emergencies contain the necessary instructions and ready-to-use documentation for the authorities to act promptly in the event of a HPAI outbreak, in particular to handle the many administrative tasks involved in those situations. However, as demonstrated in the two recent HPAI epizootics, the authorities found challenging to apply some control measures effectively due to inadequate emergency preparedness. In this context some of the components of those plans were still either missing, not detailed enough or simply not guaranteeing a prompt and effective response (e.g., missing and/or inadequate quality of epidemiological enquires, inadequate establishment of some restricted zones, and ineffective pre- arrangements to kill poultry and dispose of carcasses during large outbreaks). Therefore, those plans cannot be considered fully in line with EU requirements laid down in Article 43(2) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429 on the matters that contingency plans should at least cover.

The authorities did not fulfil the undertakings given in response to the previous audit to update and complete the national contingency plan for HPAI, to adequately reinforce the most important components of the emergency preparedness system for the high-risk areas affected by previous HPAI epizootics, and to assess, and improve if necessary, the level of preparedness of the departmental authorities to cope with an epizootic. Hence, they could not avail of sufficiently qualified and trained human resources with access to all necessary operational tools to succeed with the rapid and effective containment of the disease.

recommendations.text: To ensure that, when the authorities set up a restricted zone in response to confirmation of the presence of HPAI in a poultry establishment: · they set appropriate geographical boundaries without delay for that zone; · they apply within that zone all the necessary measures to contain the disease rapidly, such as visiting all at-risk establishments to verify their health status and application of preventive measures, and performing pre-emptive killing as necessary always ensuring that it does not contribute to spread the disease; and · if they grant derogations allowing placing on the market of poultry and products thereof from establishments situated within that zone, they do it always in compliance with EU requirements to prevent any risk of transmission of the disease. Articles 60(b), 61(1)(b) and 64(1) and (2) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429. Articles 21(1), 22(2), 25(1)(b), (d) and (e), 26(1), 28(1), (2)(a), (5) and (7), 29(2)(a), 30(1)(a)(i), 31(2)(c) and 43(1), (5) and (7) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/687. Based on conclusions 76, 78, 79 and 138, and associated findings 52 to 54, 61 to 63, 72 to 75, 107 and 115.

citations.text: During the 2020/21 HPAI epizootic, the authorities established restricted zones based on the minimum radius required by EU legislation, i.e., a 3 km protection zone and a 10 km surveillance zone, taking also into consideration relevant municipal boundaries (e.g., a zone could be slightly expanded to cover the territory of a municipality until one of those boundaries). However, the authorities did not take into account other important factors, e.g., the disease profile (e.g., whether it was more or less virulent and transmissible depending on the species and production stage affected), the high density of poultry and the network of contacts, to determine if the boundaries and size of the restricted zones were adequate to contain the spread of the disease. In addition, the audit team saw examples where due to the reduced number of epidemiological enquiries, or to have access to only partial information from them, the authorities did not have enough evidence to establish the adequate size or shape of some restricted zones.

Although the authorities established restricted zones rapidly once they confirmed the presence of HPAI in poultry establishments, they defined their size and shape without having enough information on the likely spread of the disease and without considering important criteria for doing that. In addition, they did not take full consideration of all appropriate epidemiological criteria for establishing further restricted zones and when they did establish them they did so late. Therefore, those restricted zones were not effective to stop the spread of the disease before it reached epizootic proportions and expanded far beyond the initially affected areas.

The slow start and the difficulty to apply preventive killing at early stages as planned, limited the contribution of that measure to reduce quickly the poultry population in high-risk areas. In some instances, the authorities eventually implemented preventive killing and in the end it contributed to reduce the number of birds and regain control of 20 the situation in some areas heavily affected by HPAI. However, the delayed testing of flocks moved to slaughterhouses meant that many of them were already infected, thus increasing the risk of spreading the infection during critical periods of the epizootics.

The competent authorities granted thousands of derogations to move animals and products of animal origin from restricted zones. Derogations granted for emergency slaughter contributed significantly to the reduction of susceptible animals in restricted areas. However, non-compliances with movement requirements, such as not taking certain risk-mitigating measures and not respecting certain procedural conditions before granting those derogations, compromised the health status of the areas of destination of those commodities. 5.1.4 Animal depopulation for the purpose of disease control 5.1.4.1 Animal welfare considerations

The authorities did not fulfil the undertakings given in response to the previous audit to update and complete the national contingency plan for HPAI, to adequately reinforce the most important components of the emergency preparedness system for the high-risk areas affected by previous HPAI epizootics, and to assess, and improve if necessary, the level of preparedness of the departmental authorities to cope with an epizootic. Hence, they could not avail of sufficiently qualified and trained human resources with access to all necessary operational tools to succeed with the rapid and effective containment of the disease.

recommendations.text: To take full consideration of all appropriate criteria that should be analysed in the context of a potential HPAI epizootic to decide quickly on the establishment of a further restricted zone to prevent the spread of the disease in areas where the risk of transmission is especially high. Articles 64(2)(b) and 71(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429, and Article 21(1)(c) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/687. Based on conclusion 76, and associated findings 65 and 66. 37

citations.text: As explained in section 5.1.3.1, during the 2021/22 HPAI epizootic, the central authority introduced a new strategy to immediately establish in the event of an outbreak further restricted zones in areas considered of high-risk for the introduction and spread of HPAI. When applied, this measure strengthened the application of control measures. Based on the epidemiological situation and the expected fast spread of infection, the departmental authorities, in coordination with the DGAL, established those further restricted zones even in some areas not defined as high-risk areas.

However, as mentioned in 5.1.3.1, those zones were not always applied as instructed. For example, the fast evolution of the epizootic in the Pays de la Loire region confirmed that the authorities did not properly consider the epidemiological situation when they defined the restricted zones and did not establish a further restricted zone immediately. This is not in accordance with Article 64(2)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429 and Article 21(1)(c) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/687. 5.1.3.4 Derogations to measures applied in protection and surveillance zones

Although the authorities established restricted zones rapidly once they confirmed the presence of HPAI in poultry establishments, they defined their size and shape without having enough information on the likely spread of the disease and without considering important criteria for doing that. In addition, they did not take full consideration of all appropriate epidemiological criteria for establishing further restricted zones and when they did establish them they did so late. Therefore, those restricted zones were not effective to stop the spread of the disease before it reached epizootic proportions and expanded far beyond the initially affected areas.

recommendations.text: To register all establishments keeping poultry and ensure that the authorities have access to the necessary updated information on them, so that they can plan and apply disease control measures quickly in the restricted zone established in response to a HPAI outbreak. Articles 84, 93(a) and 101(1)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429; Article 18 of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/2035. Regulation (EU) 2016/429 (Article 64(1) and (2)); Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/687 (Chapters I and II of Part II) ­ requiring the availability of accurate and updated inventories of poultry establishments in the event of suspicion and confirmation of HPAI to establish restricted zones, apply and regularly adapt those measures, and grant derogations therefrom. Based on conclusion 140, and associated findings 114 and 115.

citations.text: The authorities do not consider the databases fully updated. Notification of data to the BD Avicole database became obligatory only in 2021. The data kept in there, in particular for independent farmers and those collected from censuses in recent epizootics, show that not all commercial establishments are registered yet and, as confirmed by the 26 audit team in the départements visited, data in the database was not fully updated. For example, up to 5% of establishments registered in the database had ceased their operation, while that information had not been updated in the database. That complicates planning of official activities such as visits to establishments located in restricted zones as well as regular inspections. This is not in line with the provisions laid down in Articles 84, 93(a) and 101(1)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429, and in Article 18 of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/2035, on the respective obligations of operators to register establishments and of competent authorities to keep certain information on them in their registers.

The shortcomings above had an impact on the application of control measures laid down in Regulation (EU) 2016/429 (Article 64(1) and (2)) and Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/687 (Chapters I and II of Part II) requiring the availability of accurate and updated inventories of poultry establishments in the event of suspicion and confirmation of HPAI to establish restricted zones, apply and regularly adapt those measures, and grant derogations therefrom.

The presence of unregistered commercial establishments in restricted zones, alongside the lack of up-to-date information on the poultry population in the official databases used by the authorities to handle the HPAI outbreaks, increased the volume of control activities necessary to determine the census of poultry present in those zones at the expense of delaying other tasks that were more important to prevent the spread of the disease.

recommendations.text: To update the national and departmental contingency plans for HPAI taking into account: a) the lessons learnt from the analysis of the strengths and weaknesses identified with regard to the operation of the animal health emergency preparedness system during the 2020/21 and 2021/22 HPAI epizootics, and b) the results of the self-assessments to be carried out by the relevant départements of their specific level of preparedness to contain the disease. Article 43(1) and (2) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429; Article 4 of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/687. Based on conclusions 89 and 138, and associated findings 87, 107, 109 and 110.

citations.text: The shortcomings highlighted in the previous points are not in line with requirements of Articles 13(1)(a), 43(2)(c)(i) and (iii), and 61(1)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429, on the responsibilities of the competent authorities to have access to adequate facilities to take the necessary disease control measures, including disposal of animals that may contribute to the spread of the disease, in the event of an animal health crisis. Conclusions on animal depopulation for the purpose of disease control

Since the previous Commission audit in 2019 the authorities had not taken adequate steps and had not made the necessary logistical arrangements to ensure sufficient capacity to collect and dispose safely of the carcases in establishments where the presence of HPAI was confirmed or as a preventive measure in areas affected by the disease. This caused significant delays in the depopulation of establishments and accumulation of carcases, which significantly undermined the effectiveness of other measures to contain the spread of the disease. 5.1.5 Cleaning and disinfection

In general, the departmental Plans for Sanitary Emergencies contain the necessary instructions and ready-to-use documentation for the authorities to act promptly in the event of a HPAI outbreak, in particular to handle the many administrative tasks involved in those situations. However, as demonstrated in the two recent HPAI epizootics, the authorities found challenging to apply some control measures effectively due to inadequate emergency preparedness. In this context some of the components of those plans were still either missing, not detailed enough or simply not guaranteeing a prompt and effective response (e.g., missing and/or inadequate quality of epidemiological enquires, inadequate establishment of some restricted zones, and ineffective pre- arrangements to kill poultry and dispose of carcasses during large outbreaks). Therefore, those plans cannot be considered fully in line with EU requirements laid down in Article 43(2) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429 on the matters that contingency plans should at least cover.

However, it took the DGAL several years until this initiative resulted in an instruction and a published self-assessment tool, as they were available only since February 2021. The benchmarks included in the instruction should help the departmental authorities to better assess their preparedness for animal health emergencies, in particular regarding availability of material and human resources, and maintenance of the necessary technical and administrative skills. However, according to representatives of the authorities met, the presence of the HPAI epizootics in recent years precluded any analysis of the progress achieved with those self-assessment tools.

The DGAL presented to the audit team the main pillars of the new strategy they intend to follow in 2022, an action plan to tackle the shortcomings identified during the recent HPAI epizootics. They added that it will be the basis for updating their instructions, including the contingency plan to combat the disease.

The authorities did not fulfil the undertakings given in response to the previous audit to update and complete the national contingency plan for HPAI, to adequately reinforce the most important components of the emergency preparedness system for the high-risk areas affected by previous HPAI epizootics, and to assess, and improve if necessary, the level of preparedness of the departmental authorities to cope with an epizootic. Hence, they could not avail of sufficiently qualified and trained human resources with access to all necessary operational tools to succeed with the rapid and effective containment of the disease.

recommendations.text: To make adequate arrangements to ensure that the competent authorities responsible for controlling outbreaks of HPAI have access to all necessary resources, in particular to sufficient qualified personnel and to adequate information management tools, so that they can take the right decisions at critical times during animal health crises and apply appropriate control measures without delay. Articles 13(1)(a) and 43(2)(a), (c)(iv) and (d) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429 ­ on responsibilities of the competent authorities to have resources, to apply disease control measures effectively, and on the application of the contingency plan for HPAI. Based on conclusions 138 and 139, and associated findings 124 and 129. 38

citations.text: The authorities used information management tools that included planning and recording of the activities performed on a daily basis by the departmental disease control centres. They shared data retrieved from these centres which with experts of the ANSES and of some veterinary schools. However, during the 2020/21 HPAI epizootic they experienced difficulties to obtain and share some of the data with those experts. During the 2021/22 HPAI epizootic, although the sharing of data with experts improved, the fact that many data were fragmented in several databases and formats made still difficult their analysis, for those experts to contribute rapidly and effectively to the decision-making process to manage the crisis situations. The DGAL is aware of this and has started to make improvements in that respect.

However, despite the improvements noted in this regard since the previous audit, the human resources available were not sufficient to perform timely all the control measures necessary to contain the disease rapidly (e.g., depopulation of affected establishments and pre-emptive killing, official visits to poultry establishments in the restricted zones, completion of epidemiological enquiries). That was not in line with requirements laid down in Articles 13(1)(a) and 43(2)(c)(iv) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429 on responsibilities of the competent authorities to have qualified personnel and an effective organisation to apply disease control measures effectively, and on application of the 29 contingency plan for HPAI. 5.2.5 Availability of equipment and materials

citations.text: The DGAL issued a technical instruction containing detailed procedures regarding the registration of professional operators, their authorisation to issue plant passports, the visual examination of plants, the issuance of plant passports and the official controls on professional operators as required by Article 12(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The instruction contains guidance on how to practically implement the requirements, and examples of major and minor non-compliances. The instruction is directly used by the SRALs and the CTIFL. The FAM has developed its own procedures based on the DGAL technical instruction. The SEMAE has developed its own instructions based on international control and inspection standards (ISO 17065 and ISO 17020) and on Regulations (EU) 2017/625 and (EU) 2016/2031. Inspectors of each CA use checklists to verify if professional operators comply with the requirements listed in Article 92(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. However, these procedures contain some differences from the applicable EU requirements. 4 · The CAs sometimes grant provisional authorisation to issue plant passports as permitted under the DGAL technical instruction. In this case, they only verify whether operators possess the necessary knowledge concerning the signs, symptoms, and the means to prevent the spread of regulated pests, and to carry out the examinations as required by Article 89(1)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 after granting authorisation to issue plant passports (see also finding 14). · In line with the DGAL technical instruction, inspectors may accept as demonstration of knowledge required by EU law when the operator knows the websites to consult regarding regulated pests or has printed documents about some of these pests. However, this does not mean that the operator possesses the necessary knowledge and is able to carry out examinations, as required by Article 89(1)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. · Hand-written entries on plant passports are permitted in France. These plant passports do not comply with Article 83(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 which requires plant passports to be clearly legible, and the information on them to be unchangeable and durable (see also finding 30).

The roles and responsibilities of the different CAs are clearly regulated, with detailed procedures to assist inspectors providing a good basis for the effective implementation of EU legislation. However, minor differences in the application of some plant passport requirements and the insufficient training for inspectors mean that the CAs do not ensure that the plant passport system is implemented in a consistent manner and fully in line with EU requirements.

However, in a small number of cases, and in line with the technical instruction issued by the DGAL (see also finding 4), the SRALs grant provisional authorisation. In these cases, there is no on-site official control and documents regarding the traceability system and the format of plant passports intended to be issued are verified remotely. Operators which receive provisional authorisation are allowed to issue plant passports until the first on-site official control, after which the final authorisation can be granted. In these cases, the SRALs do not verify whether operators possess the necessary knowledge concerning the signs, symptoms, and the means to prevent the spread of regulated pests, and to carry out the examinations before granting authorisation to issue plant passports as required by Article 89(1)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. The CAs could not quantify the number of provisional authorisations granted or their typical duration. 5.3.2 Official supervision of professional operators and verification of their actions

During the official controls observed by the audit team, the inspectors used checklists containing all relevant elements of the technical instruction issued by the DGAL to verify whether authorised operators comply with Article 92(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. These controls were broadly effective. However, the audit team noted the following: · All inspectors verified the content, format and attachment of issued and received plant passports. This was done correctly in all cases and resulted in inspectors finding non-compliant plant passports. Non-compliant plant passports were issued by two visited authorised operators and were present in the garden centre (see also finding 29). · Inspectors verified the traceability of several purchased and sold lots. The lots were chosen based on a risk analysis, and inspectors considered host plants of priority pests to be the highest risk. These controls were done correctly in all cases except in the case of an imported consignment where the inspector did not know what documents are required to accompany such consignments (see also finding 3). · Inspectors correctly verified the records of examinations of plants carried out by authorised operators or contracted professional service providers in all cases. · Inspectors verified whether authorised operators possess the necessary knowledge to carry out the examination required by EU legislation. · All inspectors except one correctly verified if authorised operators identify and monitor the points of their production process and the points concerning the movement of plants, plant products and other objects, which are critical as regards compliance with the EU requirements and if they keep records concerning the identification and monitoring of those points for at least three years, as required by Article 90(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. The FAM inspector observed by the audit team did not verify whether authorised operators comply with these requirements. The particular operator did not keep such records. · All inspectors observed by the audit team verified the corrective actions taken to address non-compliances recorded during the previous official control. When inspectors find any non-compliance with EU requirements, operators are requested to provide a written plan containing actions they would take to correct such non-compliances. When the CA considers that there are only minor non- 8 compliances, the corrective actions might be verified only during the following official control. However, in one case from 2023, the SRAL had found plants for planting infected by fig mosaic virus in a nursery visited by the audit team. The operator had not provided a written action plan to the CA and the CA had not verified whether any corrective actions had been taken, with the result that at the time of the audit some of the infected plants had been sold. Contrary to the first paragraph of Article 92(2) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031, the CA failed to ensure that plants infected by fig mosaic virus, and therefore non-compliant with provisions concerning that Union regulated non-quarantine pest, were not moved within the EU. Conclusions on authorisation and supervision of professional operators for issuing plant passports

Certain weaknesses in the authorisation procedure and the annual official controls weaken the level of assurance that authorised operators fully meet the requirements for issuing plant passports. 5.4 EXAMINATIONS FOR THE ISSUANCE OF PLANT PASSPORTS Legal requirements Articles 85 to 87 of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 Articles 2 to 6, 8(2), 9, 10, 13, 14 and 17 of Regulation (EU) 2019/2072 Findings 5.4.1 Examinations by authorised operators

Authorised operators are required to keep all plant passport related records for at least three years. The plant passports provided to the audit team were generally compliant with EU requirements. However, the following examples did not comply with the requirements of Article 83(2) and (4) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 since they did not contain some required elements or contained additional information. · Plant passports contained references to traceability information outside of the plant passport, but on the same substrate, instead of having the traceability code on the plant passport itself. · Plant passports with a hole on the label which removed part of the botanical name. · After the country of origin code, plant passports containing the registry number of the operator that produced the plants as additional data. · A PZ plant passport was notified by another MS where the scientific name or code of the pest and the code of the country in front of the operator's registry number were missing. Additional data, other than the variety, were present after the botanical name of the plant species (see also section 4.2).

Furthermore, the CAs tolerate some forms of non-compliant plant passports: · The use of pre-printed plant passports with hand-written amendments is tolerated by the SRALs. In general, such plant passports often do not comply with Article 83(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 based on which the plant passports must be clearly legible, and the information on them must be unchangeable and durable. However, the CAs verify if plant passports available at the time of the official control and containing hand-written entries are legible, unchangeable and visible. · Contrary to the Annex of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2017/2313 ­ which provides that the required flag of the Union may be printed in colour (yellow stars on blue background), or in black and white, either with white stars on a black background, or vice versa ­ the colour of the substrate is tolerated as a background to the EU flag. 5.5.3 Plant passports combined with certification labels

Plant passports are attached to the trade units, replaced or invalidated by the authorised operators. However, the SRALs accept that the plant passport is only an accompanying document and is not attached to the trade units in the case of logs and plants moved in bulk, which is not in line with Article 88 of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. 5.5.5 Application of the exemptions provided for in EU law

Authorised operators issue plant passports under official supervision generally in line with provisions of the EU regulations. However, the use of some non-compliant plant passports compromises the reliability of the system developed for issuing plant passports in France. 5.6 OFFICIAL CONTROLS ON MOVEMENT OF PLANTS AND PLANT PRODUCTS WITH PLANT PASSPORTS Legal requirements Articles 69, 79 to 83, 88 and 93 to 95 of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 Articles 2 to 6, 8(2), 9, 10, 13, 14 and 17 of Regulation (EU) 2019/2072 Articles 1 to 4 of Regulation (EU) 2019/66 Regulation (EU) 2020/1770 in its entirety Findings 5.6.1 Official controls on traceability

National legislation provides a legal basis for enforcement actions in case of non- compliances with plant health requirements. When such non-compliances are detected, operators are ordered to take corrective actions. If the necessary corrective actions are not taken, the CA issues a formal notice containing the possibility of withdrawal or suspension of the authorisation for issuing plant passports. When appropriate actions are still not taken, the CA withdraws or suspends the authorisation to issue plant passports and may apply financial penalties. In 2022 and 2023, about 160 professional operators had their authorisation to issue plant passports suspended until the operator took appropriate corrective actions. However, the audit team noted that the implementation of the corrective actions is not consistently verified (see also finding 16). 14 Conclusions on enforcement actions

In most but not all cases, sanctions applied by the CAs are effective, proportionate and dissuasive thereby helping to ensure that professional operators comply with their legal obligations. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS The roles and responsibilities of the competent authorities are clearly defined. The central coordination, robust procedures and good co-operation between authorities provide a good basis for the effective implementation of the EU regulations for plant passports. The system of controls based around annual controls of authorised operators using detailed procedures and checklists is broadly effective. However, inspectors do not consistently verify that professional operators comply with all legal requirements. Consequently, authorised operators do not comply with all their legal obligations which weakens the reliability of plant passports issued in France. The non-compliant sampling procedure regarding high-risk host plants of Xylella fastidiosa which have never been grown in a demarcated area reduces the level of assurance that those plants are free from this Union quarantine pest. In general, the identified shortcomings do not significantly increase the plant health risk of plants moved with plant passports within the EU. 7 CLOSING MEETING A closing meeting was held on 22 April 2024 in the form of a videoconference between the audit team and representatives of the NPPO, during which the main findings and preliminary conclusions of the audit team were presented. recommendations.text: The competent authority should ensure that primary production fishing vessels engaged in commercial fishing activities are inspected according to the DGAL rules in place or to develop a viable system for such controls in line with Article 10 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Recommendation based on conclusion 38. Associated finding: 34.

citations.text: According to DGAL, from the 6 736 vessels of the French fishing fleet (mainland and overseas departments) 4 052 were in mainland France. The staff interviewed stated that fishing vessels are considered low risk and, due to the current pressure on staff numbers 8 and workload, the minimum frequencies are not met. The audit team saw several control reports for primary vessels with corrective measures applied. The inspection reports covered all relevant hygiene points. Facilities handling fishery products

The official control system in place covers the production chain of fishery products and is, in general, implemented as planned. However, some defined control procedures were not followed, like the inspection frequencies for primary production vessels, or were not effective in providing operators' compliance with EU rules regarding correct temperature limits in cold stores and the presence of temperature recording devices and the incorrect use of predictive tools in shelf-life studies. 5.3.2 Official controls of fishery products Legal requirements Council Regulation (EC) No 2406/96. recommendations.text: To ensure that the official controls verify that cold stores ensure that fishery products have a temperature not more than minus 18 °C and are equipped with a temperature-recording device in line with the requirements in point C(2), of part I, Chapter I, Section VIII of Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 853/2004 Recommendation based on conclusion 38. Associated findings: 36 (b),(c).

citations.text: Official staff followed adequately the procedures and appropriate follow-up, and enforcement measures were taken, where necessary. In general, the establishments were in good condition regarding structure and hygiene. During the visits, the following relevant deficiencies were noted by the audit team: a. In two establishments processing fresh fish, good hygiene practices were not respected. This included, among others, unsuitable routing of products, possible cross contamination of ice and the presence of wooden pallets when processing fish. b. One operator applied brine freezing to pelagic fish, packed it and moved it to the adjacent cold store. The temperature of the brine was minus 17.7 °C and the packaged fish was minus 17.5 °C. The HACCP system required a brine temperature of minus 20°C. The temperature limit for the cold store was set at minus 15 °C instead of minus 18 °C as written in the HACCP system. The critical control points were not defined by a decision tree. The HACCP plan had not been updated since 2019. Another establishment had applied the same temperature limit of minus 15 °C in its cold store. c. At one establishment, there was no continuous temperature recording device present. d. At several establishments a processing step called "stiffening" was applied. Smoked fish is stored between 0 °C and minus 9 °C before slicing. The EU legal requirement for this processing step is that it lasts at most, 96 hours. One operator stated that products exceeding this duration would be frozen to minus 18 °C and be labelled and sold as frozen product. This opinion was shared by the local official inspector. The CCA stated, that this is not in line with the national rules, which requires the product to be classified as unfit for human consumption. e. Regarding the prediction of shelf life of ready to eat products, an operator used a temperature/duration combination which was not in line with the European Reference Laboratory's Technical Guidance Document on challenge tests and durability studies for assessing shelf-life if ready-to-eat foods related in Listeria monocytogenes (10). (10) Available at: https://food.ec.europa.eu/system/files/2021-07/biosafety_fh_mc_tech-guide-doc_listeria-in-rte- foods_en_0.pdf. 9 f. At one establishment producing smoked fishery products, these were packed and palletised and put in the cold store for freezing. It took up to 72 hours for the product to reach minus 18 °C.

recommendations.text: To implement controls to verify compliance with relevant biosecurity measures on all poultry establishments regularly, on a risk basis and with appropriate frequency, taking account of the criteria in Article 9.1 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 Article 9.1 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Recommendation based on main conclusion No. 61 and associated findings No. 11- 17.

citations.text: A) Official controls: 7 The current "Livestock inspection campaign" runs from 2024 to 2027 and provides for annual inspections to be carried out on registered poultry and captive bird establishments at the following rates by all DDPPs as follows: - One inspection every 4 years (25% annual target) for "authorised establishments", i.e. establishments with a "health charter/trade approval/official hygiene and health control for palmipeds". - 6% annual target for inspections to be carried out on poultry or captive bird rearing sites which are neither members of the Health Charter nor approved for trade in poultry or hatching eggs or registered for official hygiene and health control. This 6% target does not vary between high-risk Departments and low-risk ones (see map showing zones in finding 75).

There is a comprehensive national technical instruction with a template inspection report form for conducting these biosecurity inspections. (i.e. DGAL/SDSBEA/2024-74). Annex 2 of the national instruction specifies the annual number of inspections to be carried out by each Department from 2024 to 2027. The planned number of annual inspections for each Department is provided by the central authority and the DDPPs decide which establishments to inspect, using the risk criteria in the national instruction, e.g. establishments located in wetlands or areas with high stocking density, unsatisfactory results of previous inspections and establishments not inspected in previous years.

In the event of major biosecurity non-compliance, the services ask the farmers by formal notice to request the support of their technical or veterinary health management in order to establish an action plan and a precise timetable for compliance. There is a system in place to follow-up identified non-compliances with re-inspections and sanctions when deemed appropriate. Results for these inspections over recent years demonstrate a continuously improving situation, e.g. 22% of inspections scored C (insufficient) or D (very insufficient) in 2024 compared to 32% for the same categories in the combined period 2022 and 2023. The audit team reviewed reports of such inspections which appear appropriate.

The competent authority provided the following data related to 2024: Table 3 Number and percentage of establishments planned to be inspected and inspected in 2024 No of registered No of No of % of planned 8 poultry and establishments establishments inspections captive bird planned to be actually implemented establishments inspected inspected during 2024 during 2024 National 35 444 2 517 (7.1%) 2 200 (6.2%) 87% Pays de la 4 908 478 (9.7%) 376 (7.6%) 79% Loire 5 305 397 (7.5%) 227 (4.3%) 57% Nouvelle- Aquitaine The above data is a combination of the establishments with an annual target inspection rate of 25% and 6%. Data provided at national level showed that: - Of the 2 517 establishments planned to be inspected during 2024: o 1 018 related to authorised establishments o 1 499 related to non-authorised establishments. - Of the 2 200 establishments inspected during 2024: o 1 070 related to authorised establishments (= 105% of planned target) o 1 130 related to non-authorised establishments (= 75% of planned target) - 1 018 planned inspections of authorised establishments in 2024 = about 4,072 authorised establishments in total (based on an inspection rate of 25% per annum - This would mean that there were about 17 178 non "authorised establishments" poultry establishments in 2024 (21 250 ­ 4 072 based on data in finding No 2) - There are 14 194 registered establishments keeping captive birds - 14 194 + 17 178 = 31 372 total number of establishments included in the 6% annual target inspection rate. o 1 499 planned inspections for 31 372 = 4.7% o 1 130 completed inspections for 31 372 = 3.6%

The Regional Directorate for Pays de la Loire provided a breakdown of the official controls of poultry establishments during 2024. Based on the numbers provided and after excluding the authorised establishments with a 25% target for annual inspections, only 3.4% of non-authorised establishments may have had an official control related to biosecurity during 2024. Of the overall inspections, 9.5% scored C or D in 2024. (further detail provided in Appendix I below).

The current approach of planning official controls to check compliance with biosecurity measures does not comply with Article 9.1 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 which requires that "Competent authorities shall perform official controls on all operators regularly, on a risk basis and with appropriate frequency, taking account of: (a) identified risks associated with: (i) animals ...; (iii) the location of the activities ...;

B) Inspections by private sector: 9 The Order of 29 September 2021 requires an annual evaluation of the biosecurity of all commercial poultry establishments by a third-party body. If the inspection is satisfactory, then the inspection can be carried out every second year. Many poultry establishments also receive an annual on-site "Animal Health Check" inspection by their veterinary practice which amongst other things allows a veterinarian to prescribe medication without visiting the establishment between inspections. The inspection includes biosecurity measures, but the competent authority could not say what percentage of poultry establishment these inspections are carried out on. On the establishments visited during the audit, the audit team saw inspection reports related to both these types of inspections and confirmed that they included biosecurity related questions. There is no national template for the inspection reports and the competent authority is not informed on the outcome of the inspections, but the reports must be available for viewing during official controls. Therefore, although both these inspections help improve the overall biosecurity standards on poultry establishments, the competent authority does not monitor their results or the extent to which they are implemented1.

recommendations.text: To ensure that enhanced passive surveillance is implemented in the vaccinated establishments and that this is verified. Article 10 and point 2.1 of Part 5 of Annex XIII of Regulation 2023/361 and Article 5.1 of Regulation 2017/625. Recommendation based on main conclusion No. 63 and associated findings No. 36- 39.

citations.text: Enhanced passive surveillance: when preparing the instruction in section 5.1 of the post- vaccination surveillance protocol (DGAL/SDSBEA/2024-546), the competent authority followed the approach set out by the EU Reference Laboratory. This instruction requires farmers to collect tracheal or oropharyngeal swabs from up to five dead vaccinated birds each week. If fewer than five dead birds are found, they must collect additional samples 3 Section 5.2 of DGAL/SDSBEA/2024-546 allows "a period of ± 10 days is allowed compared to the regulatory frequency of 30 days.") 13 from sick birds to reach five. If there are no sick birds either, they must use apparently healthy birds to complete the sample set. The audit team observed: · DGAL/SDSBEA/2024-546 defines the "representative sample" mentioned in Annex XIII, point 2.2 of Regulation 2023/361 as five samples per vaccinated establishment, regardless of flock size. · In November 2024, following advice from the HPAI vaccination steering committee (Copil), the central authority informed stakeholders that they could collect samples from sick or healthy birds when five dead birds were not available. This was initially presented as a recommendation. It became a formal requirement when the instruction was amended on 26 March 2025. · Collected samples undergo virological testing.

On the three vaccinated establishments visited, the audit team discussed the implementation of enhanced passive surveillance. In all three, farmers took samples up to a maximum of three days per week and regularly from morbid or live birds when there were not five dead birds: · Establishment 1 (around 7 000 ducks on site). The keeper stated he collected samples over three days every week (Monday to Wednesday). The keeper often sampled morbid or live ducks when fewer than five dead birds were available over the three days and occasionally sent less than five samples. · Establishment 2 (around 21 000 broiler ducks on site) and 3 (around 9 000 ducks raised for foie gras). The respective keepers stated they collected samples once a week and took samples from morbid or live ducks when there were less than five dead birds on the day of collection.

During their 30-day visits to collect active surveillance samples, the supervising veterinarian must check that farmers implement enhanced passive surveillance. The active surveillance sample submission form includes the question "is the farmer implementing enhanced passive surveillance - Yes / No". In the visited establishments, the audit team was informed by the supervising veterinarians that if the farmer answers "yes", that they do not verify it further. Supervising veterinarians have access to laboratory results and can see how many and how often farmers submit samples but cannot see if the samples came from dead, morbid or healthy live birds.

None of the three establishments visited were implementing enhanced passive surveillance in accordance with the EU requirements in point 2.1 of Part 5 of Annex XIII of Regulation 2023/361 in that: - they are collecting samples from morbid and live ducks which is not in accordance with Regulation 2023/361 which only refers to "testing of a representative sample of dead birds" - the national instruction requests that samples are collected preferentially from dead then morbid and then healthy live until 5 samples are taken during the week / seven days. No farmer collected samples from dead birds over the seven days. The procedures in place to verify the correct implementation of enhanced passive surveillance are not effective and therefore do not comply with the requirements of Article 5.1 of Regulation 2017/625. 14

recommendations.text: To ensure that official activities are only performed by the competent authority or by bodies or natural persons to whom these tasks have been formally delegated in writing, and that the competent authority audits or inspections such bodies or persons. Articles 28, 30 to 33 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Recommendation based on main conclusion No. 63 and associated findings No. 40 and 41. 30

citations.text: "Enhanced passive surveillance" in vaccinated establishments is an "animal health requirement" under point 2.1 of Part 5 of Annex XIII of Regulation 2023/361 and is therefore an "official activity', as defined in Art 2.2 of Regulation 2017/625. Competent authorities can delegate official activities to "natural persons" based on Article 31 of the OCR. This delegation is subject to compliance with the delegated conditions laid down in Article 30, (applied mutatis mutandis), being fulfilled. Within the HPAI vaccination campaign in France, farmers perform enhanced passive surveillance. They receive training for this from the supervising veterinarians, but the competent authority has not formalised a delegation of this official activity in line with the requirements of Articles 30 and 31. This constitutes a non-compliance with Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

The competent authority disagreed with the audit team and indicated that it does not consider enhanced passive surveillance to be an official activity. It stated that, under Article 10 of Regulation 2016/429, post-vaccination passive surveillance falls under the farmer's responsibility.

audits.title: to evaluate animal welfare controls during transport by livestock vessel to non-EU countries

recommendations.text: The competent authority should complete documented procedures so that they provide sufficient information and detailed instructions for staff, as required by Article 12(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, to carry out official controls at the port, including inspections carried out according to Articles 19 and 20 of Regulation (EC) 1/2005. Recommendation based on conclusion 2 Associated findings: 5 and 17

citations.text: French authorities carry out the controls at port effectively. French authorities have five staff trained on welfare issues who have also gathered some technical knowledge to ensure that vessels are constructed and equipped to transport animals without causing injury or undue suffering. There are still weaknesses as regards updating and completing the documentation of procedures and methodologies.

recommendations.text: The competent authority should take measures to ensure that inspections: · for the purpose of granting a certificate of approval or renewals of such approvals, and · on the loading of livestock vessels; are performed by a team of inspectors including at least an official veterinarian and a maritime expert, as required by Article 9 of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2023/372 and Article 5 of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/842. Recommendation based on conclusion 3. Associated findings: 9, 10, 14 and 47.

citations.text: The system is non-compliant as regards the composition of the team of inspectors and the required on-board official controls during the first voyage following approval. The team of inspectors carrying out approval and pre-loading inspections does not systematically include the required official veterinarian and maritime expert. It only includes official veterinary auxiliaries who have acquired knowledge from maritime safety experts. In addition, there is no provision for an official veterinarian to carry out official controls on board the vessel during the first voyage.

citations.section: FINDINGS ON THE FRAMEWORK FOR OFFICIAL CONTROLS
citations.text: Despite having approved ten vessels since 1 January 2024, French authorities have not implemented the requirement for an official veterinarian to carry out on-board official controls during the first voyage with animals after the approval (see finding 21). Moreover, the team of inspectors does not include a maritime expert, nor an official veterinarian (see finding 14). These two are contrary to Articles 9 and 10(1) of Regulation (EU) 2023/372.

citations.section: FINDINGS ON THE FRAMEWORK FOR OFFICIAL CONTROLS
citations.text: DGAL district has approved ten livestock vessels since Regulation (EU) 2023/372 entered into force (6). The team of inspectors for these approval inspections included veterinary auxiliaries but not systematically a maritime expert nor an official veterinarian, contrary to Article 9 of Regulation (EU) 2023/372. The approval itself is signed by the official veterinarian heading the team but participation of the official veterinarian in actual inspections is sporadic due to their wider responsibilities (which also include the controls over fisheries, bivalves, export certifications and as border control post).

recommendations.text: The competent authority should take measures to carry out official controls by an official veterinarian on board a livestock vessel during the entire first voyage following the approval of the livestock vessel and prior to the renewal of such approval, as required by Article 10(1) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2023/372. Recommendation based on conclusion 37. Associated finding 36.

citations.text: The audit team noted, in four establishments out of 13 visited, discrepancies in the approval procedures: 8 · maximal production capacities were annotated in previous approvals, but not in the most recent ones. Such capacities were indicated by the FBO itself and accepted by the CA, without a real verification of their feasibility. In two establishments visited, the capacities indicated in the PMS were not realistic in relation to the working area, equipment and staff available; · in one establishment, the conditional approval for additional buildings had been granted for premises still under construction and without the necessary equipment; · the activity of re-packing of meat products manufactured by another FBO was not included in the approval; · enlargement of buildings and equipment (consisting in adding a new drying room and another chiller was completed and put in operation without informing the CA. This was identified by the CA at the time of the next planned inspection, without imposing any sanction to the FBO. Conclusions on approval of establishments

Although the approval procedures are in line with the requirements of Article 148 of the Regulation (EU) 2017/625, they are not always consistently applied, thus resulting in some establishments operating without fulfilling all necessary conditions. 5.4 Organisation and implementation of official controls Legal requirements Articles 9, 10(1), 12, 13, 14 18(1), 34 and Chapter I of Title VII of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. recommendations.text: To ensure, as required by Article 5(1)(e) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, that the local competent authorities have, or have access to, a sufficient number of suitably qualified and experienced staff so that official controls and other official activities can be performed efficiently and effectively. Recommendation based on conclusion 31. Associated findings 24 and 25.

citations.text: In one of eight CAs visited, staff shortage was critical, with an impact on the number of inspections carried out. In this particular case the inspectors had also been poorly trained (see point 29), with an impact on the quality of official controls.

DGAL does not have adequate tools to identify similar issues in the other 94 CAs in Metropolitan France. The statistics provided by the CCA show that nationwide 85% of the planned inspections have been effectively carried out. Some activities like export certification, official activities in slaughterhouses, alerts' follow-up, approval activities and official sampling are prioritised, explaining the above completion rate. 5.2.2 Supervision of CA staff and audits

The CCA has no adequate tools to identify staff shortages and underperformance of official controls at département (CA) level. This results in a lack of overview that could impact on the overall performance of official controls as the CCA is not able to implement the appropriate corrective measures.

recommendations.text: To ensure that the competent authority takes the required enforcement action when it identifies non-compliances, as required by Article 138.1 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Recommendation based on conclusion 82. Associated finding 70.

citations.text: At establishment level, FBOs with global assessments B are issued a written warning for which they are not obliged to present an action plan. Only the global assessments C or D for establishments trigger enforcement measures: · FBOs with global assessment C are issued with a severe warning ("mise en demeure") with specific deadlines for implementation of corrective action; · FBOs with a global assessment D may be at risk of suspension of one or more activities. 14 In cases where one or more items in a report are categorized as B (minor non-compliance) or C (medium non-compliance), the entire report can still be globally categorised by the inspector as A. This A categorisation signifies that no immediate follow-up is necessary, which may allow deviations to persist until the next scheduled inspection, which can be up to three years later. This practice is not in line with the requirements outlined in Article 138 of Regulation 2017/625, as it may allow for prolonged non-compliance by FBOs. This issue was identified in audit report 2018-6450, which included a specific recommendation (recommendation 6, see section 5.5) to address this discrepancy.
